Introduction –  
Goa’s wetlands, rivers, and waterbodies are vital to its rich biodiversity and ecological health. With over 
700 wetlands recorded by ISRO and a network of key rivers —including the Terekhol, Mandovi, Zuari,  
Chapora and others—these water systems support diverse species, maintain water quality, and protect 
against floods. Recognizing their importance, the Goa State Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan 
prioritizes the conservation of these critical ecosystems to ensure a sustainable future for Goa’ s natural 
heritage. 
Broader perspective of Wetlands  - The Ramsar treaty provides a broad definition of wetlands, 
encompassing areas like marshes, fens, peatlands, or bodies of water, whether natural or artificial, with 
static or flowing water, and ranging from fresh to brackish or saltwater. UNESCO emphasizes the critical 
role of wetlands in our environment, underscoring their significance as diverse habitats, including lakes, 
rivers, swamps, deltas, tidal flats, mangroves, and coral reefs. These ecosystems, often overlooked, are 
essential for biodiversity and serve as habitats for countless plant and animal species, playing a crucial 
role in human survival due to the fundamental importance of water.  
In accordance with the Wetlands (Conservation and Management) Rules, 2017,  a “wetland” means 
an area or of marsh, fen, peatland or water; natural or artificial, permanent or temporary, with water that 
is static or flowing, fresh, brackish or salt, including areas of marine water, the depth of which at low 
tide does not exceed six. 
 
660 
 
Besides above definitions, there are several ways of looking, defining, and classifying wetlands. But it's 
most important to understand that while framing legal definition, it is ensured that pre-existing rights, 
privileges and activities ongoing traditionally (but which don’t affect the wetland character adversely 
and are the basis of local livelihood), are not impacted. However, there are detailed guidelines to regulate 
and prohibit activities around notified wetlands. There is also a provision to disallow permanent 
construction in the area of 50 meters around the high mean average of the waterscape to ensure the 
conservation of wetlands. This could be referred to as a buffer for the conservation of wetlands.  
Hence, whenever we consider wetlands as ecosystems, we should take a holistic approach based on a  
case-to-case basis, considering the ecosystem setup and biodiversity around each wetland.

 Significant services provided by wetlands 
Ecological services provided by wetland  Economical services provided by wetland  
Biodiversity Support: 
x  Wetlands support diverse plant and animal 
species, serving as habitats for many 
unique and often specialized organisms. 
x  They act as breeding and nursery grounds 
for numerous fish, amphibians, and 
waterfowl. 
 
Fisheries: 
x  Wetlands serve as important breeding and feeding 
grounds for many fish species, supporting 
commercial and recreational fisheries. 
 
Water Filtration and Purification: 
x  Wetlands act as natural filters, trapping and 
removing pollutants and sediments from 
water as it flows through them. 
x  They contribute to improving water quality 
by removing excess nutrients, heavy 
metals, and other contaminants. 
 
Water Supply: 
x  Wetlands can act as natural reservoirs, helping to 
regulate water supply for agriculture, industry, 
and domestic use. 
 
Flood Control: 
x  Wetlands function as natural buffers 
against floods by absorbing and storing 
excess water during heavy rainfall or storm 
events. 
x  They help regulate water flow, reducing 
the risk of downstream flooding. 
 
Agriculture: 
x  Some wetlands, especially floodplains, are used 
for agriculture, providing fertile soil for crops and 
supporting livelihoods. 
 
Climate Regulation: 
x  Wetlands play a role in carbon 
sequestration, helping to mitigate climate 
change by storing large amounts of carbon 
in their soils. 
x  They also contribute to regulating local 
climate conditions by influencing 
temperature and humidity levels. 
 
Tourism and Recreation: 
x  Wetlands attract tourists and outdoor enthusiasts, 
contributing to the local economy through 
activities such as bird watching, fishing, and 
ecotourism. 
 
Recreation and Aesthetic Value: 
x  Wetlands provide recreational 
opportunities such as bird watching, 
fishing, hiking, and nature tourism. 
x  Their scenic beauty and diverse landscapes 
contribute to aesthetic and cultural values. 
 
Hunting and Trapping: 
x  In some regions, wetlands are utilized for 
sustainable hunting and trapping activities, 
providing a source of income for local 
communities. 
 
Erosion Control: 
x  The vegetation in wetlands helps stabilize 
soil and prevent erosion along water 
bodies, coastlines, and riverbanks. 
 
Timber and Non-Timber Products: 
x  Wetland vegetation can be a source of timber, as 
well as non-timber products such as reeds, rushes, 
and other materials used in crafts and 
construction. 
 
 
662 
 
Groundwater Recharge: 
x  Wetlands contribute to the recharge of 
groundwater by allowing water to slowly 
percolate into the soil. 
Water Transport: 
x  Wetlands, including rivers and estuaries, have 
historically served as important transportation 
routes, facilitating trade and commerce. 
 
  
1. Nutrient Cycling: 
x  Wetlands play a role in nutrient cycling, 
recycling organic matter and nutrients 
through microbial processes, benefiting the 
overall ecosystem. 
2.  
Carbon Trading and Climate Finance: 
x  Wetlands contribute to carbon sequestration, and 
initiatives related to carbon trading and climate 
finance can generate economic benefits for 
wetland conservation. 
 
Habitat Connectivity: 
x  Wetlands act as corridors connecting 
different ecosystems, facilitating the 
movement of species and promoting 
genetic diversity. 
 
Flood Protection Infrastructure: 
x  The natural flood control services provided by 
wetlands can reduce the need for costly flood 
protection infrastructure, saving on construction 
and maintenance expenses. 
 
Educational and Scientific Value: 
x  Wetlands provide opportunities for 
scientific research and environmental 
education, helping us better understand 
ecosystem functions and the importance of 
conservation. 
 
Real Estate and Property Values: 
x  Proximity to well-maintained wetlands can 
enhance property values, contributing to the 
economic value of surrounding areas. 
 
3. Potential values 
 
x  There are many species still to be explored, and 
also there is scope to understand their role in 
dealing with climate change, ecological 
equilibrium, etc. The commercial and 
ecological importance of these species and 
wetlands as a whole is yet to be understood, 
and hence, there is scope for potential values in 
future. 
 
Wastewater Treatment: 
x  Constructed wetlands are used for wastewater 
treatment, offering a cost-effective and 
environmentally friendly alternative to 
conventional treatment methods. 
 
4.  Research and Education Opportunities: 
x  Wetlands provide opportunities for research and 
education, contributing to the knowledge 
economy and supporting academic and scientific 
institutions.

Indian Wetlands 
India joined the 'Convention on Wetlands,' commonly known as the Ramsar Convention, on February 
1, 1982. Since then, the country has identified and designated 80 wetlands, encompassing a total area of 
13,41,884 hectares, as part of the List of Wetlands of International Importance. This list includes five 
sites added during the fiscal year 2020-2021. Currently, India holds the leading position in South Asia 
and ranks third in Asia based on the number of designated sites. 

 
665 
 
 
Source – Ramsar site-  https://indianwetlands.in/wetlands-overview/indias-wetlands-of-international-
importance/ 
 
Indian wetlands with unique properties –  
1) Tampara Lake- The detonation of explosives in a conflict between the British East India Company 
and French colonists in 1766 in Ganjam district resulted in a substantial depression that eventually 
transformed into Tampara Lake. This wetland sustains a diverse ecosystem, hosting 60 bird species and 
46 fish species, including vulnerable species like common carp (Cyprinus carpio), common pochard 
(Aythya ferina), and river tern (Sterna aurantia). 
2) Hirakud Reservoir, counted among the largest artificial reservoirs in India, serves as a habitat for more 
than 130 bird species and approximately 54 fish species, including one categorized as endangered and 
six others as near-threatened. Notably, 21 of the fish species 
3) Wular Lake in Jammu & Kashmir, recognized as the largest freshwater lake in India, features vast 
marshes containing emergent and floating vegetation, notably water chestnut. These marshes play a 
crucial role in contributing significant revenue to the State Government. 
4) Sambhar Lake in Rajasthan is a substantial saline lake nourished by four streams, situated in a shallow 
wetland with seasonal variations. Encircled by sand flats and arid thorn scrub, the lake is supplied by 
seasonal rivers and streams. This location holds significance for various wintering waterbirds, notably 
hosting substantial populations of flamingos. 
5) The Sundarban Wetland is situated in the largest mangrove forest globally, the Indian Sundarban. 
Encompassing over 60% of the country's total mangrove forest area, it includes 90% of Indian mangrove 

 
666 
 
species. Within this wetland, the Sundarban Tiger Reserve, identified as a "critical tiger habitat" under 
national law and a "Tiger Conservation Landscape" of global importance, is notable. The Sundarbans 
are the sole mangrove habitat supporting a significant tiger population with unique aquatic hunting 
skills.This site is a habitat for various rare and globally threatened species, including the critically 
endangered northern river terrapin (Batagur baska), the endangered Irrawaddy dolphin (Orcaella 
brevirostris), and the vulnerable fishing cat (Prionailurus viverrinus). Additionally, it hosts two of the 
world's four horseshoe crab species, and eight of India's 12 kingfisher species are also found here. The 
uniqueness of the habitat and its biodiversity, along with the diverse local, regional, and global services 
they provide. 
6) Chilika Lake in Orissa features saline areas that support aquatic algae. The site is crucial for breeding, 
wintering, and staging for 33 species of waterbirds. It also sustains 118 species of fish, including 
commercially important ones, and provides vital resources for a significant number of people. The 
Chilika Development Authority received the Ramsar Wetland Conservation Award for 2002.  
7) Loktak Lake in Manipur, added to the Montreux Record on June 16, 1993, is a sizable freshwater lake 
and connected swamplands fed by several streams. Notably, thick, floating mats of weeds covered with 
soil, known as 'phumids,' are a distinctive characteristic of the lake. 
8) Ropar in Punjab is designated as a National Wetland, created by human intervention through the 
construction of a barrage in 1952 to divert water from the Sutlej River for drinking and irrigation 
purposes. This location holds significance as a crucial breeding ground for the nationally protected 
Smooth Indian Otter, Hog Deer, Sambar, and various reptiles. Additionally, the endangered Indian 
Pangolin (Manis crassicaudata) is believed to inhabit the area. The wetland sustains an essential role in 
the food chain with approximately 35 fish species, and it provides habitat for around 150 species of local 
and migratory birds. 
9) Bhitarkanika Mangroves in Orissa, designated as a Wildlife Sanctuary, represents one of the most 
pristine patches of mangrove forests along the Indian coast. Through 25 years of dedicated conservation 
efforts, the site has evolved into one of the most renowned wildlife sanctuaries. Notably, the Gahirmatha 
beach within the site is recognized as the largest known nesting beach in the world for Olive Ridley Sea 
turtles. 
- Date collected from Ramsar site-  https://indianwetlands.in/wetlands-overview/indias-wetlands-of-
international-importance/ 
 
Wetland classification 
Ramsar Convention recognises wetlands in 6 types namely – 
• marine (coastal wetlands including coastal lagoons, rocky shores, and coral reefs);  
• estuarine (including deltas, tidal marshes, and mangrove swamps);  
• lacustrine (wetlands associated with lakes);  
• riverine (wetlands along rivers and streams); 
• palustrine (meaning “marshy” - marshes, swamps and bogs); and 
x  human-made wetlands (fish and shrimp ponds, farm ponds, irrigated agricultural land, salt pans, 
reservoirs, gravel pits, sewage farms and canals)

Goa State - Area estimates of various wetland categories for Goa have been carried out using GIS layers 
of wetland boundary, water-spread, aquatic vegetation and turbidity. In the state of Goa 383 wetlands 
have been delineated.  In addition, 167 wetlands smaller than 2.25 ha have also been discerned. Total  
wetland area estimated is 21337 ha. (Table 4). The major wetland types are River/Stream (9362 ha), 
Inter tidal mud flats (3286 ha), Salt pans (2929 ha), Reservoirs (2363 ha) and Mangroves (1752 ha).

1. Udden Lake (Ponda) 
Udden Lake situated in Ponda taluka with an area of 0.6389 ha is a seasonal waterbody. This lake is 
enriched by rainfall and catchment runoff. It serves various purposes including supporting arecanut 
plantation, buffalo and cattle wallowing, acting as buffer against floods and sink for sediments. 
Additionally, this wetland supports some noteworthy animals like Leopard, Guppies and Frogs. 
2. Panchami Lake (Ponda) 
Located in the Ponda taluka with an area of 0.9383 ha, Panchami Lake is permanent wetland with a 
depth of 5m.Its major source of water is rainfall, groundwater and freshwater perennial springs. The 
water flows to downstream catchment area and river. It provides a number of ecosystem services 
including irrigation, fisheries, drinking source of water, recreation and tourism; and supports a number 
of migratory birds, apex species like Tiger and Leopard; and life cycle of fishes. 
 
3. Parra Lake (Bardez) 

 
674 
 
Parra Lake, also known as Boquenchi arady Tollem, is a lasting marsh situated in the Bardez taluka, 
covering an area of 0.2 hectares. Its sole water supply is derived from rainfall. The lake serves important 
ecological functions, including groundwater replenishment, accommodating cattle wallowing, water 
purification, and functioning as a sediment repository. Recognized as a significant gathering place for 
migratory waterfowl, it also sustains the life cycles of various aquatic species, such as fish and frogs, for 
example, Pseudosphro menouscupanus. 
4. Karmale Lake or Arla Keri Tollem (Ponda) 
Karmale Lake is a permanent wetland situated in the taluka of Ponda. Spread over an area of 0.805 ha, 
this lake is permanent waterbody which receives water from rainfall and natural springs. The lake's water 
is utilized to sustain the nearby cultivation of Cashew, Betel nut, Jackfruit, and Coconut. Furthermore, 
it also serves as a reservoir, mitigating the risk of potential floods in the surrounding area. Apart from 
its agricultural role, the lake facilitates recreational activities and contributes to groundwater 
replenishment while also aiding in the process of de-silting. 
5. Dhakte Lake or DiulerTollem (Salcete) 
Situated in the taluka of Salcete, Dhakte Lake is a seasonal wetland with an area of 0.469 ha. It is 
nourished by rainfall and groundwater, which later flows to downstream catchment area. The lake's water 
plays a crucial role in irrigating paddy fields, providing a source for buffalo wallowing, and supporting 
fishing activities for the local community. Other than this, it also contributes to groundwater recharge, 
water purification, and the removal of sedimentation. Notable species present in the area include the 
Skittering Frog, African catfish, Water Hyacinth, and Water Lily. 
6. Ita Lake(Salcete) 
Ita Lake is located in the Benaulim village of Salcete taluka, occupying an area of 0.3425 ha. The lake 
is sustained by water from rainfall, which than flows to downstream catchment area and to the sea. The 
wetland provides a number ecosystem services such as irrigating paddy fields, fishing, cultivation of 
Acrostichum aureum,  cattle wallowing, groundwater recharge, water purification, de-siltation and 
supports life cycle of fishes. 
7. Maem Lake (Bicholim) 
Situated in the Bicholim taluka within the North Goa district, the lake spans an area of 10.2348 hectares. 
Its primary water sources include rainfall and groundwater. The placid waters of this lake make it ideal 
for boating and bungee jumping. Its water is utilized for irrigation and local people use this lake for 
Ganesh idol visarjan. Additionally, the lake is responsible for water purification and groundwater 
recharge.  
8. Macasana Lake(Salcete) 
Macasana Lake, located in Salcete taluka, covers an area of 0.6609 hectares. This permanent waterbody 
is sustained by rainfall and when water levels are low, the Paroda canal. The lake's water serves various 
purposes, including paddy and fish cultivation, buffalo wallowing and groundwater recharge. During the 
winter months, the lake becomes a habitat for migratory birds. 
 
9. Bandolem Lake(Salcete) 
 
675 
 
Situated in Sancoale village of Mormugao taluka, Bandolem Lake is a permanent waterbody with an 
area 0.8452 ha. Its main source of water is rainfall, catchment runoff and salt water intrusion during post 
monsoon season. This water later ends in river. Local use it for fishing and Ganesh visarjan. It acts as a 
reservoir providing de-siltation and supporting fishes complete their life cycle and winter migratory 
birds.  
10. Orlim Lake(Salcete) 
Orlim Lake is a part of Orlim village in Salcete taluka. It is a permanent lake with an area of 6.3898 ha. 
This wetland collects water from rainfall and few natural springs which end up in river Sal. Ecosystem 
services such as irrigation, buffalo wallowing, recreational activities, groundwater recharge, water 
purification, de-siltation and supporting life cycle of fishes is provided by this lake. Notable species here 
includes Otters, Water Lily and more. 
11. Dhulpe Lake or Chicungal Tollem (Ponda) 
Dhulpe Lake, also recognized as ChicungalTollem, is located in the Ponda taluka, covering an expanse 
of 1.3153 hectares. This seasonal wetland is nourished by rainfall and natural springs. Noteworthy flora 
and fauna, such as the Dhobi tree, Leopard, and Crocodile, thrive in this environment. The lake's water 
serves various purposes, including sustaining Arecanut plantations, providing a space for buffalo 
wallowing and facilitating the reproductive cycle of fish species like Pittol and Chikal. Additionally, 
Dhulpe Lake functions as both a water purifier and a repository for sediments. 
12. Sapu Lake or Tollem Bandar (Salcete) 
This lake is a permanent water body situated in Ambelim village of Salcete taluka covering an area of 
20.7789 ha. It is fed by rainfall, catchment runoff, and natural springs, eventually flowing into rivers and 
recharging the groundwater table. The lake provides water for paddy cultivation and buffalo wallowing. 
It also sustains the life cycle of various fish species like Pintod, Tiggur, Kumbaruka, and Chikalo. The 
stored water aids in replenishing groundwater, facilitates de-silting and purifies water. Noteworthy 
species in the area include Bittern, Green bee-eater, Pond heron, Common, Kevda, Palm tree, crocodile, 
otter, Kingfisher, and Lesser cormorant. The local residents engage in worship at the foundation stone, 
reflecting a cultural connection with the lake. 
13. Vodle Lake (Salcete) 
Vodle Lake, located in Benaulim village of Salcete taluka, covers an area of 0.442 ha. It is a seasonal 
lake that is replenished by rainfall and groundwater, eventually flowing into the downstream catchment 
area. The lake is home to various species, including Nymphea sp., Water lily, Water hyacinth, Catfish, 
tilapia, frog, and migratory species like stork. This lake plays a crucial role in providing essential 
ecosystem services. It serves as a water source for agriculture, functions as a reservoir, acts as a natural 
buffer against floods, and contributes to water purification and de- siltation. 
14. Talaulim Lake or TalsalTollem(Ponda) 
Talaulim Lake, also recognized as Talsal Tollem, is located in the Ponda taluka, covering an expanse of 
0.5225 ha. This permanent wetland is nourished by rainfall and catchment runoff ultimately ending in 
downstream catchment area and sea. Noteworthy flora and fauna, such as coconut, cashew, mango, 
banana, Wild boar, Leopard, Crocodile and many others thrive in this environment. The lake's water 
serves variouspurposes, including sustaining paddy cultivation and facilitating the reproductive cycle of 
 
676 
 
fish and amphibians. Additionally, Talaulim Lake functions as both a water purifier and a repository for 
sediments. 
15. Moingal Lake (Ponda) 
Found in the village of Shiroda in Ponda taluka, Moingal Lake is a seasonal waterbody that spans 0.2717 
hectares. Its existence relies on rainfall and catchment runoff, eventually benefiting the downstream 
catchment area, river, and groundwater recharge. The lake's water is essential for sustaining paddy fields, 
arecanut, and coconut plantations. Beyond its agricultural contributions, the lake plays a vital role in 
water purification and desiltation processes. Moreover, it serves as a crucial water source for agricultural 
activities and supports the life cycle of various species such as sungat, Tiggur, Shiggur, Pittol, and 
Volayu. 
16. Betal Lake (Ponda) 
Betal Lake is located Querim village in Ponda taluka. It is named after the Betal temple next to it.  This 
lake is a permanent waterbody covering 0.44 ha of area. Water from rainfall, catchment runoff and 
natural springs collects here forming a large reservoir. The lake’s water is used for irrigation, fishing and 
cattle wallowing. Important festival like Sangoda Palki is performed here. It also supports noteworthy 
species like Water Lily, Egrets, Common Kingfisher etc and other small fishes. 
 
17. Adsule Lake (Salcete) 
Adsule Lake is a permanent water body situated in Benaulim village of Salcete taluka with 0.3 ha of 
area. It receives water from rainfall which flows to downstream catchment area. It supports sched ule 
species like crocodile, monitor lizard and Oriental darter. Fishes like Tilapia and African catfish are 
found here. The lake acts a large reservoir thus leading groundwater recharge and water purification. 
18. Kodal Lake (Bicholim) 
Situated in the Karapur village of Bicholim taluka, Kodal Lake is a permanent waterbody covering an 
expanse of 0.753hectares. The lake is sustained by rainfall and groundwater ultimately contributing to

Wetlands with biodiversity perspective – 
Wetlands are often referred to as “biological super “due to their capacity to generate significant amounts 
of sustenance, fostering an impressive diversity of species. In terms of both quantity and diversity of 
supported organisms, wetlands rival the richness found in rainforests and coral reefs. The presence of 
shallow water, abundant nutrients, and elevated primary productivity makes wetlands an optimal 
environment for the thriving of essential organisms forming the foundational components of Earth ’s 
food web.6 
Wetlands encompass a broad range of environments, spanning both inland and coastal areas. Inland 
wetlands comprise rivers, lakes, marshes, swamps, and other waterlogged regions. However, the Ramsar 
Convention expands its definition to include coastal wetlands, incorporating saltwater marshes, 
estuaries, mangroves, lagoons, and coral reefs. Recognizing both inland and coastal wetlands is crucial 
because of their interconnectedness and their relationships with the surrounding terrestrial landscapes. 
To emphasize this interconnected web of aquatic ecosystems, members of the IUCN Species Survival 
Commission advocate for the concept of the aquascape. This term underscores the connectivity among 
freshwater, marine environments, and transitional waters, such as estuaries, lagoons, and deltas, as well 
as the ecological processes that span across them.7 
Wetlands can be likened to the agricultural fields of aquatic ecosystems, as they generate substantial 
quantities of food, primarily in the form of plant material. The significant nutritional value of wetland 
plants is realized when the decomposition of their dead leaves and stems in the water produces small 
organic particles known as “detritus”. This nutrient- rich detritus serves as the primary food source for 
numerous small aquatic invertebrates, various shellfish, and forage fish, which, in turn, become prey for 
larger predatory fish. Ultimately, these larger fish are harvested and consumed by humans. 8 Species of 
songbirds, waterfowl, raptors, marsh birds, and shorebirds undertake migration across the Great Lakes, 
heavily relying on nearshore habitats as crucial refuges along their journey. The vast expanse of the lakes 
poses a significant challenge both in the fall and spring, serving as an initial obstacle and a final hurdle 
for many of these long-distance migrants. Audubon, through its Great Lakes initiative, has prioritized 
 
5 https://gswa.goa.gov.in/ 
6 https://www.wetlands-initiative.org/high-biodiversity 
7 https://www.iucn.org/crossroads-blog/202001/wetlands-ultimate-biodiversity-hotspot 
8 https://dec.vermont.gov/watershed/wetlands/functions/fish

conservation efforts directed at the vital coastal stopover habitats essential for migratory birds and other 
wildlife. These stopover sites serve as crucial locations for birds to rest, refuel, and find shelter during 
their bi-annual migration, which is the most perilous stage of a bird ’s life cycle.9 Rainfall often washes 
various pollutants from urban and agricultural areas, carrying them overland and depositing them into 
water bodies. These pollutants encompass soil particles, fertilizers, pesticides, as well as grease, oil, and 
road salts from vehicles. Wetlands play a crucial role in enhancing water quality by effectively extracting 
pollutants from surface waters. Three key processes through which wetlands contribute to pollutant 
removal are sediment trapping, nutrient removal, and chemical detoxification. These mechanisms 
collectively help mitigate the adverse impacts of pollutants on aquatic ecosystems and contribute to 
overall environmental health.10 
Wetland soils are characterized by low levels of oxygen, making them anoxic, which slows down the 
decomposition process and results in the buildup of organic matter. The extent of this storage varies 
based on factors such as wetland type and size, vegetation, soil depth, groundwater and nutrient levels, 
pH, and other environmental factors. In addition to the organic matter within the wetlands, these soils 
serve as reservoirs for carbon transported from upland areas, either through soil erosion or the movement 
of leaves and tree debris. Wetlands not only accumulate carbon but also release it, influenced by natural, 
seasonal changes. However, human interference can disrupt the equilibrium of wetland ecosystems, 
leading to more substantial releases of carbon. Understanding the dynamics of carbon storage and release 
in wetland soils is crucial for managing and conserving these ecosystems and mitigating their potential 
impact on the global carbon cycle.11   
Some freshwater wetlands serve as points where surface water enters an underground aquifer, 
replenishing groundwater resources. Conversely, wetlands often act as sites for groundwater release onto 
the land surface, such as through springs. This groundwater discharge plays a crucial role as a local 
drinking water source and in sustaining stream flows for the well-being of fish, animals, plants, and other 
organisms during dry summer periods. In accordance with the Vermont Wetland Rules, wetlands that 
significantly contribute to safeguarding or improving the quality of surface or ground water are deemed 
important. When assessing whether a wetland holds significance for the Surface and Ground Water 
Protection function, the Secretary or Panel must, at the very least, evaluate the extent to which the 
wetland: 
a. Replenishes a drinking water source, such as a well head or source protection area. 
b. Diminishes levels of contaminants in surface waters that recharge underlying or neighboring 
groundwaters. 
c. Adds to the flows of Class A surface waters. 
d. Augments or safeguards water quality through chemical processes, nutrient removal, sediment or 
organic matter retention or removal, or by mitigating the adverse water quality effects of soil erosion or 
stormwater runoff.

Causes of Wetland Depletion: 
1. Excessive Pollutants: Dumping industrial effluents, domestic waste, and agricultural runoff into 
wetlands surpasses their recycling capacity. 
2. Habitat Destruction and Deforestation: Altering wetland species populations through habitat 
destruction and deforestation disrupts ecological balance. 
3. Land Use Changes: Conversion of wetlands for agriculture and encroachment by the public and illegal 
activities contribute to depletion. 
4. Overfishing and Aquaculture: Overfishing and fish farming (aquaculture) impact wetland ecosystems. 
5. Overgrazing: Overgrazing in marshy soils harms the vegetation and biodiversity. 
6. Sand Removal: Extraction of sand near seas weakens wetlands, making them susceptible to wave 
action and tidal bore. 
Mitigation Measures: 
1. Demarcation and Enforcement: Employ advanced technology for wetland demarcation, enforce laws 
rigorously, and impose strict penalties on violators. 
2. Aquaculture Regulation: Prevent unsustainable aquaculture and shellfish cultivation. 
3. Effluent Treatment: Treat industrial effluents and agricultural runoff before discharging into wetlands. 
4. Sustainable Use: Utilize wetlands sustainably, allowing for natural regeneration, and implement 
artificial regeneration for rapid recovery. 
5. Ecological Management: Implement afforestation, weed control, and prevention of invasive species 
to conserve wetlands. 
6. Invasive Species Prevention: Take preventive measures to stop the introduction of exotic invasive 
species like water hyacinth. 
7. Soil Conservation: Implement soil conservation measures and afforestation around wetlands. 
8. Grazing Control: Prevent grazing in the peripheral areas of wetlands. 
9. Wildlife Conservation and Tourism: Promote wildlife conservation, sustainable tourism, eco-tourism, 
and raise awareness among the local populace. 
10. Eutrophication Abatement: Process nutrient-rich discharges into water bodies to reduce 
eutrophication. 
11. Community Involvement: Involve local communities in wetland conservation efforts. 
Measures to Protect Wetlands: 
1. Ramsar Convention on Wetlands: Adhere to international agreements like the Ramsar Convention on 
Wetlands. 
 
688 
 
2. Ramsar Sites in India: Identify and protect wetlands listed under Ramsar Sites in India. 
3. Wetlands International: Collaborate with organizations like Wetlands International for global wetland 
conservation efforts. 
4. National Wetlands Conservation Program (NWCP): Support and implement national initiatives like 
the NWCP for wetland conservation.13 
Invasive Species documented in wetlands of Goa 
1.Red eared slider turtles were sighted in Khandepar, Mormugao and Taleigao during a research survey 
by Trupti Jadhav. This species poses significant threat to Indian wetland biodiversity as they threaten 
native species by competing with them for food, nesting, basking spaces and hiding places. Being an 
invasive species, they don’t have natural predators thus proving to be a threat to native aquatic plants 
and animals. Additionally, the native turtles lack immunity to the parasites and other diseases spread 
through the Red-eared Sliders.1415 
2.Pistia stratiotes, commonly known as water cabbage is an invasive aquatic species that is widely 
distributed. It forms dense mats that clog waterways and degrade water quality by blocking the air-
water interface, thus greatly reducing dissolved oxygen levels. This results in fish die-off and the 
overall reduction of aquatic faunal and floral diversity.16 
3.Water hyacinth has worldwide distribution. It has become invasive due to its ability to grow rapidly. 
It forms a thick mat of green vegetation of the water surface cutting off the oxygen supply eventually 
eliminating underwater fauna such as fish. It affects the native floral diversity of the wetland by 
surrounding them at water’s surface and below.171819 
4.Salvinia molesta is a free-floating aquatic plant that forms a thick mat on the surface of the water. It 
harms the waterbodies by shrinking wetlands and destroying indigenous animal and plant 
biodiversity. It interferes with irrigation system and fishing, and provides breeding ground for 
mosquitos.2021 
5.African Sharptooth Catfish is an air breathing fish, native of North Africa. this species is a hardy fish 
which can easily breed in tough conditions as it is a voracious feeder and feeds on all type of food. 
This exotic fish poses a threat to the local fishes and sustainability of aquatic ecosystem. It has been

Traditional practices associated to wetlands around the nation – 
Wetlands play a crucial role in sustaining diverse ecosystems, and their significance is deeply 
intertwined with cultural practices across different regions in India. During the winter season, 
depressions that were once part of rivers; courses fill up post-monsoon, transforming into wetlands that 
serve as natural capital 
for local fishing communities. 
x  In Guwahati, the Deepor Beel is cherished by fishers and Bodo-rice farmers, becoming a life-
giving elixir celebrated during Bihu festivals. Fish-catching equipment like bamboo jakoi, dolonga, 
and sepa are integral to these festivities. 
x  The Chhath Puja is dedicated to the Sun God and is predominantly observed in the states of Bihar, 
Jharkhand, and parts of Uttar Pradesh. During this festival, devotees perform rituals near water 
bodies such as rivers, ponds, or lakes. The setting sun and rising sun are worshipped, and the rituals 
often involve taking a dip in the water. Wetlands, being crucial water ecosystems, may play a role 
in these ceremonies. 
x  Ganga Sagar Mela is an annual gathering of Hindu pilgrims at Sagar Island in West Bengal, where 
the river Ganges meets the Bay of Bengal. Pilgrims take a holy dip at the confluence of the river 
and the sea, believing it will cleanse them of sins. Wetlands near river deltas often serve as sites 
for such religious gatherings. 
x  Celebrated in South India as the harvest festival, Pongal or Makar Sankranti involves offerings to 
the Sun God. People often gather near water bodies to perform rituals and cook the first rice of the 
harvest. Wetlands and rivers can be important locations for these festivities. 
x  In Kerala, the Vaikom Mahadeva Temple celebrates Vaikathashtami, where devotees undertake a 
pilgrimage by walking through wetlands and water bodies to reach the temple. This ritual is 
believed to be purifying and spiritually significant. 
x  Celebrated in Assam, Magh Bihu is an agricultural festival that marks the end of the harvesting 
season. People take part in traditional dances, feasts, and rituals near water bodies, emphasizing 
the connection between agriculture and water resources. 
x  The Yamuna River is considered sacred in Hinduism, and in Vrindavan, devotees perform aarti on 
the banks of the Yamuna. This practice highlights the reverence for the river and its ecological 
importance. 
 
22 https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/goa/tigur-species-under-threat-from-african-
catfish/articleshow/53052396.cms 
23 https://india.mongabay.com/2020/10/commentary-tilapia-how-an-invasive-fish-came-to-dominate-

690 
 
x  The Kaveri River holds cultural significance in South India, and Pushkaram is a festival celebrated 
when the river enters a particular zodiac sign. Pilgrims take a holy dip in the river during this 
period, and the festival involves various rituals performed near the river and its tributaries. 
x  In Assam, Morigaon district, the Jon Beel mela, a three-day festival, has been observed since the 
15th century. Indigenous communities engage in bartering goods along the Jon Beel, emphasizing 
fish from the Beel as a central component of the nuan puja marking the bountiful harvest. The 
Kaibarta fishing community, reliant on seasonal wetlands, has developed rituals to safeguard their 
sensitive livelihood, including Ghot Puja and Ganga Puja to appease deities associated with 
wetlands. 
x  In arid regions like Rajasthan, transient wetlands, and human-made structures are essential for 
pastoralists; sustenance. Nadis, shallow ponds, exist in community conservation areas like the 
sacred grasslands called Orans. These Orans serve as grazing grounds for local livestock and 
support biodiversity, including the critically endangered Great Indian Bustard. 
x  Guardian deities play a significant role in the spiritual connection to wetlands. In Pulicat, Tamil 
Nadu, terracotta figurines of Thambi and Thangachi Selais, are considered early warning systems, 
and the custodian goddess Kanni is worshipped by fisher communities. Guardian deities like 
Ayyanar protect villages in Tamil Nadu, marking the landscape and boundaries. The Mahamaham 
tank in Kumbakonam is believed to have received nectar spilled from the celestial pot, leading to 
the Mahamaham festival celebrated every 12 years. 
x  In Uttarakhand, water is perceived as divine, and springs are revered in the Garhwal Himalayas, 
playing a crucial role in rituals and symbolism. In Odisha, crafts like Sholapith, Golden Grass, and 
Nalia are examples of wetland resource extraction tied to local culture. Sholapith craft, linke d to 
the worship of Lord Jagannath, involves crafting ornaments and headgears from waterlogged stems 
harvested during specific months. 
x  Wetlands also hold deep spiritual significance in Meitei mythology of Manipur. Nungjen Pukhri, 
a pond in Kangla Palace, is believed to be the abode of Lord Pakhangba, and rituals like Lai 
Haraoba celebrate deities of sacred groves. In Bundi, Rajasthan, the Nawal Sagar wetland houses 
a temple dedicated to Lord 
x  Varuna, the Vedic God of water, and stepped ponds like Rani ki Vav in Patan have inbuilt shrines 
and sacred imagery, depicting the personification of sacred rivers. In the Sundarbans, Bonbibi, a 
Forest God, is worshipped, and the Bonbibi festival ensures communities respect the ecosystem 
and regulate resource extraction. Kashmiris revere springs, and folklore speaks of Tasrufdars 
dwelling around streams, rivers, and wilderness. Springs were used as oracles in ancient times, 
emphasizing the importance of caring for these water sources. 
x  In Vedanthangal, Tamil Nadu, Diwali is celebrated quietly to coincide with the bird migratory 
season, respecting the wetland bird sanctuary. Traditional norms in Uttarakhand prohibit fishing 
in Dodital and Devariyatal lakes, and temple ponds in Assam, like Kamakhya, contribute to turtle 
conservation efforts. These examples highlight the intricate relationship between wetlands, cultural 
practices, and spiritual beliefs across diverse regions in India. 
 
Rivers and wetlands 
Goa, situated along India's western coast, is geographically divided into three distinct regions. 
To the west lies the Coastal Plain, characterized by sandy beaches, estuaries, mudflats, and 
 
691 
 
marshes, occasionally interrupted by low tablelands with laterite-capped surfaces. In the central 
region, known as the Midland, are the moderately high hills running in a northwest-southeast 
direction, separated by undulating expanses of weathered plains. To the east, the imposing 
Western Ghats form a high, steep escarpment, running generally from north to south, with the 
Karnataka plateau bordering the state further east. 
The Coastal Plain ranges in elevation from 2 to 15 meters above sea level, while the flat 
tablelands along the coast rise to heights of 50-80 meters above sea level. The Midland's ridges 
vary in elevation from 100 to 400 meters, with the intermountain plains at 30 to 60 meters above 
sea level. The Western Ghats an average elevation of approximately 800 meters above sea level 
within the state of Goa. 
The terrain of Goa is drained by a network of nine estuarine rivers, including the Terekhol, 
Chapora, Mandovi, Zuari, Baga, Sal, Saleri, Talpona and Galgibag River. The major rivers 
mostly originate in the Western Ghats but gradually lose the gradient as they flow through the 
Midland and Coastal Plains before emptying into the Arabian Sea. The gentle slopes in the lower 
reaches of these rivers allow tidal waters to penetrate several kilometers inland. Two smaller 
rivers Harmal and Mandrem also drain smaller watersheds in the northern part of the state. 
As of 2005, the Central Water Commission estimated that Goa possesses ample surface water 
resources, totaling approximately 8437 million cubic meters.

 Heritages of Wetness – Khazans of Goa 
Khazans are distinctive features of Goa's coastal areas, situated at the junction of land and water. 
These constructed fields, found along the Mandovi and Zuari rivers and their tributaries, shape 
Goa's dense wetlands and coastal zones. 
Characteristics and Creation 
x  Khazans take advantage of tidal movements, reclaiming land from shallow waters. 
x  They create linear and organic patterns visible from surrounding plateaus. 
x  Mythically, these lands are associated with Parashurama's arrows reclaiming land from the 
ocean. 
x  The technical knowledge behind khazans is attributed to indigenous populations, ancestors of the 
Gaudde and Kunbi communities. 
Technical Aspects 
x  Sluice gates, derived from the Dutch word 'sluis', are crucial in regulating water flows and soil 
salinity. 
x  Khazans balance natural elements: oceanic and river water, salt, and soil. 
x  They enhance interactions between atmospheric systems, the ocean, rivers, and the Western 
Ghats. 
Conceptual Significance 
x  Khazans embody an 'in-between' space, belonging to both water and land. 
x  They bring coastal characteristics inland, following tidal movements. 
x  These landscapes are both perennial and ephemeral, changing with seasons. 
Cultural and Aesthetic Value 
x  Khazans form a vital layer in Goan village organization. 
x  They complement the built structures of houses, temples, and churches. 
x  Their value lies in how change is controlled and re-enacted. 
Contemporary Relevance 
x  Khazans face challenges from abandonment and pollution. 
x  They represent a delicate balance between natural processes and human control. 
x  These landscapes are significant for their natural, cultural, and aesthetic value. 
Khazans thus serve as important markers of Goa's cultural heritage, blending natural landscape 
features with human ingenuity and traditional knowledge.2425

Conservation of Poeteracia coarctata 
Poeteracia coarctata member of Poaceae, act as pioneer species in the succession process of mangrove 
formation along the estuaries of India (Jagtap, 1985). This species establish on the newly deposited 
sediments and help enhance sedimentation, developing favourable substratum for the growth of 
mangroves (Plate 1). Porteresia coarctata, though of great significance to estuarine and deltaic 
environments, is very poorly understood ecologically, compared to other marine and estuarine 
vegetation. Temporal and spatial patterns in growth and biomass production of P. coarctata were 
evaluated with regard to its immediate environmental characteristics at selected localities along the 
banks of Mandovi estuary, Goa, India. The open mudflats along the estuaries and creeks are generally 
subjected to the intensive erosion, particularly because of speedy runoff during monsoon period as well 
due to the strong waves caused by blowing of speedy winds during the period of pre-monsoon. The 
Porteresia beds, which generally grow towards the waterfront, could be of importance in minimizing 
erosive processes and enhancing the sedimentation rate. The predominant sandy nature of substratum 
indicated the adaptability of P. coarctata to establish on newly deposited unstable sediments and helps 
further enhance the land building process.

Introduction 
Goa's rich natural heritage is defined by its diverse avifauna and entomofauna. The state's bird species 
and insect communities, including odonates, wasps, ants and butterflies, play vital ecosystem roles as 
pollinators, predators, and environmental indicators. 
This chapter of the GSBSAP provides a comprehensive assessment of Goa's avifaunal and 
entomofaunal diversity. It examines the status of endemic species and those under IUCN threat 
categories, highlighting the need for targeted conservation. The chapter also identifies threatened 
ecosystems and outlines specific strategies and action points to address these challenges. 
Importantly, the proposed monitoring framework aligns these efforts with the 23 National Biodiversity 
Targets outlined in India's 2023 NBSAP. This ensures Goa's avifauna and entomofauna conservation 
initiatives contribute to the broader national biodiversity goals, while addressing the state's unique 
priorities. 
As a key component of the GSBSAP, this chapter reaffirms Goa's commitment to safeguarding its rich 
faunal heritage through collaborative, evidence-based, and impactful conservation interventions.

1. Climate Change and Goa 
 
Global temperatures have already risen by about 1.1°C over the period 1880 to 2020 [IPCC-
A6] in response to the GHG build-up in the atmosphere since the pre-industrial times. Indian 
sub-continent is also warming rapidly, particularly since the 1980s. As per IMD (2021) 
analysis, the annual mean temperature during 1901-2020 period has risen by about 0.73C. As 
GHG build-up is projected to further rise in the 21st century, in future temperatures are 
expected to rise even further. A mere temperature rise of 1.1 Deg C is causing distress to 
human societies as well as different flora and fauna around the World. A temperature rise of 
1.5-2C is regarded as the dangerous threshold for climate change. The Paris Agreement aims 
to limit warming below these levels. Going forward, at all India level Chaturvedi,et. al. 2012 
project that “under the business as usual (between RCP6 and RCP8.5) scenario, mean 
warming in India is likely to be in the range of 1.7  to 2°C by 2030s and 3.3 to 4.8°C by 
2080s relative to pre-industrial times”, further they project that “all India precipitation under 
the business as usual scenario is projected to increase from 4% to 5% by 2030s and from 6% 
to 14% towards the end of the century (2080s) compared to the 1961-1990 baseline”. 
 
 
Climate Profile of Goa state- 
 
Figure xxx shows the mean annual temperature map of Goa over the long-term period of 
1951-2014. Methodology and data source for this figure is described in Venkateswaran and 
Chaturvedi (in Preparation). Mean temperature in Goa is found to be 26.70C, which is higher 
than the national average annual temperature which is about 23.3C (Chaturvedi et.al. 2012). 
While spatial temperature variability is not high in goa, hilly areas in the eastern parts of the 
state are generally cooler than the coastal areas in the west.

Figure xxx: Long period average (1951-2014) spatial distribution of mean temperature 
(deg C) in Goa 
  
Goa experiences a hot summer (April- June) followed by pleasant monsoon (June-
September) season, temperatures temporarily rise again in the month of October, following 
pleasant winter months (November to March). Figure xx. shows the seasonal and monthly 
mean monthly temperature profile in the Goa based on the long-period mean temperature 
average over the period 1951-2014.

Figure xxx: Long-period average (1951-2014) annual temperature profile in Goa 
  
Rainfall Profile in Goa: 
Average annual rainfall in Goa is about 3000 mm, which is about three times higher than the 
national average.  
Figure xxx. shows the mean monthly rainfall profile in the state in monsoon, pre-monsoon 
and post monsoon months. Figure xxx shows that much of the rainfall in Goa takes place in 
the monsoon months, whereas winters are usually dry.

How Climate is changing is Goa? 
 
Mean temperature trend in Goa is shown in Figure xx. Figure xxx suggests that Goa is 
witnessing higher levels of temperature increase compared to the national average (IMD, 
2013) as the mean temperature in Goa has increased by about 1C over the period 1901-2018. 
Figure xxx also shows that much of the warming in Goa has been witnessed after 1970s. 
 
 
Mean annual rainfall trend in Goa is plotted in Figure xx. It shows that mean annual rainfall 
in Goa has increased by about 68% over the last century.  Results in Figure xxx are supported 
by mean annual rainfall trend in North Goa as reported by Kaur et al 2017, where mean 
annual rainfall in North Goa is found to have increased from 3000 mm in 1901 to 5000 mm 
to 2015 (an increase of 66%).

Projected Climate Change in Goa 
In this section we aim to assess climate change projections in Goa in the 21st century based 
on high resolution regional climate models. To be more precise, what does climate change 
projections under the different Representative Concentration Pathways (RCPs) mean for the 
State of Goa in the 21st century? As GHG build-up is projected to rise in the 21st century, 
temperatures are expected to rise even further. The projected climate change scenarios 
(temperature and rainfall) are for the two scenarios of RCP8.5 and RCP4.5. Under RCP8.5 
scenario atmospheric CO2 concentration is going to rises to 940 ppm by 2100, whereas under 
RCP4.5 scenario atmospheric CO2 concentration rises to 538 ppm by 2100.  
Figure xx shows that the mean temperature projections for the state of Goa from 1901-2100 
under two scenarios of RCP4.5 and RCP8.5. Under the RCP8.5 scenario temperature rises by 
4.5C compared to the base of 1901-1950, however if the GHG emissions are controlled to 
RCP4.5 scenario then Goa witnesses a mean temperature rise of only about 2.5C compared to 
1901-1950 base. 
 

 
111 
 
 
Figure xx: Projected mean temperature trend (deg C) in Goa under different climate 
change scenarios 
  
Figure xx shows the mean annual rainfall projections for the state of Goa from 1901-2100. 
The figure shows that generally annual rainfall is projected to decrease in Goa in the 21st 
century, however the variability in rainfall projections for Goa state are very high. 

 
112 
 
  
Figure xx: Projected rainfall trend (mm/day) in Goa under different climate change 
scenarios 
 
Figure xxx shows the future mean annual temperature projections in the short term, medium 
term and long-term. As per Figure xx, mean annual temperature in Goa increases to 28.3°C 
by 2035, and to 30.3°C, compared to the present annual temperatures (1985-2015) of 26.8°C .

Projection of Extreme Temperature 
Extreme temperatures are projected to increase under climate change scenarios. For Goa, it is 
projected that by the year 2040, maximum temperatures of 40C or more will become 
commonplace, minimum temperatures in Goa are also expected to increase by 3-7 degrees C.

in the 21stcentury 
  
Projection of Extreme Rainfall 
IPCC special report on weather extremes (IPCC, 2012) project likely increase in the 
frequency of heavy precipitation in the 21st century over many areas of the globe. We 
quantify the expected future change in extreme rainfall events over India by using the daily 
precipitation data from the multiple model ensemble of the CORDEX models. Figure xxx 
shows that very heavy rainfall events will increase in Goa in the 21st century, under both 
RCP4.5 and RCP8.5 scenarios.  

 
116 
 
Figure xx: Rising frequency of very heavy extreme rainfall events in climate change 
scenarios 
  
Similarly, exceptionally (rare) very heavy extreme rainfall events which are rare and 
exceptional in today’s climate will become commonplace in climate change scenarios of 
RCP4.5 and RCP8.5.

Climate change and its impact on biodiversity 
 
Climate change has already been seen to have an effect on biodiversity and natural 
ecosystems. Growing world population, urbanization, land and water degradation, 
biodiversity loss and food insecurity are concurrent and interact with climate change (IPCC, 
2022). Globally, freshwater, terrestrial, and marine ecosystems have all been impacted by 
climate change. Effects are more pervasive, having both immediate and longer-lasting effects 
than anticipated (IPCC, 2022). Ecosystems are impacted by climate change in a number of 
ways. For instance, warming may compel some species to move towards higher latitudes or 
altitudes where the climate is more suited for their survival. Similarly, as the sea level rises, 
saltwater intrusion into a freshwater system may cause certain important species to disappear 
or be driven to new locations. The effects of climate change that have already been seen and 
expected to increase are (i) coral bleaching (ii) habitat shifts (iii) species migration (iv) 

 
118 
 
seasons shifting (CCC, 2015). Not all species within a community will probably adapt to 
climate change equally or fast. Some animals may move easily across landscapes as habitats 
are transformed by rising temperatures and shifting biological circumstances. Less mobile 
species will experience distribution shifts more gradually. Certain species, such as some tree 
and plant species can only move through reproduction and seed dissemination (UCS, 2003). 
The 1°C rise in the average global temperature is modifying species' genetic makeup, 
behaviours, and capacities for survival in significant and unexpected ways. Climate change is 
bringing about changes in species themselves that endanger their survival in addition to 
higher rates of disease and deteriorated habitats. 
 
Effect of extreme events on biodiversity 
 
Major ecosystem disruptions are caused by cyclones and floods (Kupika et al., 2021). 
Floods are said to account for 34% of all natural disasters worldwide (Petit-Boix et al., 2017). 
Floods are becoming more common and destructive as a result of climate change and 
anthropogenic pressures (Ge et al.,  2021). Extreme floods have submerged large areas, 
including 27% of cropland worldwide (Ballesteros-Canovas et al.,  2020). Drought has a 
general impact on biodiversity by reducing ecosystem productivity and increasing mortality. 
Competitive species, species adapted to cold and wet conditions, and species with slow 
reproduction rates appear to be the most vulnerable (Archaux& Wolters, 2006). Relevant 
stakeholders must be made aware of the impact of climate change-related extreme events on 
biodiversity and wildlife resources to promote adaptive biodiversity management measures.  
• Drought-tolerant crops/crop varieties appropriate for Goa should be promoted. 
• Rainwater harvesting and aquifer recharge are advised in all available locations other 
than high and moderate landslide-prone zones. Irrigation techniques with higher 
efficiency like drip irrigation should be promoted. Soil and water conservation 
techniques like soil mulching and cover crops should be encouraged to conserve soil 
moisture. 
• The drought affected regions may be brought under the village adoption programme 
by multiple agencies like universities, colleges, R&D organizations, NGOs, etc. 
• The State of Goa experience extreme weather events such as droughts, cyclones, 
floods and untimely rainfall. These risks are further compounded by climate change 
• Despite significant progress in the agricultural sector, climate extremes periodically 
result in losses to livelihoods and yields that produce distress in the farming 
community 
• Hence long-term measures are needed to develop climate-resilient agriculture 
production systems that can contribute to food security and poverty reduction.

7.     Socio-economic aspect- people’s contribution towards the sector and implications on people 
Climate Change on Forests and Western Ghats 
• Forest-dependent communities will be affected as there’s a rapid loss of forests due to climate change and climate change induced 
stressors like rising temperature, and extreme events. Forest-dwelling communities will face a severe impact on their livelihood. 
• Ecotourism might also be impacted due to extreme events 
• Forest resources may become scarce 
• Human activity, such as burning of fossil fuels, greenhouse gas emissions, farming, deforestation are largely to blame for current climate 
change 
• The prime impact climate change is on agricultural production and food security 
• Rising water scarcity, sea-water intrusions and rising temperatures will threaten crop yields, food security, and make India dependent on 
food imports 
• Crop failures and increased infestation of pests and insects are common place. It would not be an extrapolation to link farmers' suicides to 
climate change 
• Also leads to malnutrition and child-stunting 
• Increasing temperatures will enhance vector-borne diseases such as malaria and diarrheal infections

11. Good practice example from other states / Interesting discoveries/ did you know facts or any other interesting piece related to the sector 
➢ Management of Coastal Saline Soils   
 
➢ ICAR-CSSRI, Karnal and several SAUs in India, understanding the problems of salt-affected soils, poor-quality irrigation wa ters, 
water dynamics, causes of salt accumulation and behaviour of plants under salt stresses, recommendations ha ve emerged as 
technologies for reclamation and management of salt-affected soils, viz. gypsum technology for reclamation of sodic soils, 
developing salt tolerant crop varieties, guidelines for use of poor quality waters, rehabilitation of salty lands using fores try 
species, etc. 
 
➢ Rainwater Harvesting and Irrigation Methods 
 
➢ Rajendra Bhat farmers from Badlapur in Maharashtra, owns a lush five-acre farm with 187 varieties of fruits, vege tables and 
medicinal plants 
 
139 
 
➢ He executed raised-bed farming to evenly distribute water and prevent water runoff. He also made long and n arrow trenches on 
the ground and planted seeds on raised strips. Next, he made optimal use of earthworms for capturing rainwater and preparing 
nutrient-rich manure. 
➢ Earthworms make it easy for water to seep into the ground, and increase its holding capacity.  
➢ Earthworms make tunnels in the soil and make it very porous. Raindrops go through these tunnels and make the place much better 
than what it would be if the leaves and weeds were not there. It is like the entire field starts drinking rainwater. 
➢ This helps to prevent loses in drought-like and floods situations.

Chapter X – Biodiversity Management Committee (BMC) 
Goa, a smallStatein India, has 205 BMCs, (191 village panchayats, 13 Municipalities and 1 
corporation) which are constituted at the Village Panchayats, Municipaland corporation level 
to ensure decentralised & effective Governance at the grassroots level. These BMCs are 
constituted in accordance with the Section No. 41 of Biological Diversity Act, 2002 at local 
body level within its jurisdiction area for the purpose of promoting conservation, sustainable 
use and documentation of habitats, conservation of land races, folk varieties and cultivars, 
domesticated stocks and breeds of animals & microorganisms and chronicling of knowledge 
relating to biological diversity. 
The section also mentions that the National Biodiversity Authority & the State Biodiversity 
Boards shall consult the BMC while taking any decision relating to the use of biological 
resource occurring within the territorial jurisdiction of the BMC, it also gives power to BMC 
to levy charges by way of collection fees from any person for accessing or collection 
purposes from areas falling within its territorial jurisdiction.  
Rule No. 22 of The Biological Diversity Rules, 2004 gives an outline of the roles and 
responsibilities of the BMCs as well as the procedures for their establishment and 
 
141 
 
functioning. Each BMC consists of seven members: one chai rperson, two women members, 
one SC/ST/OBC member, two local members, and one secretary, who are responsible for 
overseeing the various tasks and operations of the BMC. 
In accordance with NBA guidelines, the Goa State Biodiversity Board ( GGSBB) has 
provided Technical Support Groups (TSGs) to each BMC; these TSGs help BMCs with one 
of their core responsibilities, which is making the People's Biodiversity Register (PBR). The 
PBR is a comprehensive documentation of the biodiversity found within the jurisdiction of 
each BMC, and TSGs are responsible for providing scientific assistance to the BMC for the 
compilation and maintenance of the PBR. As of now, 204 BMCs are provided with TSGs, 
which include NGOs like ICLEI South Asia and institutions like TERI. Whereas Penha de 
Franca BMC has set an example for the entire Sstate by preparing its own PBR without any 
TSG and by getting their PBR validated at all three levels, namely, the BMC level, the Gram 
Sabha level, and the State level, by the Goa State thematic expert committee on PBR and its 
validation.

Plan (GSBSAP) they require to strengthen themselves forthat they require space and 
infrastructure of each BMC, more financial assistance and grants to organize more 
conservation activities annually, support from local bodies, which also calls for convergence 
of governance wherein institutions like Goa State Pollution Control Board could do the 
analysis of suspected polluted habitat or ecosystem and further on BMCs want to be 
financially strong to pay such institutions to  understand their respective ecosystem closely as 
part of their social commitment, they also want to understand the quality and contaminant 
already present in soil, air, and water in their respective jurisdiction area.  
BMCs showed a requirement for funding for activities such as 
• Constant capacity-building, training, and awareness programs for both BMC members 
and local people. 
• Organize more events like PBR updates and validations in a year. 
• Flagship species analysis in their respective areas and their monitoring by the 
installation of cameras and telescopes. 
• Installation of CCTV cameras around Biodiversity Heritage Sites (BHS). 
• Funds and grants transportation, Travel, refreshments, and meetings. 
BMC representatives also discussed on whom to consider inactive member and process of 
removal and gave following points – 
• Inactive members will be those who have not attended three consecutive BMC 
meetings. 
• Unjustified reasoning for being inactive. 
• Escalation of the complaint to remove the member to Gram Sabha.The Gram Sabha 
decision will be the final decision. 
• A change in BMC members and chairperson will be decided by BMC internally, and 
Sarpanch can be involved in the case of dispute. 
• Internal voting system needs to be used for all the BMC changes, in case of dispute at 
Gram Sabha level, MS, GSBB’s decision will be final. 
Representatives also suggested to constitute subcommittees under them involving college and 
school students that will be responsible for focusing on different aspects of biodiversity, for 
example, the subcommittee for avifauna, which will monitor bird counts and update such 
things in PBR. These subcommittees will also be required to present their observations in 
front of BMC members monthly. 
They also requested to extend the support provided by village panchayats and the Sarpanch 
for funds to maintain the green cover or environment protection funds to support all the 
mentioned activities.

Chapter XX – Goa State Biodiversity Board- 
Goa State Biodiversity Board (GSBB) is an autonomous body of Government of Goa 
constituted as per the provision made in Section 22 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002 for 
the establishment of State Biodiversity Boards, the State Government of Goa constituted the 
Goa State Biodiversity Board in the year 2004.  
Functions of the Board:  As per section 23 of the Biological Diversity Act, 2002, the 
functions of the Board are:  
a) Advise the State Government, subject to any guidelines issued by the Central Government, 
on matters relating to the conservation of biodiversity, sustainable use of its components and 
equitable sharing of the benefits arising out of the utilization of biological resources;  
b) Regulate by granting of approvals or otherwise requests for commercial utilization or bio-
survey and bio-utilization of any biological resource by Indians;  
 
152 
 
c) Performs such other functions as may be necessary to carry out the provisions of the 
Biological Diversity Act, 2002 or as may be prescribed by the State Government.  
The Goa State Biodiversity Board is acting on the following lines to achieve the goal:  
A) To make people aware of the biodiversity and its importance for human wellbeing  
B) Constitution of Biodiversity Management Committees (BMC’s) at the Panchayat and 
Municipal level for decentralized management of Bio-resource. 
C) Documentation of Biodiversity, its uses, traditional knowledge and practices associated 
with it, in the form of People’s Biodiversity Registers (PBRs), involving local people through 
the concerning BMCs to follow Goa SBB Mandate.Goa State is one of the richest 
repositories of biological diversity. It has six wildlife sanctuaries including one bird sanctuary 
and one National Park. The primary mandate of the Board is to conserve biodiversity, 
sustainable use of its components and fair and equitable sharing of the benefits arising out of 
the utilization of biological resources. 
During the meeting it was felt that empowerment of GSBB is required to implement 
GSBSAP for next year.

BMC Success story – Penha De Franca PBR 
Penha de Franca BMC, which is in the Bardez Taluka, is one of the BMCs whose PBR was 
validated after successfully completing the 3-tier validation process. This BMC collaborated 
with two High Schools, Dattaram K. Chopdekar Memorial High School and L.D. Samant 
Memorial High School, to prepare PBR. In this practice, teachers and students worked 
together to tag trees and count the plants in the area under their jurisdiction. Additionally, it 
required the active involvement of BMC members and locals, such as Mr. Ghanashyam Naik 
and Mr. Ganpat Vishnu Sidhaye, the former secretary & present Chairperson of the BMC. To 
record locals' traditional knowledge about the flora and identification in the area, Penha de 
Franca (BMC) also included locals like Late Krishna Madkaikar and Mr. Ramesh 
Dhargalkar, and for Scientific assistance BMC members reached out to Forest Department 
and Goa State Biodiversity Board. After the completion of PBR, Penha de Franca BMC also 
converted a garbage dumping ground into a well-managed Butterfly garden with the help of 
Goa State Biodiversity Board. 
 
BMC Success story – Curtorim BMC office 
Members of the Curtorim BMC identified a primary government school in Curtorim that 
would meet their needs for an office, and they contacted GSBB to ask for assistance in 
acquiring the space in the school from Education Department so that they could use it as the 
BMC office. GSBB and the BMC also contacted the Directorate of Higher Education to 
request permission to allow the BMC to acquire space at the school for office purposes, 
which was later approved. Presently this space also houses the Community Seed Bank, which 
is another story of the BMC. 
 
Success Story – Community Seed Banks- 
The Goa State Biodiversity Board, in collaboration with two Biodiversity Management 
Committees, established two community seed banks in Curtorim on September 16, 2022, and 
Bandora, Ponda, on July 2, 2023. The goal of these seed banks is to preserve and conserve 
local plant species while also promoting sustainable agricultural practices. Farmers who have 
deposited their indigenous seed varieties in both community seed banks received Beej Mitra 
cards or seed purchase cards. The cards’ purpose is to identify these farmers and facilitate 
 
158 
 
their connections with bulk buyers or individuals interested in purchasing local varieties from 
these seed banks. 
 
Success Story – Vaidya Mitra & Certification of Traditional Healers  
The traditional healers certification project is being implemented with the financial 
sponsorship of the Goa State Biodiversity Board under a grant-in-aid for the benefit of 
traditional healers in Goa. The oral evaluation of the knowledge and skills and field 
verification of the traditional healers who applied for their assessment, field verification, and 
certification as Traditional Community Healthcare Providers (TCHPs) was held. Firstly, 
eligible healer applicants aged 50 years and above and having an experience of 50 years and 
above were identified by the respective Biodiversity Management Committees with the help 
of the Goa State Biodiversity Board. They were assessed and field-verified by a four-member 
TCHP Advisory Board. During the first batch, 30 were certified under the project.

Introduction – 
Communication, information, awareness, and capacity building are considered crucial when it 
comes to biodiversity and conservation, holding significant power to sensitize the citizens of 
Goa. The print, broadcast, and internet media can be powerful allies in educating and 
enlightening the public on biodiversity conservation. Mass media, reaching every household and 
people of all ages, can be used as a crucial source to sensitize the public, regardless of caste, 
colour, or geographical location.1 
The strengthening of this sector and its inclusion in the Goa State Biodiversity Strategy and 
Action Plan is of utmost importance. Therefore, this chapter presents inputs from experts who 
have been working in the aforementioned sector for years. It outlines the strategies, plans, gaps, 
and monitoring frameworks that should be taken into consideration while preparing this 
document, which will be implemented for the next 10 years in the State of Goa. 
This comprehensive approach aims to leverage various media channels to create a well-informed 
citizenry that understands the importance of biodiversity conservation. By incorporating expert 
knowledge and tailored strategies, the plan seeks to ensure long-term, sustainable conservation 
efforts across Goa, fostering a culture of environmental stewardship among its diverse 
population. 
 
1. Baseline Study - 
A brief history of environmental journalism in Goa 
• The occurrence of dead fish in River Zuari gained space in the media and therefore caught 
attention of the public in a major way in the late 1970s. This was caused due to effluents being 
released by the factory into the waters and the issue caused a furore. 
 
1 https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/readersblog/world-of-words/role-of- media-in-conserving-biodiversity-
34046/ 
 
160 
 
• Mechanisation led to indiscriminate mining of iron ore in Goa by mid to late 1980s and ill-
effects of extraction beyond prescribed limits began to be reported in the media. Marathi daily 
Tarun Bharat was the only newspaper which would report freely on ill-effects of mining as 
rest of the media houses in Goa were mostly owned by mine-owners. 
• Nylon-66 agitation in 1989-90 was the first village level organisation of an environment 
movement to protest in Goa. 
• Post 1990s saw arrival of electronic media in Goa and reporting on environmental issues 
received a boost. 
• Around this time the movement against Konkan Railway line was seen in Goa, while Khazan 
land conservation also started getting reported. 
• Tourism boomed in Goa in late 1990s to early 2000s and many star hotels were reported to be 
carrying out constructions along Goa’s coast by destroying sand dunes. A report submitted 
before the high court had recorded more than a 1000 cases of CRZ violation. 
• It is in the post 2000s era that the stranglehold of mine-owners on newspapers reduced and 
illegal mining related issues in Goa could gain more prominence in the media 
• Post 2000 also saw the meta strips agitation against the unit was melting scraps in plant using 
a hazardous process. 
• Around the same time, media began raising awareness against the killing of bull frogs for 
consumption in Goa. 
• Mid-2000s saw a boom in construction industry in Goa as well, leading to rise in illegal sand 
extraction being reported. 
• By 1994-96, due to efforts of a Catholic priest, turtle conservation began in Morjim and the 
efforts were reported in the media. 
• In a major event in 2001-02, the coastline in North Goa was seen changing due to grounding 
of the River Princess vessel in Candolim. Coastline erosion also began to be reported in 
newspaper and measures were taken for the first time to prevent sand erosion. 
• In 2002, the Corporation of City of Panaji’s initiative to make Panaji a bin -less city was 
widely reported in the media. The initiative was introduced after drains were found choking 
with plastics. 
• The Goa Bachao Andolan against the new Regional Plan to prevent land-use conversion made 
headlines. 
• Coco beach near Nerul saw massive erosion in 2006, and beach on this stretch nearly 
disappeared within a short period of time. 
• Nearly all media outlets in Goa began reporting rejuvenation of environment post the mining 
ban in 2012. 
• Over the last decade, the rise of social media and alternative media outlets has seen an 
explosion on reporting on environmental issues.

7. Socio-economic aspect- people’s contribution towards the sector and implications on people.  
• The social, cultural, political, and economic circumstances of a group, community, organization, or individual can be described 
using socio-economic elements. Socio-economic aspects can be categorized into several areas, including economic, demographic, 
and social and public services. Numerous facets of social and economic life, such as trade, migration, employment, investing 
behavior, decisions about product uptake, and social mobility, are influenced by social connections. 
Numerous new persons that one might not have otherwise encountered will be met. People from all backgrounds will be introduced 
to and one will get the chance to hear their tales. This makes it possible to obtain fresh insight that will help in both life and work. 
• The media has the potential to be a powerful tool for fostering understanding between the public and authorities as well as for 
providing helpful criticism that advances society. Journalism is a symbol of free expression. It upholds the public's right to free 
speech and the means of disseminating opinions. The world is also connected via journalism. Without journalism, nations would 
exist in isolated bubbles, existing and disappearing within themselves. If there was no journalism, ignorance would flourish. 
• The goal of journalism is to inform the public with current, pertinent information. Our activities have an effect on other people's 
lives, either directly or indirectly, because we live in a global economy. A journalist finds readers for his particular writing style 
while assisting in the assessment of these effects and placing them in the context of people everywhere. Mass media and journalism 
are frequently referred to as sources of truth since they aid in the understanding of the subject at hand and offer reliable news free 
from political prejudice. A journalist's job is to provide the facts, not to trivialize, sensationalize, or fragment themes in order to 
force their opinions on readers.  
 
167 
 
• By influencing public opinion, journalism can promote social change. This is accomplished by providing the general public with 
access to sophisticated information in a comprehensible and straightforward style. This makes it easier for people from different 
social classes to comprehend the problem as a whole and to formulate opinions based on their perceptions of it.

Success stories 
• In February 2023, Uttar Pradesh’s Amethi district’s 35-year-old Mohammad Arif brought home an injured sarus crane he found in his 
village. Arif was booked under a number of wildlife laws for keeping the sarus in his possession without informing the concerned 
authorities. The bird has been shifted to a zoo in Kanpur, Uttar Pradesh.  The duo became famous on social media, and officials came 
knocking. Media took an interview of Mohammad Arif and also tweeted about the bird on social media. Many videos went viral about the 
sarus cranes and Arifs bond.  Through all these awareness on social media the concerned authorities reached out to Arif and rescued the 
bird and shifted it to Zoo.  
• The year 2023 has indeed been special for millets as The United Nations General Assembly at its 75th se ssion in March 2021 declared it 
the International Year of Millets. The International Year of Millets 2023 has surely raised awareness about millets and their nutritional values. 
Advertising and publishing various millets on social media. Awareness among locals through programs and events.   
• Arvind Mishra, of Bihar, formed the Mandar Nature C lub to save the Great Adjutant Stork from near exti nction and created a sa fe 
habitat for the species with the help of locals. 
• Akul Biswas started planting mangrove saplings alon g the banks of the Bidyadhari River in 2005. Locals  came to know about him  
through social media and took notice of his work an d joined his mission. Today, Biswas and over 200 wo men have formed the 
Jharkhali Sabuj Bahini that works towards revival o f mangroves in the Sundarbans. This information is published in papers and  
various platforms of social media. Through this man y locals are aware of it and help him in the same.
