Introduction 
Epidemiology, the study of health and disease patterns in populations 1, plays a crucial role in shaping 
Goa's Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan. This chapter explores how epidemiological insights inform 
our understanding of the intricate relationships between biodiversity, ecosystems, and human health in 
the State. By examining disease emergence, recorded cases by Department of Health Survey, data from 
Integrated Disease Surveillance Program, transmission dynamics, and environmental factors, 
epidemiology provides valuable tools for predicting and mitigating potential health risks associated with 
biodiversity loss and ecosystem changes. This chapters talks about the diseases like Kyasanur Forest 
Disease, Leptospirosis, Climate change related illness and their potential due to changing climate, and 
other such diseases in the State of Goa. This interdisciplinary approach was taken into consideration to 
enable the State Biodiversity Board to develop more comprehensive and effective strategies for 
preserving Goa's rich biodiversity while safeguarding public health. 
 
1. Baseline Study- Primary data and Secondary data compilation and analysis 
• Surveillance of outbreak prone diseases is been carried out by Integrated Disease Surveillance 
Programme (IDSP) as well as NVBDCP under Directorate of Health Services to detect and respond to 
disease outbreaks quickly 
 • Major diseases of public health importance which are linked to Climate and environment: Malaria, 
Dengue, Chikungunya, KFD, Influenza including Covid-19, Leptospirosis, Acute diarrheal diseases etc. 
 • With increasing environmental temperatures and scarcity of potable water cases of Diarrheal disease 
will be on rise this is especially evident in late summer season, also with high temperatures cases of heat 
stroke & exhaustion will rise.  
 • Air Pollution if not controlled will be a problem Goa will face which will increase burden of acute 
respiratory illnesses. 
 • Diseases directly or indirectly linked to open garbage 
Climate change induced diseases prevailed in Goa – 
 
➢ Air Pollution related illnesses

COPD (Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease) has risen to the 4th leading cause of DALY (Disability-
adjusted life years) in Goa with 4% contribution compared to its 2.6% contribution in the 90’s.

- With COVID pandemic, cases of lung involvement are also expected to add to above burden. 
 Asthma is a genetic disease triggered by both extrinsic and intrinsic factors. Cases are expected to rise 
with increase in air pollution levels. 
 
➢ Heat-related illnesses  
With changing climate and increasing rates of deforestation Goa will soon start experiencing heat waves. 
Hence, there will be a need to ramp up Trainings and Surveillance activities in the State of Goa in the  
near future, as well as modify infrastructure of health centres to be able to handle these in the future. 
 
➢ Vector borne diseases  
Vector borne diseases such as Malaria, Dengue, Chikungunya are also identified threat for the state of 
Goa and there is a separate programme called as National Vector Borne Disease Control Programme  
headed by Dr. Kalpana Mahatme and all the preventative and curative measures are followed as per 
national guidelines. As the breeding of mosquitoes is one of the important causative factors for the 
disease, wherein the intersectoral coordination plays a pivotal role in source reduction and disease 
prevention.

 During the year 2019-20, there was a decline in the malaria cases due to following reasons- 
 
173 
 
- Regular Monitoring of Vector Borne Diseases at the highest level, State level Committee for Vector 
Borne Disease meetings under the Chairmanship of Secretary (Health). 
- Screening of Rokhda labourers for early detection and prompt treatment at construction sites. 
- Use of Ultra Low Volume (ULV) & thermal fogging machine by use of Pyrethrum Aquafog and 
Pyrethrum 2% ext. in and around high-risk areas respectively. 
- Regular anti-larval activities by use of Temephos & MLO. 
- The facility for detection of malaria with Rapid Diagnostic kits is extended to all the health centres in 
the state so that immediate results are obtained for treatment of labourers. 
- Information, Education, Communication/Behaviour change Communication measures were taken up at 
all level with the involvement of Local bodies, NGOs and community at large by organizing advocacy, 
Inter-sectoral meetings and other Information, Education and Communication programme. 
The number of malaria cases in the table is showing a steady decrease since 2015 and there have been 
no deaths reported since 2018. The state of Goa is in the Malaria Elimination phase as the API (Annual 
Parasite incidence is the number of positive cases per one thousand population) in both the districts is 
less than one.  
Practices like throwing coconut shells, discarding tyres in open makes the people of the state more 
vulnerable towards these vector diseases as the changing climate is in favour of breeding of the vectors 
such diseases the states need to be prepared for upcoming surge. 
 
➢ Disaster related health issues 
Goa is prone to landslides, and unchecked hill cutting and development make it more vulnerable to them. 
Changing climate is adding to this vulnerability. Fluctuations in rain patterns, an expected increase in 
cyclonic activities in the Arabian Sea, and an expected increase in heat waves are all threats to the health 
of Goans. Hence, there will be a need to ramp up training and surveillance activities in the state of Goa 
in the near future, as well as modify the infrastructure of health centres to be able to handle these 
challenges in the future.

Introduction- 

 
194 
 
The variety and variability of animals, plants and micro-organisms that are used directly or indirectly for food 
and agriculture, including crops, livestock, forestry and fisheries. It comprises the diversity of genetic resources 
(varieties, breeds) and species used for food, fodder, fibre, fuel and pharmaceuticals. It also includes the 
diversity of non-harvested species that support production (soil micro-organisms, predators, pollinators), and 
those in the wider environment that support agro-ecosystems (agricultural, pastoral, forest and aquatic) as well 
as the diversity of the agro-ecosystems.1 
➢ Konkan Goa, being the part of Western Ghat Biodiversity Hotspot, has enormous 
Biodiversity in flora and fauna which encompasses the wealth of Agro-biodiversity 
also.   
➢ Goa State’s Agro-Biodiversity spans across total area of about 3702 square km under 
different topographical situations like Coastal plains including estuaries, Foot hills and 
Hilly terrains.   
➢ Nevertheless, Goa’s Agro-Biodiversity is flourishing under the annual average 
precipitation of about 3000 mm, it is also under the onslaught of natural calamities and 
the threat of excessive anthropogenic activities.   
➢ On one hand, Goa’s Agro-Biodiversity is catering to the needs of the state, while on the 
other hand, it is under the exploitative demographic pressure of 15.3 lakh population 
besides the manifold enormous demographic pressure of dynamic tourists population.   
➢ Though Agro & Allied sector Biodiversity contributes <5 % to the State’s GDP, share 
of Agriculture & allied sector in GVA (Gross Value added) at current prices is Rs 
55,06,000 for 2021-22 and forms a fulcrum for the sustainable Development Goal 
(SDG) for the state. 
 
Current Status:   
• Complete information for the state is not available. Rice germplasm of Goa (Alvares 
2002)2 as cultivated in different locations of the state as given as table 1 
• 28 traditional varieties of rice are documented by ICAR-CCARI and Goa University.   
(Bhonsle & Krishnan, 2011; Manohara et al., 2019)34 
• Jaya and Jyoti are two popular rice varieties in Goa. Some local varieties like Korgut, 
Asgo, Muno, etc are tolerant to salinity. (plate 1)

• Apart from above, minor millets like finger millet or nachni (Elusine coracana) and 
vari millet or little millet (Panicum sumatrense) are also traditionally cultivated. 
Alasando, a bold seeded cowpea, ground nut, sesame are other crops. Wild types of 
pigeon pea, sesame and castor are abundantly seen.  Goa’s cowpea 3 is an improved 
variety of alasando. (plate 2) 
• There are many varieties of horticultural crops including 77 mango (Dhandar et al. 
1997) varieties are reported earlier, local banana varieties like Myndoli (GI 
Registered), Saldatti, Velchi, Amti, Sakri, Savarboni, Rasbali and other crops like 
Karonda, Guava, Tamarind, Ber, Chunna (Zyzipus sp), Kanera, Bimla, Carambola, 
Wax apple, Rose apple, Rambutan etc. (plate 2,3) 
• The plantation crops include cashew (Desai & Singh. 2011), arecanut, coconut 
(Arunachalam & Salgaonkar, 2021)5, chara and species of spices like black pepper, 
nutmeg, kokum, turmeric, ginger etc.   
• Tuber crops like Katekanaga, Greater Yam, Karando, Jhad kanaga, Sweet potato, 
Coclcasia Spp (Alu madi, Dhave alu, Taro bhaji) etc. These are is largely maintained 
and used for domestic consumption as well as livelihood security.   
• Vegetable crops include Brinjal (Local varieties: Agassaim & Taleigaon), Chilli: 
Kholla local, Harmal chilli (Both GI Registered), Okra: Local types : Seven ridged, 
Amaranthus (Thangam & safeena2018). Amaranthus germplasm of goan origin are 
rich in betacyanin.  (Arunachalam et al., 2016, 2022)6 and also useful as nematode 
trapping for management of root knot nematode (Vaingankar et al., 2018)7 
• Short duration medium size and long shelf-life onion variety of goan origin are popular 
•  Sahyadri gourd germplasm of goa is documented (Vasudeo et at. 2023)8

Agro ecosystem of Goa 
1)Awadhis of Madkai 
  
Pictures of mud heaps (Awadhi) in Madkai 
Source- pictures taken by Soniya Gaude, Intern, GSBB 
 
             
Small mounds of mud, evenly distributed across the field, quickly catch the attention of newcomers. These 
mud heaps, known locally as Awadhi, have a history spanning no more than 80-90 years. The use of inputs 
such as cow dung and dry fish manure in large quantities disrupts the water-field level, necessitating the 
removal of excess soil to restore the previous balance. 
One area is irrigated solely through tanks, while the other relies on a nallah. Only on the nallah side, the 
flattened tops of these Awadhis are employed for cultivating vegetables. In the Madkai fields, excess soil is 
gathered in corners and utilized for growing bananas. 
Other noteworthy aspects of these fields include their vulnerability to inundation during the rainy season, 
resulting in the deposition of mud along with various materials like straw, sticks, and stones. 
Crops: banana, vegetable13 (Alvares, 2002) 
2)Khazan 
 
13 Claude Alphonso Alvares, Vidyadhar Gadgil, Goa Foundation, Fish Curry and Rice: A Source Book on Goa, Its Ecology, and Life 
Style  

 
205 
 
  
Khazan Field Khazan Manas (Bund) 
Source – Khazan Society of Goa 
 
Khazan, referring to non-irrigated lands, utilizes gates to keep saline water at bay during the monsoon. Crops 
are cultivated in these areas after the heavy rains have washed away the salinity. However, the cultivation is  
limited to highly salt-tolerant but low-yielding varieties of paddy. 
The term 'Khazan' is commonly used in Konkani in Goa to describe coastal saline soils. These soils are 
prevalent in agro climatic zones No. 11 and 12, along the East and West coasts of India. Similar soils in 
Maharashtra are referred to as 'khar,' 'kharvat,' and 'khazan,' in Karnataka as 'Gazzani,' and in Kerala as 'pokkal' 
and 'Chemeen kattu.' 
To understand the khazan lands of Goa, a comprehensive study is essential, treating them not as individual 
units but as integrated systems specific to each estuarine region, floodplain, and river basin, all of which 
significantly influence their ecology. (Alvares, 2002)14 
 
 
 
 
 
3) Puran farming (Puran Sheti) 
 
14 Claude Alphonso Alvares, Vidyadhar Gadgil, Goa Foundation, Fish Curry and Rice: A Source Book on Goa, Its Ecology, and Life 
Style 

 
206 
 
 
Puran sheti at the banks of Mhadei river 
Source- Tradable Bioresources of Goa 
 
Puran farming, a distinctive agricultural practice, is deeply intertwined with the community life of 
Sattari Taluka, nourished by five rivers. Among these rivers, Mhadei holds a special status as the 'great 
river' or the 'great mother.' As Mhadei flows into the Arabian Sea, it transforms into the Mandovi.  
For centuries, the people have engaged in puran farming, also known as flood farming, along the banks 
of the Mhadei. This unique method, passed down through generations, has effectively alleviated the 
pangs of hunger for the residents. Villages like Velge, Dhamshe, and Guleli serve as examples, 
showcasing their near-total dependence on puran farming for sustenance. (Alvares, 2002) 
The farming technique was under threat of extinction due to land use change, reliance on hybrids, new 
generation seeking new opportunities leading to loss of traditional practices. 
4)Kulagar 
 
Dabhal’s Kulagar plantation 
Source - timesofindia.indiatimes.com15 
 
15 https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/goa/with-mines-in-govt-control-dabhal s-kulagar-plantations-thirst-for-
water/articleshow/100237509.cms 
 

 
207 
 
The Goa and Konkan region of Maharashtra, situated within the Western Ghats, boasts a remarkable 
diversity of flora and fauna. The area's hot-humid climate, coupled with heavy monsoons, designates it 
as a biodiversity hotspot. In this context, local farmers employ a traditional, multitiered homestead 
gardening system known as "kulagar," passed down through generations, to cultivate and conserve 
indigenous crop plants in close proximity to their households. 
The kulagar is an integrated system with areca nut palms serving as a foundational component. Various 
crops, including cash crops, plantation crops, spices, fruits, local vegetables, medicinal and aromatic 
plants, and flower crops, coexist within this system. Some kulagars also incorporate animal components, 
enhancing cost-effectiveness and holism. Noteworthy features of the kulagar include bioresource 
conservation, crop diversification, resource recycling, value addition, processing, and the utilization of 
byproducts.To enhance sustainability and economic viability, the new generation of farmers is 
integrating advanced crop production technologies into the kulagar system, ensuring its continued 
relevance and success.16(Maneesha S R, et.al, 2019)  
5) Kumeri cultivation 
The traditional source of livelihood for many tribal communities in various parts of India involves a 
practice known as kumeri or shifting cultivation. This method, known by different names such as jhum 
cultivation in North India, slash and burn, or swidden agriculture, has been a common and longstanding 
practice. In the context of Goa, this form of shifting cultivation is locally referred to as kumeri cultivation 
or kaamat in Konkani.17 (PriyankaVelip,2016)

Capacity building of owners of Goan Agro biodiversity 
1) Training on grafting mango 
Conducting training for grafting mangoes in Goa is imperative for several reasons. Firstly, it enhances 
productivity by allowing farmers to combine favorable traits from different varieties, resulting in improved 
yield and fruit quality. Additionally, training promotes disease resistance, market competitiveness, 
biodiversity conservation, skill development, and community collaboration, collectively contributing to the 
overall sustainability and economic viability of mango cultivation in the region. 
2)  Training on seed production of vegetables 
Organizing training on seed production of vegetables in Goa serves as a strategic initiative for various 
compelling reasons. Firstly, it empowers local farmers with the knowledge and skills needed to produce 
high-quality vegetable seeds, ensuring self-sufficiency and reducing dependency on external sources. This 
training fosters agricultural sustainability by promoting the use of locally adapted seed varieties, enhancing 
crop resilience to regional conditions. Moreover, it contributes to economic viability as farmers gain the 
ability to produce seeds for commercial purposes, creating opportunities for income generation and 
strengthening the overall resilience of the agricultural community in Goa. 
 
3)  Training on nursery management  
Conducting training on nursery management in Goa is pivotal for several reasons. Firstly, it equips farmers 
with essential skills for proficient seedling cultivation, ensuring a reliable and healthy supply of plants for 
subsequent transplanting. Effective nursery management contributes to crop uniformity, improved yield, 
and enhanced resilience to environmental stressors. Additionally, this training empowers farmers to engage 
in sustainable agricultural practices by promoting resource-efficient techniques such as water conservation 
and optimized nutrient use. By enhancing nursery management capabilities, the training supports the 
overall agricultural productivity and environmental management in the region. 
4) Training on air layering  
Implementing training on air layering in Goa holds significant benefits for local agriculture. Air layering 
is a propagation technique that allows for the cloning of plants with desirable traits, offering advantages 
such as quicker maturity and enhanced yield. By providing farmers with expertise in air layering, the 
training facilitates the propagation of high-quality plants, contributing to improved crop varieties and 
increased productivity. Moreover, air layering is a cost-effective method, reducing the need for excessive 
plant material and promoting sustainable agricultural practices. This training not only empowers farmers 
with a valuable horticultural skill but also enhances their capacity for efficient plant propagation, ultimately 
boosting agricultural resilience and success in the Goa region.

7. Socio-economic aspect- people’s contribution towards the sector and implications on people  
1. Local public plays a vital role in in-situ conservation of agrobiodiversity for sustainable utilization. 
2. Agricultural feasts (harvest feasts) should be given great importance. 
3. The public should be encouraged to take up agriculture as a profession. 
4. Agrotourism can be increased through Kulagar systems and farms. 
5. Preparation of wild plant-based products can provide employment opportunities. 
6. The 'Plant Utsav' annual show provides a marketing platform for plant sellers. 
7. Promotion of millet cultivation through events like 'Nachneachem Fest' can revive traditional crops. 
8. Wild vegetable cultivation can generate livelihoods, promoted through events like Raan bhaji 
festivals. 
9. The Beejamitra scheme can help farmers generate livelihoods via community seed banks. 
10. Myndoli Banana cultivation and product development can generate employment for village people. 
11. Feni production and its medicinal uses can be promoted as an important local product. 
12. Promotion of local varieties of rice, such as Korgut and Assgo, can help preserve traditional crops 
while providing economic opportunities for farmers. 
13. Development of value-added products from local fruits like cashew, kokum, and jackfruit can create 
new income streams for rural communities. For the same projects like GoVan should be promoted. 
14. Establishment of farmers' markets focusing on local agrobiodiversity can improve direct farmer-
consumer connections and boost local economies. 
15. Incentivizing organic farming practices can help preserve agrobiodiversity while potentially fetching 
premium prices for farmers. 
16. Developing ecotourism around unique local crops and farming practices can provide additional 
income for rural communities. 
17. Creating cooperatives for processing and marketing local agrobiodiversity products can strengthen 
the economic position of small-scale farmers. 
18. Integrating local agrobiodiversity into school meal programs can create a stable market for farmers 
while improving nutrition for children. 
19. Promoting beekeeping with native bee species can support pollination of local crops while providing 
additional income through honey production. 
20. Encouraging home gardens with diverse local varieties can improve household food security and 
nutrition. 
21. Developing geographical indications (GIs) for unique local varieties can add value to traditional crops 
and protect farmers' interests.

Success Stories 
• Agriculturists of Goa: Shri Sanjay Anant Patil : Inovative Kulagar farmer of Goa. An innovative 
farmer from Goa has been given the innovative farmers award 2023 by the ICAR, for his outstanding 
contributions to Natural farming and zero energy micro irrigation system.  
• Shri. Shekhar Parashtekar from pernem won Fr. Inacio Almeida Organic farming award. As he 
uses vermicompost and vermiwash to maintain soil health and manage effective biomass.   
• Shri. Rajat Prabhu a farmer from ponda was awarded the Krishi Ratna awarded for his integrated 
farming system model with excellent diversity of fruits, vegetables, livestock, and value addition 
products.   
• The Krishi Vibhushan was shared by Shri.Rajendra Dessai from Dharbandora, and Shri. Gaspar 
Fernandes from Anjuna. Shri. Rajendra Dessai practices year-round vegetable production with 
modern scientific practices such as mulching, drip irrigation and trailing. Fernandes has adopted 
mechanised paddy cultivation and even provides custom service to other farmers with the help of 
his tractors and power tillers.  
• Shri. Sanjay Rane from Bicholim won the Krishi Vibhushan for creating employment opportunities 
in Agriculture for many others with his enterprising skills.   
• Dr. John Fernandez, an ex-scientist with the National Institute of Oceanography (NIO) purchased 
his 3.6-hectare Khazan Land in 2000. In his land, John has started a few experiments that has yielded 
him with bumper harvests and more importantly, knowledge. Since he was with NIO, he had heard 
about institutes like TERI (The Energy Research Institute), ICAR (Indian Council of Agricultural 
Research) and Local Farmer Clubs. These were places where he picked up the scientific approach 
to getting better yields. In addition to this, he also went about visiting the village elders and would 
inquisitively ask about traditional methods of farming and the logic behind several practices.  
 
221 
 
• Mrs. Uma Prabhudesai she is an Agriculture Graduate who turned into an entrepreneur and started 
Jaggery production along with her father. She has trained her brother and many other people from 
her village. Uma managed to make jaggery in three forms – powder, candy and block. 
• Mrs. Junku Pereira  is from Thivim, Pedne Taluka, North Goa, Goa. Mrs. Junku Pereira is 
progressive woman goat farmer maintaining twenty-seven Osmanabadi goats at her goat farm in 
Thivim village, Pernem Taluka of North Goa. Before starting of the Osmanabadi goat farm, she had 
undergone five days training on “Scientific Goat Farming” at ICAR – KVK North Goa. During the 
training KVK had arranged lectures on scientific housing, feeding, breeding and health care 
management and one exposure visit to one goat farm near Dharbandoda, South Goa. Mrs Junku got 
all the information regarding goat farming and marketing of the goats from this training. She 
purchased 15 female and five male Osmanabadi goats from Latur District of Maharashtra which is 
a home tract of Osmanabadi goats in December 2019. Before that she constructed low cost raised 
platform goat shed by using locally available resources like coconut flanksforslatted floor. She also, 
planted CO-5 perennial fodder in half acre and started hydrophonic unit producing 60-100 kilo 
hydroponics green fodder per day to solve the problem of green fodder. In addition to this she is also 
buying goat feed ingredients and dry fodder from the market. To make goat farming more profitable 
she is drying goat manure and packing in one kilo plastic pouches and selling to nearby apartments 
in the same town. She is also cultivating her own organic vegetables using some goat manure. This 
in turn saved money as she was not buying vegetable from market. She practiced all the scientific 
practices of goat farming i.e. feeding, breeding, housing, health care management and marketing 
(selling her goats on the basis of body weight with a premium rate). 
 
Good practice example from other states  
• Ram Saran Verma is the Indian most affluent farmer who brings advanced and more profitable 
farming techniques. Moreover, he is the only farmer who brings these techniques to small Indian 
farmers and rural villages in his state. Ram Saran Verma has been felicitated by several Indian 
farming awards for his work. He started farming in 1990 with 5 acres of land. His constant efforts 
and modern farming techniques made him successful. Now, he has approx. 200 acres of agricultural 
land. He use his 100 acres of land for banana plantations and 100 acres for tomatoes and potatoes. 
His farming techniques have been considered and replicated across his state.  
• Ramesh Chaudhary, a farmer living in Jaipur in Rajasthan, also has his status. He is the owner of 
three Greestein Polyhouses and one Green House in Jaipur. He cultivates tomato, cucumber in a 
polyhouse and floriculture in the greenhouse. Apart from this, he cultivates maize in the open field. 
From all these, Ramesh earns a quarter of two crore rupees a year. He also has many expensive cars 
and luxurious bungalows. In these bungalows, he also parks his buffaloes along with the cars. 
• Harish Dhandev, a prosperous farmer. He also left his government job to start Aloe Vera farming in 
Rajasthan. After that, he decided to work on his ancestral land in Jaisalmer. Harish’s starting 80,000 
trees quickly grew in number to seven lakh within six months. Next, Harish headed to get ten clients 
for his Aloe Vera stock within Rajasthan itself. But soon realized that they were selling the removed 
pulp at much higher prices. So he trained his labourers to remove the pulp, giving them all some 
extra income. After many years, Harish has bought more land and currently grows Aloe Vera over 
hundred acres. In addition, he runs his company, Dhandev Global Group, located in Dhaisar, 45 
kilometres from Jaisalmer in Rajasthan. And currently, his turnover ranges between Rs. 1.5 to 2 
crores. 
• Rajiv Bittu, full-time farmer also. According to him, he makes more revenue from farming than his 
chartered accountancy firm. At first he took some land for lease in Kuchu village, 32 km far away 
from Ranchi. Sometimes he did not arrange the funds to pay rent for the land. So, he offered the 
 
222 
 
landlord 1/3rd production of the produce he grew. And thus, his journey into agriculture began. He 
used the latest technologies, like drip irrigation and mulching, to get maximum production at his 
farm. In Mid-2014, Rajeev had a good production of watermelon and muskmelon. But the profit was 
not as satisfactory as his investment. So he decided to divide the land into small sections and evaluate 
his investment and the profit earned from each part. Rajeev Bittu has acquired 32 acres of the farm 
on lease and grows brinjal, cucumber, watermelon and many vegetables. He earns a profit of around 
Rs 15 lakh to 16 lakh every year. 
• Vishwanath Bobade, a farmer from Bahirwadi, Maharashtra, the drought-prone Beed district. He 
has earned Rs 7 lakh from farming by just one acre of land. He decided to try multi-cropping and 
estimated that he could increase his crop by forming a wire fence and planting creepers and climbers 
on them. Vishwanath also fixed a pipeline by his first-year profits to water his plants. He has also 
chosen many farming methods like raised-bed farming and mulching, which has proved very 
beneficial. He takes the help of only two labourers at his farm. However, he and his wife worked the 
entire 24×7 to take care of the plants. Hence the cost of the return is less, giving them better profits.

Introduction – 
 
The Marine and Freshwater Fisheries & Biodiversity subcommittee is a crucial component of Goa's 
State Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan, given the state's rich aquatic heritage along its coastline 
and river systems. This subcommittee focuses on preserving and managing Goa's diverse aquatic 
ecosystems while ensuring sustainable fishing practices that balance ecological conservation with 
local livelihoods. In the face of growing challenges like climate change, pollution, and overfishing, 
the subcommittee's integration into the state's biodiversity strategy is essential for maintaining both 
environmental sustainability and the socio-economic wellbeing of Goa's fishing communities. 
 
Flora (341 species / taxa): 177 plants, 49 green algae, 47 brown algae, and 68 red algae 
Fauna (763 species / taxa): 18 cnidarians, 144 crustaceans, 156 molluscs, 16 echinoderms, 18 
elasmobranchs, 389 teleost, 7 reptiles, and 15 mammals

20. Mangrove covers in Goa 
 
 
Figure 1: Distribution of Mangrove habitats in the state of Goa 
Source - Nagi, H. M., Rodrigues, R. S., ManiMurali, R., & Jagtap, T. G. (2014). Using remote 
sensing and GIS techniques for detecting land cover changes of mangrove habitats in Goa, India. 
 
Goa houses 16 mangrove species and many associates such as Acrostichum aureum. Chorao 
Island in Mandovi river is home to most of the species found in Goa. 
 
  
Bruguiera gymnorrhiza Kandelia candel 

 
278 
 
 
  
Acanthus illicifolius Avicennia officinalis 
 
  
Excoecaria agallocha Rhizophora mucronata 
 
  
Species wise description of mangroves found in Goa 
  
• Rhizophora mucronata: Moderate-sized tree with rough bark, elliptic leaves, and yellowish-white 
flowers. Radicle 15-40 cm long. Flowers Dec-June.  
• Rhizophora apiculata: Similar to R. mucronata but with lanceolate leaves and white flowers. Radicle 
up to 30 cm. Flowers Dec-May.  
• Bruguiera gymnorrhiza: Tall tree (up to 30m) with buttressed stem. Red calyx, 15-20 cm radicle. 
Flowers Nov-Apr.  
• Bruguiera cylindrica: Medium to tall tree with smooth bark. White to greenish flowers, 10-15 cm 
radicle. Flowers Nov-Apr.  
• Ceriops tagal: Small tree or shrub (1-2m) with buttress and lenticels. White flowers. Localized to 
Terekhol river. Flowers Jan-Apr.  
• Kandelia candel: Small tree (5-6m) with reddish bark. White flowers, 30-40 cm radicle. Flowers twice 
yearly.  
• Avicennia officinalis: Tree with smooth bark, silvery leaves. Yellow flowers. Flowers Mar-Aug.  
• Avicennia marina: "White mangrove" with white bark. Yellow or white flowers. Flowers Mar-Aug.  

 
279 
 
• Sonneratia alba: Moderate-sized tree with orange-brown bark. White or pale green flowers. Flowers 
twice yearly.  
• Acrostichum aureum: Erect fern up to 1.5m high with pinnate leaves.  
• Sonneratia caseolaris : Moderate-sized tree with rose-tinged flowers. Found in low salinity areas. 
Flowers twice yearly.  
• Aegiceras corniculatum: Small shrubby tree with white umbel flowers. Flowers Feb-Apr.  
• Excoecaria agallocha: Tree up to 5m with poisonous latex. Dioecious flowers in catkins.  
• Acanthus illicifolius: Shrub up to 2m with spiny leaves and light blue to violet flowers. Flowers Feb-
Apr.  
• Lumnitzera racemosa: Small tree up to 10m with knee-shaped pneumatophores and white flowers. 
Flowers Mar-Sep.  
• Derris heterophylla: Evergreen climber with compound leaves. Flowers Jun-Dec.1

❖ Traditional Knowledge associated with Marine Biodiversity 
1. Shravan celebration in Goa –  
The fifth month of the calendar is Shravana, which is celebrated religiously by the Hindu 
population in the state, who visit temples and abstain from non-vegetarian eating. As the fifth 
month in the Hindu calendar is considered the holiest, with many auspicious days throughout, 
people eat more vegetables, which are abundant during those months. Since fish are breeding 
during these months, fishing activities also drastically decrease, giving fish more time to breed and 
multiply. 
 
2. Mugger pooja in Goa - 
The Mannge Thapni ritual is a distinctive tradition observed by farmers and fishermen along Goa's 
Cumbarjua canal and Zuari river. During this ceremony, participants craft a crocodile statue from 
mud, which they then worship by offering flowers and coconuts. This practice is rooted in the 
belief that it safeguards fishermen from crocodile attacks while emphasizing the importance of 
coexistence between humans and wildlife. The ritual serves to foster respect for the local 
ecosystem, indirectly supporting crocodile conservation efforts. It also plays a role in preserving 
traditional ecological knowledge and serves as a reminder of the delicate balance in nature. Mannge 
Thapni exemplifies how cultural practices can complement modern conservation goals, 
particularly in areas where human activities intersect with wildlife habitats.

❖ practice example from other states / Interesting discoveries/ did you know facts or any other interesting piece related to the sector 
 
Establishing Sustainable Clam Fishing in Ashtamudi Lake 
Situated in the Kollam district, Ashtamudi Lake is the second largest lake estuary of Kerala. Spread over an are of nearly 6,140 ha, 
it remains connected to Arabian Sea throughout the year. Kallada river empties into it and is the main source of its fresh water. 
About 173 ha area near the bar mouth is clam fishing area. Introduction of processing expanded the market of these clams for export 
to countries like Vietnam, Thailand and Malaysia. The result was intensification of fisheries. The catch rose to the p eak of 10,000 
tonnes of 1991. But then, declined 
to 5000 tonnes in 1993, mainly because of unregulated fishing. This created a demand from fishermen for action against 
indiscriminate fishing, particularly organised mechanical dredging, especially during spawning seasons. Spawning of clams 
commences by December and lasts till February. Clam beds have abundant young clams from January to March. Based on its 
 
293 
 
studies on the fishery and biology of short-neck clam of Ashtamudi Lake undertaken since the late nineteen seventies, CMFRI in 
association with local fisheries introduced the 
following regulations: 
• A closed season from October to January, 
• Mesh size restrictions for nets used in fishing, 
• A minimum export size of 1400 clam meats per kg, and 
• Mechanical Clam fishing methods prohibited. 
Clam fishery has since sustained landings of around 10,000 tonnes per year in the last decade, with relatively stable CPUE over the 
same period. The Ashtamudi estuary short-necked clam fishery has been certified Marine Stewardship Council (MSC) standards 
compliant since 5th November 2014. Its Certificate Code 
is F-ACO-0055. Receipt of MSC has constantly encouraged streamlining of practices. For example: 
• Minimum Legal Size (MLS) of 20mm shell length was introduced in July 2015 on the basis of the stock and the catch size 
composition. 
• Opening area for fishery for 2016 season was delayed until 1 March at the request of the fishermen, to allow time for the clams to 
grow in the early part of the year. 
• Fishery is now open for five rather than six days per week. Weekend closure was introduced in response to the change in sto ck 
distribution and decline in biomass observed during 2015. 
In response to the southward movement of stock distribution, a new management area was established during the 2015 fishing 
season. This has remained in place during 2016 and 2017. 
 
Case Study: Mainstreaming coastal and marine biodiversity conservation into production sectors in Sindhdurg coast 
In the fishing district of Sindhudurg in the state of Maharashtra, the lives of thousands of people are inextricably linked with the 
sea for sustenance and livelihood. A pilot project co-funded by GEF, Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Cha nge and 
UNDP (2012-2017) was taken up in Sindhudurg maintaining the livelihood-ecosystem balance with the aim of mainstreaming 
biodiversity conservation in production sectors. 
Outcomes of the project include: 
(i) 100 % adoption of CIFT developed by-catch removing square mesh nets by fishers. 
(ii) Mangrove eco-tourism through Self-Help Group of women. 
Sindhudurg was declared a ‘tourism district’ in 1997. The recorded number of visitors to the Sindhudurg fort grew from 100,00 0 
to 700,000 between 2006 and 2010. Tourists are attracted by the many cultural sites (notably the forts), the beautiful beaches, the 
cruises, the backwaters and snorkelling/diving.  
(iii) On pilot basis, mud crab-farming model on private lands by fisher women and men for which 28.5 acres of land in 15 villages 
has been used and 149 beneficiaries trained. 
(iv) Oyster and mussel (bivalve) farming as alternative livelihood option for fishing communities. 
 
294 
 
(v) System of Rice Intensification (SRI) comprising set of practices for plant, soil, water and nutrient management to revive native 
species of rice that fetches higher price than the hybrid varieties. 
(vi) Cleaning of the seabed of debris such as ghost nets and marine waste through the newly trained scuba divers including women 
divers. 
(vii) Effective behavioural change making people not to dump litter or waste in the sea. 
An expedition of living marine resources in Angria Bank has identified 160 species including 153 coral species, 18 fish species, 9 
seaweed species and 9 echinoderms. 
The State Government of Maharashtra has established Mangrove and Coastal and Marine Biodiversity Conservation Foundation 
for long term sustainability and for expanding the project approach to the rest of the 
coastal areas in the state.

Scope of Sub-committee: The sub-committee covers a wide range of topics, related to 
the plant diversity including medicinal plants. The objective of the study is to 
understand the status of plant diversity and vegetation, threats and measures to conserve 
them. This committee deliberated on the baseline data on flora, medicinal plants, 
threats, current status, suggested actions, invasive species, current policies and schemes 
of different departments for identified areas of priority, strategy and action, and People’s 
contribution towards the sector and conservation.  
 
Current scenario for the State of Goa 
Flora general 
 
• Post liberation, the first work to be published on the plants of Goa was by Vartak (1966). 
This work included plants from adjacent Maharashtra and Karnataka. A later work of 
the Botanical Survey of India (1985-86) published in two volumes for Goa, Diu, 
Daman, Dadra and Nagarhaveli recorded about 1115 species for Goa alone. 
• A subsequent work (Naithani et al. 1997) titled Forest Flora of Goa, dealt with 494 taxa, 
predominantly trees and shrubs. Datar and Lakshminarasimhan (2013) of the Botanical 
Survey of India published ‘Flora of Bhagawan Mahavir (Molem) National Park and 
Adjoinings’. They reported 721 species of flowering plants under 490 genera and 119 
families.  
• A project report was submitted by Janarthanam et al. (1999) from Goa University to the 
Goa State Council for Science and Technology, Government of Goa (August 1999). 
According to the study, 1741 specimens were collected from Goa, mainly outside the 
forest areas. These specimens are available at Goa University Herbarium. They have 
reported 1305 wild plant species in the study, including 283 species not reported 
previously from Goa. Four hundred and two species of them have been identified as 
economically important species. 
• Pteridophytes (including ferns) were generally not in focus. However, Datar and 
Lakshminarasimhan (2010) reported 47 Pteridophytes in 32 genera under 20 families. 
Benniamin (2023) reported 69 species of ferns and seven species of fern allies under 42 
genera for Goa. Dominant families recorded from Goa are Pteridaceae (15 species), 
 
297 
 
Thelypteridaceae (11 species), Dryopteridaceae (7 species) and Polypodiaceae (6 
species). 
• Works on Bryophytes are meagre. Phatak et al (2007) brought out a preliminary account 
of bryophytes of Goa. However, several documentation studies on smaller areas and 
groups have been carried out, especially by the students of Goa University.  These have 
not come to public domain.   
• Kerkar and Madkaikar (2003) reported 46 species (under 23 genera and 7 families) of 
freshwater blue green algae from Goa. Kerkar (2009) reported 44 species of (26 genera 
14 families) green algae from Goa. However, Bongale (1981) was the first one to report 
algae for the first time from Goa from Panjim paddy fields. Gaunker and Kerkar (2004) 
recorded algal diversity of two temple ponds from North Goa wherein they reported 41 
species of Chlorophyta and 12 species of Cyanophyta. Kanolkar and Kerkar (2009) 
reported 96 species of freshwater green algae from Parsem of Pernem taluka, Goa. 
Shetiya and Kerkar (2004) reported 30 species of green algae and 16 species of blue-
green algae from the paddy fields of Tiswadi taluka of Goa. Prabhudessai et al. (2019) 
worked on phytoplanktons and reported 25 species of green algae and three species of 
blue-green algae from Chapora and Sal estuaries. D'Souza e Gomes et al. (2011) 
recorded 90 species of blue green algae from paddy fields of different habitats. 
Tetraselmis indica, a new species from Chlorodendrophyceae was described from salt 
pans of Goa (Arora et al. 2013). 
• Untawale and Dhargalkar (1975), for the first time reported the Seaweed resources of 
Goa. Agadi and Untawale (1978) reported 50 marine algal species from Goa coast of 
which 28 species were reported for the first time. Agadi (1983) also worked on. 
intertidal ecology of marine algae along Anjuna coast of Goa. Pednekar et al. (2012) 
recorded Harmful Algal Species from Goa and recorded a total of 54 of them from 
Mandovi and 46 from Zuari estuaries. Al Usmani and Ansari  (2020) compiled 
information on marine and coastal Biodiversity of Goa and reported 145 Marine Algae, 
15 Mangrove species, 106 species of sand dune vegetation, 2 sea grasses, 96 
phytoplanktons and 78 marine fungi. 
• With National Institute of Oceanography and Goa University and its affiliated colleges 
in Goa, several works on algae (freshwater and marine) have been carried out. Most of 
them are available in the form of dissertations and reports. Huge efforts are required to 
compile this information. 
 
Endemic flora 
• The occurrence of 113 endemic plants was reported by Joshi and Janarthanam (2004) 
from the Western Ghats of Goa based on actual fieldwork. Based on the herbarium 
records and literature, they have not considered several plants as endemics to the 
Western Ghats any more. They have identified strict endemics of the Western Ghats in 
Goa and found that most of these herbaceous endemics are on lateritic outcrops 
(plateaus), and most are habitat-specific and do not grow outside lateritic plateaus. 
Datar and Lakshminarasimhan (2011) recorded 127 endemic plants in Bhagwan 
Mahaveer National Park. These endemic Plants were distributed in various habitats, 
such as Plateaus, evergreen forests, semi-evergreen forests and moist deciduous forests. 
Singh (2016) reported 357 endemic taxa of flowering plants of Western Ghats from 
 
298 
 
Goa, with eight strictly endemic to the state. However, this work is based on literature 
without applying any further filters.  
 
Three red-listed tree species, viz. Myristica fatua Houtt. var. magnifica, Syzygium 
travancoricum and Semecarpus kathalekanensis were reported by Prabhugaonkar et al. 
(2014) from the freshwater swamps of Goa. Benniamin (2023)  reported Osmunda 
hilsenbergii, Bolbitis feeiana, Bolbitis semicordata, Bolbitis beddomei as endemic 
Pteridophytes to Goa.  
 
New taxa 
 In the last three decades, several new species have been described from Goa. It 
shows that more studies are required to document the plant wealth of Goa completely. 
All of them are endemic and except one all others are confined to lateritic outcrops, and 
these habitats are disappearing fast due to various developmental activities. Some of 
the species are: 
• Glyphochloa henryi (Janarthanam et al., 2000) 
• Glyphochloa veldkampii (Fonseca & Janarthanam, 2003) 
•  Ischaemum yadavii (Poaceae) (Gad & Janarthanam, 2007) 
• Dimeria veldkampii (Poaceae) (Kiran Raj & Sivadasan, 2008) 
• Dipcadi goaense (Hyacinthaceae) (Prabhugaonkar et al., 2009) 
• Cuscuta janarthanamii (Convolvulaceae) (Kolte et al., 2019) 
• Ischaemum janarthanamii (Poaceae) (Bokil et al., 2020) 
• Canscora shrirangiana (Gentianaceae) (Kolte et al., 2018) 
• Sonerila konkanensis (Melastomataceae) (Resmi et al., 2021) 
• Eriocaulon goaense (Eriocaulaceae) (Kolte et al., 2022) 
 
Group-specific and habitat-specific works 
Jalal (2022) brought out a book on The Wild Orchids of Goa that dealt with 67 species, 
including few which were not reported from Goa. Out of these, 23 are endemic to the 
Western Ghats. It is also shown using the MaxEnt algorithm that the species richness 
of orchids is very high in the Western Ghats belt. Several Goa University students have 
worked on different groups, primarily for their postgraduate degree dissertations, which 
are mostly untraceable. Gad (2007), in her thesis on grasses for Goa, recorded 155 
species and five varieties. This includes new additions to Goa (55 species). These 
results were never published and attempts must be made to publish these works. 
 
Mangroves occupied a specific place and have been in focus among the habitats. Salim 
Ali Bird Sanctuary which is basically a mangrove habitat, its proximity to the capital 
city, importance in sustaining livelihood of locals and generally their role in lessening 
the effects of storms is probably some of the reasons for this special focus. Several 
documentations, both scientific as well as popular books with colour photographs, have 
come out. Wafer and Untawale (2000) have even come out with a book in Marathi 
language for spreading awareness among the public. 
 
 
 
 
299 
 
Current Status:  
Information on plants, plant diversity and vegetation are available in bits and pieces. 
There is no single source where the plant wealth of Goa could be referred to. Though 
there are comprehensive accounts on Pteridophytes as a group, Orchidaceae as a family 
and Mangroves as a habitat are available, for the whole of the state a Flora of 
angiosperms is still wanted. When we refer to information it includes the preserved 
specimens in the form of herbarium on the basis of which the descriptions were written 
or their presence is reported. Very often than not, these accounts do not refer to the 
herbarium specimens but only photographs are printed. Either herbarium is not made 
or not available in Goa. When it comes to lower groups of plants such as Bryophytes, 
the information is very scant.  
The majority of our forests are under protected areas such as Wildlife sanctuaries or 
National Park. But for the Bhagwan Mahaveer National Park and Mollem Wildlife 
Sanctuary, the flora is not worked out. Obtaining permission to enter the sanctuaries, 
logistics of travelling within the sanctuaries and lack of funding are probably the 
reasons for the absence of studies. 
The plateau vegetation and private holdings outside the protected area are under great 
threat. Developmental activities, including road constructions, the establishment of new 
settlements and the expansion of industrial estates, are some of the well-known 
causative factors. Flora outside Protected Areas, especially that of plateaus, is under 
great threat. When an area is degraded, the first ones to establish are invasive weeds. 
These species are eliminating native species from their original habitat.  
Barring a few efforts, no new attempts are made to bring wild edible/useful species 
under cultivation. 
• Tree plantation in open areas such as plateaus (greening) is a direct threat to herbaceous 
species, especially endemic ephemerals. 
• Disconnection between people and plants is increasing the threat. 
• Baseline phenology data not available for climate change studies. 
• Floral biodiversity of Goa is vast and more primary research is needed and to be 
encouraged and funded.

• Floral Biodiversity of Goa  
 
Ramachandra et al(year), reported that Goa’s flora is diverse with a total of 1041 species 
belonging to 494 genera and 151 families. Dominant family was Fabaceae with 124 
species followed by Poaceae with 60 species, Malvaceae with 51 species. The flora of 
Goa is notable for its high variety of species having as estimated 2000 to 3000 plant 
species. About 390 tree species were found in the floral diversity along with 595 shrubs 
and herbs and 56 species of lianas.  
 
 
• Medicinal plants of Goa 
i.A survey was conducted by Radhika, K. P., & Rodrigues, B. F. (2010) to study 
Arbuscular mycorrhiza on 36 medicinal plants under 25 families at North and South 
Goa of Western Ghats. A total of 30 medicinal plant species were found to be 
mycorrhizal and six plant species showed absence of Arbuscular Mycorrhizal (AM) 
fungal colonization. Glomus was found to be the most dominant genera and  Glomus 
fasciculatum the most dominant AM fungal species. 
 
 
ii. A Case study on Medicinal Plants-An Integral part of Goan rituals of Goa was carried 
out by Ananth Nag, B. (2016). Hindu Goans use ethno medicinal plants very 
interestingly for the treatment of dysentery, boils, cough and cold, typhoid, kidney 
stones, fever, body ache, toothache, headache, rheumatism, asthma, skin disease etc. 
The rare medicinal plants are given religious importance by the ancestors and the same 
knowledge is passed orally from generation to generation. No proper documentation is 
being done till the date. To draw the attention of plant workers and pharmacologists 
research scholars for further scientific research in this specific topic this paper was 
published.3

• Mangroves and associates of Goa 
 
1. Rhizophora mucronata: 
It is a moderate sized tree, much branched, very rough bark, leaves elliptic, broad, 
opposite, pale beneath with black dots, flowers yellowish white, four petals, radicle 
slender, elongated, 15 to 40 centimeter s. long, flowering & fruiting takes place in 
between December to Mid-June. Locally known as Kandal, it is available in plenty in 
the high salinity areas in all the estuaries. 
  
2. Rhizophora apiculata: 
It is a moderate sized much branched tree with rough bark, leaves elliptic, lanceolate, 
dark green above, base tapering, pink petioled, clustered towards end of branches, 
infloroscence 3-4 times forked, 4-8 flowered, flowers white, radicle thick, short and 
cylindrical, upto 30 cms. in length. Flowering and fruiting takes place in between 
December to May. It is seen mainly in between R. mucronata trees, which is dominant 
species. The species is found occasionally here and there and its total occurrence is 
quite less in Goa. 
  
3. Bruguiera gymnorrhiza: 
It is a straight stemmed, buttressed tall tree, up to 30m. in height, dark colored, fissured 
bark, leaves elliptic, pointed, pale beneath, crowded at branchlet end, flowers solitary, 
petals bifid with hairs at the base, calyx red to bright red, radicle 15-20 centimeters. 
long, faintly ribbed, alike ladyfinger. Flowering and fruiting takes place in between 
November to April. It is found in low salinity areas and can be seen in the interior areas 
of the State. The tree has a conical shape and is seen mainly in Zuari & Chapora rivers. 
  
4. Bruguiera cylindrica: 
It is a medium to tall buttressed tree with smooth grey bark, leaves oblanceolate, thin, 
elliptic, flowers white to greenish, radicle 10-15 cms., short. Flowering and fruiting 
takes place in between the months of November to April. The species is observed in 
most of the river estuaries of the State and smaller size trees only are seen. It does not 
form a colony and is seen scattered here and there. 
  
5. Ceriops tagal: 
It is a small, 1to 2 m. tall straight stemmed tree or shrub forming buttress. Stem has lot 
of lenticels, leaves simple, opposite narrowed downwards, collected at branchlet end, 
flowers white, small and in cyma inflorescences. The species is localized to Terekhol 
river only and also planted in Chapora river. Flowering and fruiting take place in 
between January to April. 
  
6. Kandelia candel (K. rheedi): 
It is a small, 5-6 tall tree with smooth reddish bark, leaves dark green, polished above, 
shortly petioled, elliptic, flowers white, radicle 30-40 cm. long and slender. Distributed 
in all estuaries of Goa. Flowering and fruiting take place two times in a year, 
prominently from December to April and also from September to December. 
  
 
314 
 
7. Avicennia officinalis: 
A tree with smooth yellowish grey bark, low branching, leaves very fine, silvery white, 
tomentose beneath. Flowers yellow, collected in small clusters, capsule velvety, 
compressed, obvate and pointed. It is found in all estuaries and make colonies. Profuse 
seedings & regeneration is observed. Flowering & fruiting takes place in between 
March to August. 
  
8. Avicennia marina: 
It is known as “White mangrove” due to its white bark, leaves opposite, shortly petioled, 
glossy green on upper side & dull grey or silvery white tomentose hair on lower side, 
flowers yellow or white, fruit a compressed capsule. Found in all estuaries and make 
colonies. Flowering & fruiting takes place in between March to August. Profuse 
seedings & regeneration is observed. 
  
9. Sonneratia alba: 
It is much branched moderate size tree, bark orange brown / grey, branches silvery grey, 
swollen, leaves leathery, opposite, elliptic, thickened, flowers solitary or in threes, 
white, pale green, fruit about 3 centimeters. dome shaped. It is available in plenty in 
higher salinity areas. Profuse regeneration forming pure patches is observed. Flowering 
and fruiting take place twice in a year, from January to April and September to 
December. 
  
10. Acrostichum aureum: 
It is erect fern, attaining height upto 1.5m having small bushy appearance, fibrous 
typical fern like roots but without any aerial roots. Pinnate leaves with a terminal leaflet. 
  
11. Sonneratia caseolaris: 
It is a moderate sized tree, brown rough bark, leaves 5-10 cms. long, broadly obvate, 
flowers tinged with rose colour, fruit fleshy, cushion shaped. It is found in low salinity 
areas, on the higher reaches of the rivers. Flowering and fruiting takes place twice in a 
year, from January to April and September to December. Fine patches showing 
excellent growth are seen at many places, particularly along Zuari river, in Khazan land 
in Borim and Shiroda. 
  
12. Aegiceras corniculatum: 
It is a small shrubby tree, bark brown with reddish tinge, leaves alternate, elliptic, 
flowers white, in umbels, fruit cylindrical, curved, very small. Available in plenty in 
low salinity areas. Flowering and fruiting take place in between February to April. 
  
13. Excoecaria agallocha: 
It is a much-branched tree, upto 5 m high. Bark greyish, leaves pale green, alternate, 
elliptic, produce latex which is poisonous & dangerous to eyes. Flowers dioecious, 
arranged in sessile axillary catkins. Male and female plants found separately with 
distinct characters. Found in all the estuaries and is a common species in Goa. 
  
14. Acanthus illici folius:  
 
315 
 
It is a shrub, upto 2 m high, aerial root formation is seen. Leaves glabrous, decussate 
with pair of spines. Flowers light blue to violet. Fruit 2-3 cms. long. It is found in 
abundance in all the estuaries. Flowering and fruiting take place in between February 
to April. 
  
15. Lumnitzera racemosa: 
A small tree upto 10 m. high. Bark grey and fissured. Pneumatophores are thin, knee 
shaped. Leaves small, fleshy, oval, clustered towards end of branches Flowers white. 
Fruit hard, ovoid. Flowering and fruiting in between March to September. Localised to 
Siolim area, along the bunds. 
  
16. Derris heterophylla: 
A climber, much branched shrub, evergreen, perennial, tap roots deep sunken and 
without any aerial growth, compound leaves, 3 to 5 leaflets. Flowering in June to 
December.7 
 
 
• Plants used as fodder in Goa 
1. Maize : African Tall variety , seed required 75 kg/H,  production approx  50T/H 
in 80- 90 days  
          
African tall maize is a variety of maize that is grown as green fodder for animals. It is also 
known as fodder maize.  
Characteristics 
• It is a tall-growing variety that can reach heights of up to 6 feet.  
• It has a high dry matter content and crude protein content.  
• It has a high number of leaves per plant.  
• It is suitable for mixed cropping.  
• It can be used for silage, stacks, and maize flour.  
Growing conditions 
• It grows best in temperatures between 20°C and 35°C.  
• It grows well in soil that is medium to heavy, deep, sandy, well drained, and has more organic 
matter and water holding capacity.  
• It can be used for green fodder, silage, stacks, and maize flour.  
 
7 hƩps://www.forest.goa.gov.in/mangroves - Forest Department, Government of Goa 

 
316 
 
Uses 
• It is a good fodder for cows, buffaloes, goats, and sheep.  
• Consumption of this green fodder increases milk production.  
• It can be used as a fodder bank that can be used throughout the year.  
Selection  
• Some varieties are bred for drought resistance, while others may be better suited for high-
rainfall areas. 
 
2. Jowar :  Richira , Maldandi , MP Chari 6, 50kg/H, 40-50T/H in 80-90 days  
          
 
 
Ruchira is a variety of jowar, also known as sorghum, that was developed by the Mahatma 
Phule Krishi Vidyapeeth in Rahuri, Maharashtra. It's a multi-cut variety that's recommended 
for cultivation in Maharashtra.  
Characteristics Medium-tall plants, High yielding, Green fodder quality, Multi-cut ability, and 
Yields 40–50 T/Ha (tons per hectare) Green Fodder and 8.2 T/Ha Dry Matter.  
Growing conditions  
• Grows in medium to heavy, well-drained soil 
• Can be grown in Kharif, Rabi, and summer 
• Kharif sowing time is June–July 
• Rabi sowing time is September–October 
• Summer sowing time is February–March 
Health benefits 
Jowar is known for its heart-healthy properties due to its rich content of phytochemicals like 
phenols, tannins, and plant sterols. It's also gluten free.  
 
 
Maldandi jowar is a variety of sorghum that is grown in India, including Goa. Jowar is a staple 
crop in many regions of India and is a vital source of protein, iron, gluten-free, high in fiber, 
and has a slightly sweet taste. It is mainly grown in the Solapur and Satara districts of 
Maharashtra.  
Features 
Nutrition: High in fiber, protein, calcium, iron, potassium, and phosphorus  
Uses: Used to make bhakri, papad, and roti  
Health benefits: Helps with digestion, regulates blood sugar, and promotes bone health  
Other characteristics: Small grains, yellowish in color, and larger than Desi/Dagdi Jowar  
• Jowar is a vital staple crop in Goa 
• Jowar is planted in the state usually after harvesting the paddy crop 
• Jowar atta is available in Goa 

 
317 
 
• Maldandi jowar flour is a versatile addition to your kitchen and is suitable for those managing 
diabetes or following a healthy lifestyle  
• It is also a good choice for babies, sporty, healthy, and fit people to include in their diets  
Potential side effects  
• Jowar's high fiber content may lead to bloating, gas, or stomach discomfort 
• Some individuals may have an allergy to jowar, which can cause symptoms like itching, 
swelling, or digestive upset. 
• It is drought-resistant 
• It can be consumed throughout the year 
• It can be used to replace wheat rotis 
• It can help promote weight loss, control blood sugar levels, and enhance gut and heart 
health 
Jowar benefits  
• It helps to keep the bad cholesterol away. 
 
M.P. Chari  is the most important cereal fodder crop grown in summer/ rainy season and 
gaining more popularity in India because of its high yield. Covering the maximum cultivated 
area among fodder crops, sorghum is grown in all parts of the country except the cool hilly 
areas. It has high tolerance to drought and excessive rain fall. There are single, two multicut 
varieties/ hybrids of sorghum giving one to six cuts per crop producing 50-100 tonnes of green 
fodder/ hectare. To avoid prussic acid or cyanide toxicity to livestock, the crop should be 
harvested at about 50% flowering or after irrigation at the preflowering stage. The crop is also 
useful for hay and silage making.Cultivate such variety of Jowar which has very low HCN (a 
poison) content and can be cut many times. M.P. Chari is suitable variety for it. 
 
 
3. Oat : 100kg/H, 46-50T/H ( Not widely used in Goa ) 
 
Oats are not commonly grown in Goa, but there are many retailers that sell oats and oat-based 
products, including rolled oats, steel-cut oats, instant oats, and flavored oatmeal.  Oats are a 
type of cereal grain belonging to the “Poaceae” grass family of plants. Its scientific name is 
“Avena sativa”. Oats are popular because of their high nutritional value. The grains came from 
edible seeds of oat grass which we eat. When we cook oats they give us a mushy texture. Oats 
have enormous health benefits. They have soluble fiber, vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants 
in rich amounts. They can help lower cholesterol and blood sugar level. Oats are high in a fiber 
called beta-glucan which boosts your immunity and keeps your heart healthy. Being rich in 
fiber, oat keeps you full for a longer time. They also contain an antioxidant “avenanthramides”. 
Various studies have proven that it helps in reducing inflammation and regulating blood 
pressure also. 
 
4. Bajra: 5kg/H,  

 
318 
 
 
Bajra, also known as pearl millet, is a staple food in Goa and is an important crop in many parts 
of India. It's a hardy cereal grain that's well-adapted to arid conditions.  
Importance of Bajra  
Bajra (pearl millet) is an important source of nutrients and has many health benefits. It's high 
in fiber, protein, and minerals, including iron, calcium, magnesium, and potassium. Bajra is 
also gluten-safe.  
Nutritional benefits 
Bajra is a good source of protein, fiber, and vitamins. It's also a high-energy food that can help 
improve heart health. 
Health benefits 
• Digestion: Bajra's fiber helps with digestion and prevents constipation.  
• Heart health: Bajra's magnesium helps regulate blood pressure, and its fiber and nutrients help 
lower cholesterol and blood sugar.  
• Blood sugar: Bajra's low glycemic index means it has a slower impact on blood sugar levels.  
• Anemia: Bajra's iron can help prevent and address anemia.  
• Metabolism: Bajra's nutrients help convert food into energy.  
• Skin and hair: Bajra's iron, zinc, and B vitamins contribute to healthy skin and hair.  
Climate adaptability 
Bajra can thrive in poor soil conditions and requires less water than other cereals. 
Economic viability 
Bajra cultivation can be profitable for farmers, especially in regions with limit ed resources. 
Other benefits 
Bajra is resistant to drought, heat, and some forms of contamination that affect other grains.  
Bajra is an important source of dietary energy for people in the third world countries, 
particularly in Africa and Asia.  
 
 
Fodder crops  
Multicut varieties  
First cut after 4 mths and subsequent cuts every 3 months 
Varieties  
Napier Hybreed , Also known as Gajraj in India  

 
319 
 
     
Napier Bajra is a hybrid grass that can be used as fodder in Goa. It's a perennial grass that can 
grow in a variety of soils and temperatures. Napier bajra can grow to be 1.5 –2 meters tall, but 
can potentially reach 6 meters. It's a fast-growing, perennial grass that's often used as fodder 
for livestock.  
Height and other characteristics 
• It has stiff, tapering leaves with minimal hair on the upper surface  
• It can be cut every 6–8 weeks, with up to 8 cuts annually  
• It's drought tolerant and can grow in almost any soil, but does best in deep, fertile, well-drained 
soils  
• It's vulnerable to disease and pest attacks  
• It can be intercropped with various forage legumes  
• It's used as a soil stabilizer in soil conservation methods  
Features  
• A tropical grass that can grow in areas with rainfall over 1000 mm 
• Can withstand drought for a short spell and regenerate with rains 
• Grows well at high temperatures and can tolerate drought conditions for a fairly long spell 
• Can grow on a wide range of soil with varied fertility status 
• Provides nutritious and palatable fodder all the year round 
Uses  
• Ideal for green fodder, silage and hay 
• Optimizes feed efficiency and agricultural productivity. 
 
 
Para Grass  
  

 
320 
 
Para grass (Urochloa mutica) is a perennial grass that grows in Goa and is used as fodder, hay, 
and for green soiling. It's a vigorous grower that can spread up to 5 meters in a season.  
Features Grows well in heavy rainfall areas and water logging conditions, Can withstand 
prolonged flooding, Propagated by roots and stem cuttings, Highly palatable and nutritious, 
and Sensitive to heavy grazing.  
Uses  
• Used as green fodder, soiling, and even for dry hay 
• Rotational grazing is recommended 
• All types of soils especially low lying, moist and water logged soils are best suited 
Growth  
• It can spread 5 m in one season 
• It generally takes 12 months for a stand to develop properly 
• It should not be grazed before the stand reaches 30-70 cm high and should not be grazed below 
20 cm 
Distinguishing features  
• The flower-head is a loose panicle up to 30 centimetres (12 in) long with spreading branches 
• The paired spikelets are arranged in uneven rows and are elliptical and 2.5 to 5 millimetres (0.1 
to 0.2 in) long 
 
 
Guinee Grass 
              
Megathyrsus maximus, known as Guinea grass and green panic grass. Guinea grass is a fast-
growing, highly palatable perennial grass that can be used as a fodder crop. It can be cut 
multiple times a year.  
Description  
• A tall, tufted grass that can grow to be 1–4.5 meters tall 
• Has a short creeping rhizome 
• Can be established by seed or by planting rooted slips 
• Suitable for all types of soil with good drainage 
Varieties  
Hamil, PPG -14, Makuni, Rivers-dale, Co1, and Co2. 
Cultivation  
• Can be intercropped with Hedge Lucerne (Velimasal) at a 3:1 ratio 
• Can be harvested together and fed to animals 
• First cut is 75–80 days after germination or 45 days after planting of slips 
• Subsequent cuts at intervals of 45 days 
 
Rhodes Grass 

 
321 
 
       
Rhodes grass ( Chloris gayana ) is a tropical grass that can be found in tropical countries, 
including India. It's a leafy grass that can be used as pasture or hay. It can grow in many types 
of habitat. It is also cultivated in some areas as a palatable graze for animals and a groundcover 
to reduce erosion and quickly revegetate denuded soil. It is tolerant of 
moderately saline and alkaline soils and irrigation  
Appearance  
• Can be annual or perennial 
• Can grow to be 1–2 meters tall 
• Has linear leaves that can be flat or folded 
• Has an open hand shaped seed head 
• Has light greenish brown inflorescences that turn darker brown as they mature 
Uses  
• Used as pasture or hay 
• Used for erosion control 
• Can be used as permanent pasture or a short- to medium-term pasture ley 
Growth  
• Spreads by rhizomes, rooting stolons, and seeds 
• Forms strong bunch type stools with runners that rapidly cover the ground surface 
• Can invade rainforest fringes and smother native ground cover species 
• Well adapted to colonize bare ground (fallows, roadsides) 
Control 
• Control strategies require an integrated approach that includes tillage, crop selection, and 
herbicides  
• Effective long-term control can be achieved by using a combination of strategic practices  
 
 
Dinanath Grass 
     
Deenanath grass (Cenchrus pedicellatus) is an annual grass that is native to India and tropical 
Africa. It is also known as desho grass, kyasuwa grass, and bare.  

 
322 
 
Features  
• Deenanath grass is a leafy grass with erect, branching stems. 
• The leaves are flat, hairless, and 15–25 cm long. 
• The flower clusters are pink to purple and form cylindrical panicles. 
• The spikelets are 4 mm long. 
Growing conditions  
• Deenanath grass prefers warm climates with annual rainfall between 800–1250 mm. 
• It grows best on medium textured, light soils. 
Uses  
• Deenanath grass is ideal for livestock feed. 
• It can be sustainably cultivated on small plots of land. 
 
 
 
Marvel Grass  
    
Marvel grass ( Dichanthium annulatum ) is a tropical grass that's native to India and North 
Africa. It's a popular fodder grass in India and is used for grazing livestock. This is a 
popular pasture grass in many areas. It can be used in fields for grazing livestock, and cut for 
hay and silage. It is tolerant of varied soil conditions, including soils high in clay and sand, 
poorly drained soils, and soils that are somewhat alkaline and saline. It forms a turf that can 
stand up to grazing pressure. It can recover from fire and drought, but it is less tolerant of frost 
and shade. It does not require fertilizer but it does respond well to a small amount of 
supplemental nitrogen. Horses and cattle find it very palatable.  
While it can aggressively outcompete many other plants, it thrives with some types 
of companion species , such as the grasses Bothriochloa insculpta , Dichanthium aristatum , 
and D. caricosum, and the legumes Medicago sativa, Stylosanthes hamata, and S. seabrana.  
The grass can also be used to revegetate degraded grasslands. It is a very effective binding 
plant for erosion control. 
Characteristics  
• Can grow up to 100 cm tall 
• Has a deep root system that can go down to 1 meter 
• Tolerant of water stresses 
• Tolerant of alkaline and saline soils 
• Can recover from fire and drought 
• Less tolerant of frost and shade 
Uses  
Used in pastures, Cut for hay and silage, Used to re-seed degraded grasslands, and Used as an 
effective binding plant for erosion control.  

 
323 
 
 
Anjan Grass  
 
Local names: Buffel grass, African foxtail 
Anjan  grass is  a  most  important  perennial grass with a marked tussocky habit of growth.  It 
is leafy prostrate and rhizomatous grass of  the tropics  up to an altitude of 1500 meters. It 
shows best growth in monsoon. It can withstand drought and is an excellent grazing grass for 
hot dry areas in tropics and sub-tropics. It is a good soil binder and hence used as a cover crop 
on bunds for soil and water conservation. Depending on rainfall, the yield varies greatly and in 
arid tract with less than 300 mm rainfall, a well established pasture produces 90-110 tonnes/ha 
green matter. 
Features  
• Grows best in the monsoon and can withstand drought 
• Grows well in light textured soils and even low pH soils 
• Thrives in arid and semi-arid areas 
• A prolific seed producer that responds quickly to light rains 
• Flower spikes are densely packed with bristly fruit that resemble burs 
Uses 
• Excellent grazing grass for hot, dry areas in the tropics and sub-tropics  
• Suitable for open grazing and pasture land  
• A go-to option for creating lush, resilient lawns and landscapes  
Growing  
• Planting is preferred in the monsoon season 
• First harvest at 70-75 days after planting and subsequently after 50-60-days 
• Can produce 30-40 tonnes in 3-4 cuttings per year depending on growth 
 
Other varieties ( leguminous ) 
Lucern Grass : Chikhaldhara & Sirsa 9 varieties available , seeds required 20kg/H, 100T/H 
 

 
324 
 
Lucerne (Medicago sativa), also known as alfalfa, is a perennial, flowering plant that's used as 
a forage crop for livestock. It's a legume that's high in protein, vitamins, and minerals.  
Uses 
• Grazing: Lucerne can be grazed directly by livestock.  
• Hay and silage : Lucerne can be conserved as hay or silage to feed livestock when 
pasture quality declines.  
• Green manure: Lucerne can be used as a green manure and cover crop.  
Growing conditions 
• Lucerne can be grown in a variety of soils, but well-drained, fertile soils with a neutral 
pH are ideal.  
• Lucerne can't thrive in alkaline soil, but it can grow in acid soils if lime is applied.  
• Lucerne can tolerate low temperatures, but it doesn't like to get wet.  
• Lucerne should be cut at the bud stage for the best compromise between yield and 
quality.  
 
 
Berseem : seed requirement and production is same as lucern  
    
Berseem (Trifolium alexandrinum) 
Local name: Egyptian clover 
One of the most significant fodder crops is berseem, which is appropriately referred to as the 
"king of fodders." It is a highly valued feed that holds a specific role in national animal 
husbandry programs. Despite being an Egyptian immigrant, it has lived in this area for the past 
60 years and may be regarded as an Indian native. It offers a lot of appealing features. A 
maintenance ration consists of 10 to 15 kg of feed and straw. When balanced with straws, it 
can promote growth and milk production on ad lib feeding. 
It grows in a variety of soil types, with the exception of usar regions, however it cannot 
withstand acidic soils. In plains, the crop is sown from mid-September to the end of October; 
in hills, it is sown from mid-August to the first week of September. This crop necessitates 
careful land preparation. Giant berseem is another kind of berseem that is now available. Giant 
berseem has the benefit of requiring less irrigation. While the seed rate of ordinary diploid 
berseem is 20-25 kg that of giant berseem is 30-35 kg per hectare. 
For the first cutting, the crop is available 55 –60 days after seeding. In the winter and spring, 
subsequent cuttings are taken at 30-day intervals. Up until the middle of May, all five or six 
cuttings are available. The yield per hectare may range from 500 to 600 quintals. For taking 
the seeds, plots are left uncut after February and in that case 4-5 quintals seeds per hectare may 
be obtained. Berseem tetraploid has been regarded as a high-yielding cultivar. 

 
325 
 
Nutritive value 
Berseem is highly  palatable fodder and it  contains 17% crude protein and 25.9% crude fibre. 
The total digestible nutrients content is 60-65%. Berseem contains saponins, if fed in high 
quantity to ruminants leads to bloat. 
 
Chavali : 50kg/h, 30T/H, widely practiced in Goa alongwith maize and jowar 
    
The cowpea (Vigna unguiculata ) is an annual herbaceous legume from the genus Vigna. Its 
tolerance for sandy soil and low rainfall have made it an important crop in the semiarid regions 
across Africa and Asia. It requires very few inputs, as the plant's root nodules are able to fix 
atmospheric nitrogen , making it a valuable crop for resource-poor farmers and well-suited 
to intercropping with other crops. The whole plant is used as forage for animals, with its use as 
cattle feed likely responsible for its name.

Dashrath  
 
Dasharath grass is a perennial fodder crop with good nutritional value of dicotyledonous fodder 
year round. Estimated nutritional value of green areas in Dasharath is 22.31 for protein, 2.61 
for fat, 24.30 for fiber and 43.97 for carbohydrates. 
 It's used to feed livestock such as cows, goats, sheep, rabbits, and poultry.  
Features  
• Nutritional value: High in protein, vitamins, and minerals 
• Yield: High yield of nutrient-rich grass 
• Drought resistance: Requires minimal water once established 
• Soil health: Improves soil structure and fertility 
• Farm productivity: Enhances overall farm productivity 
Growing Dashrath grass  
• Can be cultivated throughout the year under irrigated conditions 
• Can be cultivated during monsoon under rainfed conditions 
• Grows in all types of soils 
• Requires immediate irrigation after sowing 
• Requires life irrigation on the third day and thereafter once in a week 
• Requires hoeing and weeding as and when necessary 
Uses  
• Used as fodder for goats, cows, buffalos, and sheep 
• Used to increase the weight gain and improve productivity of milk yield 
• Used as a sustainable feed source 
• Used in mixed farming systems

Giripushp  
 
Giripushpa is another name for the Gliricidia sepium tree, a fast-growing, nitrogen-fixing tree 
legume. 
Description  
• A medium-sized tree that can grow up to 39 ft (12 m) tall 
• Has smooth bark that can range in color from whitish gray to deep red-brown 
• Has bright pink to lilac flowers with a white tinge and a pale yellow spot at the base 
• Has fruit that's a pod that's green when unripe and yellow-brown when ripe 
• The pod contains four to ten round brown seeds 
Uses 
• The leaves can be fed to livestock  
• The wood can be used for firewood, charcoal, and construction  
• The tree can be used to stabilize soil, prevent erosion, and reclaim denuded land  

 
328 
 
• The tree can be used as a shade tree for plantation crops, especially cacao, but also tea and 
coffee  
• The tree can form hedges and provide green manure  
• The tree can be used as a trellis for climbing crops  
• The juice of the leaves, bark, and roots is traditionally used to treat eczema and to alleviate 
itches and wounds  
Seeds 
The seeds of the Gliricidia sepium tree are a valuable source of fodder for livestock and can be 
used as green manure to enrich soil fertility.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Subabhul 4kg/h, 30t/h 
 
Leucaena leucocephala is a small fast-growing mimosoid tree. It was promoted as a "miracle 
tree" for its multiple uses. It has also been described as a "conflict tree" because it is used for 
forage production but spreads like a weed in some places.  
The legume is promoted in several countries of Southeast Asia (at 
least Burma, Cambodia, Indonesia, Laos,  and Thailand), most importantly as a source of 
quality animal feed, but also for residual use for firewood or charcoal production. 
The legume provides an excellent source of high-protein cattle fodder. However, the fodder 
contains mimosine, a toxic amino acid. Horses and donkeys which are fed it lose their hair.

Shevri is used as a good windbreaker and provides shade and support for other plant species
