Socio- Economic Aspects: 
• People who hold land along the streams and rivers shall be suitably rewarded to preserve the natural vegetation.0- 
 
342 
 
• Stopping (illegal) sand / gravel mining will not be appreciated by the beneficiaries. 
• Awareness based participation in elimination of weeds. 
• Restoration of grazing land. 
• Availability of wild vegetables 
• Regeneration of native flora 
• Festivals like Bonderam, Tounshache Fest (Cucumber) and Konnsanche fest are celebrated throughout Goa in different villages to mark 
the Harvest period. A variety of dishes are prepared using newly harvested grains. In certain parts of Goa, a part of the new harvest is 
offered to God such festivals should be encouraged on interstate level.  
• State level also local producers should be promoted for example Millet festival, Raan Bhaji festival, Fruit festival, Tuber (Kongache) 
festival, Cashew fest. 
• Just like Community Seed Banks, a medicinal plant processing unit should also be created at BMC level from where Ayurvedic companies 
can buy raw material. 
• Since most of the things are done online in the modern times local people should be made aware about new things online by creating social 
media groups: like Comp post villa group which takes and shares knowledge. 
• Cultivation of wild vegetables should be promoted by locals with the help of cultural events like Raanbhaji festivals where scientific experts 
should be involved to discuss livelihood generation by wild vegetables Availability of wild vegetables 
• Use of native flowers should be promoted to make bouquets and garlands during festivals and purchase of imports should be avoided. 
• Nurseries should be encouraged to regenerate and distribute native flora over exotic species. 
• To mitigate climate change, tree plantation is one of the widely prescribed strategies. Environmentally conscious citizens are doing their 
level best in greening the open unwooded areas and grasslands, mainly lateritic outcrops. Various studies have shown that these are rich in 
monsoonal ephemerals which are habitat specific and endemic. They prefer the open areas. It is observed by some of us that plantations 
done in these areas eliminate the local plants, especially endemics. The digging for plantation also provides good substratum for the weeds 
to establish. This is happening in Goa.  
• More and more awareness regarding Beejamitra scheme must be provided to the farmers which will help them generate livelihood via 
community seed banks. so as to preserve the germplasm of various species in various forms. 
• Knowledge about plants like Indian gooseberry, Devil tree, Matti, V oval, Bael, Khair, White teak, Apto etc. must be given to people by 
celebrating years dedicated to these trees to pass on traditional knowledge. 
• Preparation of wild plant-based products such as perfumes, food items, etc. as it will provide employment to the people also will be 
protected from getting extinct in the biodiversity. 
 
343 
 
• ‘Plant Utsav’, the annual plant show which has been delighting plant enthusiasts for three decades is held in Goa so as to create awareness 
among the youths regarding conservation of plants and it provides a marketing site for people who are interested in selling plants. 
• As this year is celebrated as the 'International Year of Millets,' many programs are being held throughout India in various parts of the 
country to make people more aware of the millets as it has several health benefits, such as the 'Nachneachem Fest' in Goa to bring back the 
cultivation of Ragi in Goa as it was cultivated in large areas which have now vanished due to the li festyle of the current generation. It is 
also important to raise awareness of its health benefits. 
• ‘Govan’ is one of the best examples, which does post-harvest management of various fruits and vegetable by producing various products 
out of it like mango pickle, nutmeg candy and many other products where in all the raw materials such as fruits and vegetables are collected 
from Gaon farmers itself and prepared by women of Goa; which aims in 3 major things i.e.  
-Women empowerment, preparation of herbarium from each taluka by a group of farmers so as for easy understanding of plant heritage in 
each taluka. 
-Providing market to the Goan Farmers and fishermen.  
-Aiming to prepare products from every part of every fruit and vegetable, so that no part goes to waste or is lost.

Success Story of Any Successful intervention for conservation/protection/ sustainable use of bioresources in respective sectors in 
the state of Goa and India.  
Environmentalists of Goa: Claude Alvares and his wife Norma Alvares. 
Norma Alvares: The wife of Claude Alphonso Alvares, is an Indian lawyer, social worker and environmental activist. Under the aegis of 
the Goa Foundation that was started by her husband, she initiated a public interest litigation in 1987 to save the sand dunes of Goa. This 
was the first ever PILfiled in the state. She has been involved in over 100 PIL’s. Her efforts are reported to be winning a favorable court 
order for blocking a DuPont factory and another one with restricted mining activities in Goa. She is the president of Goa branch of People 
for Animals. She was honored by the government of India, in 2002, with the Padma Shri award.  
Shri. Ramesh N. Zarmekar: has been awarded the Biodiversity Enthusiast Category Biodiversity conservation award (North Goa) for his 
contribution in protecting and rescuing wildlife species and rehabilitation of snakes and wild animals. 
Shri. Johnson Stephen: has been awarded the Biodiversity Enthusiast Category Biodiversity conservation Award (South Goa), for his 
contribution in protecting and rescuing wildlife species and rehabilitation of snakes and wild animals. 
Jadav Payeng: The Forest Man of India, Jadav Payeng is a famous environmentalist in India. Hailing from the North eastern state of Assam 
which is an abode of greenery, Payeng has over the course of several decades planted a forest on a sandbar of the river Brahmaputra. Named 
Molai forest after his name Jadav ‘Molai’ Payeng, this unique initiative earned Payeng the honor of being bestowed with the Padma Shri, 
the fourth highest civilian award in India. 
SumairaAbdulali: is an Indian environmentalist with a difference. Her thrust on highlighting unconventional forms of environmental 
hazards such as noise pollution and sand mining has earned her several awards. The Co-Chairman of the Conservation Sub Committee and 
Honorary Secretary of Asia’s oldest and largest environmental NGO, the Bombay Natural History Society, Abdulali has also set up the first 
ever network for protection of activists in India. 
RaghavjibhaiPrajapati: might not be an environmental activist per se but with his unique innovation that is a huge step forward in making 
the environment more sustainable is sure a crusader for a greener earth. The fridge that he made out of clay, called the Mitti Cool Fridge is 
one of his eco-friendly inventions and can surely go a long way in promoting the conservation of the environment. 
And there are many other great personalities who have contributed their life in conservation of plant biodiversity; one of them is Rahibai 
Soma Popere who was born in 1964, is an Indian farmer and conservationist. She helps other farmers return to native varieties of crops, 
preparing hyacinth beans for self-help groups. Rahibai Soma Popere farm land, where she grows 17 different crops.   
 
347 
 
She developed a series of hyacinth beans for self-help groups and families in nearby villages. She was described by RaghunathMashelkar, 
the erstwhile Director General of the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research as 'Seed Mother'. She is an active member of the self-
help group Kalsubaiparisar Biyanse Sarvdhan centre. She has created her own methods to harvest water hyacinth on farms; turning 
wasteland into space she can use productively. She trains farmers and students on ways to select seeds, keep fertile soils and manage pests. 
She is skilled in four-step paddy cultivation.    
Another great personality who has played a huge role in conservation of plant biodiversity is Tulsi Gowda who is an Indian environmentalist 
from Honnali village, Ankola taluk in Karnataka state. She has planted more than 30,000 saplings and looks after the nurseries of the Forest 
Department. Her work has been honoured by the Government of India and other organisations. In 2021, the Government of India awarded 
her the Padma Shri. She is known as the "Encyclopedia of the Forest" for her ability to recognise the mother tree of any species of tree. 
Gowda spent over sixty years working at the Karnataka Forest Department. 
Gowda is known by environmentalists as the "Encyclopaedia of the Forest" and by her tribe as the "tree goddess" because of her knowledge 
of the forest and its plants. She is known for her ability to identify the mother tree of every species of tree in the forest no matter where it 
is. Mother trees are significant because of their age and size, which make them the most connected nodes in the forest. These underground 
nodes are used to connect mother trees with saplings and seedlings as the mother tree exchanges nitrogen and nutrients. Gowda is also an 
expert in seed collecting, the extraction of seeds from mother trees in order to regenerate and regrow entire plant species. It is a difficult 
process as the seeds must be collected at the peak of germination from the mother tree in order to ensure the survival of the seedlings and 
Gowda is able to work out this exact time.  
Gowda cannot explain how she gathered her knowledge of the forest, but says it is as if she can "speak the language of the forest." In the 
traditions of her tribe, the HalakkiV okkaliga, the matriarchy is connected to nature and cares for the land.

Dr K P Dinesh 
I hail from coffee growing communities of the 
Western Ghats, and started my early research 
life roaming around the hill ranges of 
Kudremukh and Mullayanagiri in search of 
birds and butterflies. After completing doctoral 
research in coffee genetics, government 
service provided me an opportunity to kick 
start my new interest in amphibian taxonomy. 
In the process of addressing taxonomic issues, 
I ended up working on phylogenetics, 
phylogeography and evolutionary history of 
amphibians of the Western Ghats. As part of 
my postdoctoral project at CES, IISc (2011-
15), I attempted to examine the extent and 
patterns of distribution of genetic diversity 
within the Ranid family of the Western Ghats. 
I assessed species-wide phylogeographical 
structuring within the ranid frogs to make 
inferences about gene flow between 
geographic locations on the either side of the 
Palghat Gap in the Western Ghats. I continue 
to elucidate problems in taxonomy, 
systematics and delimitation of the species, 
and are attempting to define the altitudinal and 
latitudinal range of distribution for ranids and 
other frogs. In the past 20 years of my 
amphibian research in India I am involved in 

 
355 
 
the discovery of more than 50 new species of 
amphibians new to science which includes two 
new species of frogs and two new species of 
caecilians from Goa. As an additional research 
interest involved in the DNA barcoding 
(generated more than 500 DNA barcodes) and 
phylogeny of parasitic hymenopterans, moths, 
butterflies, termites, cockroaches, centipedes, 
spiders, molluscs fishes amphibians and 
reptiles. Involved in the more than 130 
publications including 42 Indian Journal 
Research Articles and 38 Foreign Journal 
Research Articles.

Introduction- 
Inclusion of lesser-known habitats in the Goa State Biodiversity Strategy and Action Plan 
(GSBSAP) is crucial due to their unique ecological roles and high biodiversity value. These 
habitats, often overlooked, include microhabitats like leaf litter and dead logs, specialized 
ecosystems such as Myristica swamps and hypersaline salt pans, and coastal features like 
seagrasses and coral reefs. They support diverse species, including endemic and threatened 
species, which are essential for maintaining ecological balance, nutrient cycling, and water 
conservation. 
These ecosystems face significant threats from urbanization, tourism, pollution, and climate 
change, making their conservation urgent. By incorporating them into the GSBSAP, Goa can 
better monitor, protect, and sustainably manage these habitats. This approach not only safeguards 
biodiversity but also strengthens ecosystem resilience, supports sustainable livelihoods, and 
helps mitigate climate change impacts. Additionally, the GSBSAP can foster community 
engagement and awareness around these habitats, promoting a more comprehensive and 
inclusive strategy for biodiversity conservation in Goa 
➢ Spiders and their habitat   
 
357 
 
Spiders are widely distributed animals. They have high abundance and high diversity in almost all 
microhabitats (Rajeevan, et.al. 2019). They are known to inhabit varied habitats such as the water 
surface, thick foliage, on flowers, the forest floor, grassland, under stones, logs, barks, houses, as 
well as in agricultural fields. According to the World Spider Catalog (Version 24.5, 2023) around 
51,817 species belonging 4,361 genera and 136 families have been identified. Till now 1952 
species belonging to 503 genera under 62 families are documented from India (Caleb & Sankaran, 
2024).  
207 species under 45 genera and 22 families of Spider have been documented from the state of 
Goa so far. The present checklist includes 74 species of spiders which are Endemic to Western 
Ghats, and there are four species of spiders which are endemic to the state of Goa. Spiders are 
known to occupy mostly of the terrestrial habitats (Vairale & Wagh, 2021).

Ecosystem of spiders according to their families 
1. Araneidae: This family inhabits a wide range of terrestrial ecosystems including 
wooded and forest area of India. Majority of species belonging to this family are found 
in shrub land, grassland and bushland. They spin large sticky webs between adjacent 
1trees to trap prey. Species inhabiting forest, prepares medium sized radial

358 
 
symmetrical webs between adjacent shrub twigs or branches. Species belonging to 
genus Cyclosa spin smaller delicate, geometrical webs in between bushes and shrubs. 
These spiders are commonly known as the orb-weaver spiders as they build spiral 
wheel-shaped webs in the houses, gardens, tree branches, tall grasses, agricultural 
fields, and bushes (Singh, et.al, 2023). 
2. Clubionidae: Commonly known as sac spiders, species belonging to this family are 
found in tropical and subtropical party of the world. These spiders construct flattened 
dense white tubes that often have two openings, usually made on rolled leaves, under 
barks or under rocks for retreat (Singh, et.al, 2023). Genus Clubiona specially prefers 
shrublands. 
3. Corinnidae: Species of this family are hunters and build silken retreats, or sacs, 
typically on plant terminals, between leaves, under bark or under rocks (Singh et al., 
2021a) 
4. Ctenidae: Ctenidae family consists of wandering spiders which are comparatively 
large, nocturnal and active ambush-hunters found in tropical region (Singh, et.al, 
2023).  
5. Eresidae: Members of this family are referred as velvet spiders. Only one species of 
this family is found in Goa. Spiders belonging to this genus Stegodyphus are social 
and usually build large silken nests in vegetation and hundreds of individuals live 
together (Singh, et.al, 2023).  
6. Gnaphosidae: Gnaphosid spiders are commonly known as the ground spiders. They 
are nocturnal species and hide during the day under the rocks and logs, and in leaf 
litter typically in a tubular silken retreat (Singh, et.al, 2023). 
7. Hersilidae: Hersiliidae is a small family of tropical and subtropical spiders, commonly 
called long-spinnered or two-tailed spiders. Normally these solitary creatures are seen 
moving on large tree trunks, moving very fast and camouflaging with trunk. They lay 
light coating of thread on tree bark waiting for prey and feeds on variety of smaller 
insects inhabiting the tree trunks (Singh, et.al, 2023). 
8. Lycosidae: Spiders belonging to this family are known as wolf spiders. Wolf spiders 
are usually diurnal and are observed in grasses, leaf litter, agricultural fields, sandy 
and stony areas, and near water surfaces actively hunting on prey. They can also be 
observed in man-made constructions (Singh, 2021). Genus Lycosa is found in the leaf 
litter near the banks water. 
9. Miturgidae: These are medium to large sized spider commonly known as prowling 
spiders. They are nocturnal creatures living on ground and keep their eggs under rock 
or other debris (Singh, et.al, 2023). 
10. Oxyopidae: These spiders are found mainly on trees, shrubs and herbs. Architectural 
attributes such as size, shape and spatial arrangement of substrate are some of the 
factors that affect their habitat selection. Oxyopids were predominantly found on the 
grasses (Rajeevan, et. al, 2019; Sebastian, et. al, 2012). Hamadruas hieroglyphica can 
be found in secondary forest.  
11. Philodromidae: Commonly known as false crab spiders, these species are found in the 
foliage, branches, stems of bushes and trees. They are also observed at ground level 
 
2(https://www.sahapedia.org/the-spiders-of-western-ghats). 
 
 
359 
 
2and on vertical surfaces. Moreover, they construct wooly egg sacs on various 
surfaces such as leaves, under bark, etc (Singh, et.al, 2023).  
12. Pholcidae: Pholcid spiders are also known as cellar spiders. The cellar spiders are 
found in areas such as caves and rock piles, damp cellars, basements, crawl spaces, 
garages, dark undisturbed places, dark corners of remote vacant houses and buildings, 
hallow tree trunks, and medium to smaller size pits through the side cuttings of rocks. 
In human habitats, they can be seen at the corner of a wall or a ceiling in their webs 
(Singh, et.al, 2023). 
13. Pisauridae: Pisauridae includes nursery web spiders and fishing and raft spiders (semi-
aquatic species). They hunt in low vegetation or in ambush and rarely use webs for 
procuring prey. The semi-aquatic species, the fishing spiders and raft spiders, are 
found near water bodies and predate upon variety of aquatic insects sometimes even 
on larger preys such as small tadpoles and fishes (Singh, et.al, 2023). 
14. Psechridae: Species belonging to Psechridae are commonly known as lace-sheet-
weavers. They are mostly found in forest, rocky areas, and even in caves (Singh, et.al, 
2023). 
15. Salticidae: The members of the family Salticidae is commonly called as jumping 
spiders. Jumping spiders have a widespread distribution in terrestrial ecosystems 
including agricultural fields and are also found in human dwellings and home gardens, 
searching for their prey on the walls of buildings or among foliage (Gajbe, 2020). 
Myrmarachne plataleoides, the ant mimicking spider is found in close vicinity of 
weaver ants  
16. Scytodidae: Spiders of family Scytodidae are also known as spitting spiders. They are 
nocturnal species, and prefer the warm and cozy confines of caves or houses, dark 
crevices, closets, and under rocks during the day  and even in caves (Singh, et.al, 
2023).  
17. Sparassidae: These spiders are known by varied names such as huntsman spiders, 
giant crab spiders, wood spiders, rain spiders or lizard-eating spiders depending upon 
the habit and habitat. Most of these species are cursorial and live under rocks, barks 
and undisturbed places (Singh, et.al, 2023). 
18. Tetragnithidae: These spiders are found mainly on trees, shrubs and herbs. Their 
habitat selection is dependant on a variety of biotic and abiotic factors together with 
the architectural attributes of the habitat. Architectural attributes such as size, shape 
and spatial arrangement of substrate are some of the factors (Rajeevan, et. Al, 2019). 
19. Theraphosidae: Commonly known as Tarantulas, these species are found in forests. 
They usually live in the selfmade burrows but sometimes hide in larger crevices of 
forest lands. In Goa, they were sighted in the burrows on the mud bund parallel to 
road passing through forests, other than this they also occupy the crevices of tree 
trunks (Borkar & Seth, 2020). 
20. Theridiidae: Members of this family are found mainly on trees, shrubs and herbs. 
Theridiids are usually found at the bottom of leaves. Their choice of habitat depends 
on a range of factors, including the physical architectural attributes. These attributes

21. Thomisidae: These spiders are referred to as crab spiders or flower crab spiders due

including paddy fields, fences, and shrubs found next to the highway (Babu et.al, 
2022). 
Spider species are known to exhibit preferences for habitats influenced by the physical 
organization of environmental parameters. They are particularly sensitive to changes in habitat 
arrangement and microclimate conditions (Halarnkar & Pai, 2018). The habitat heterogeneity 
hypothesis suggests that greater complexity in habitats provides more diverse niches, leading to 
increased species richness (Tews et.al, 2004; Halarnkar & Pai, 2018). 
➢ Leaf litter: Leaf litter, the layer of decomposing leaves and organic matter beneath trees 
forms one of the important micro habitat. Its consistent temperatures and high humidity 
levels provide perfect habitat to a wide range of organisms. Typical residents of this 
microhabitat include earthworms, millipedes, spiders, and springtails, which facilitate soil 
formation and decomposition. This layer gives the forest floor a steady supply of organic 
matter, which is necessary for the cycling of nutrients3. Pill millipedes (Oniscomorpha) are 
slow-moving little creatures that move along the leaf litter and curl up into balls when 
threatened4. 
➢ Tree trunks: Tree trunks support rich biodiversity including orchids, ferns, butterflies, 
moths, birds and more 5. Many predators often conceal themselves on tree trunk lying in 
wait for their next meal, one such example is of bark mantis (Mantodea) with a flat, brown-
grey body that camouflages perfectly onto the tree trunks it inhabits, hunts insecting on 
moths, flies, and a variety of arthropods6. 
➢ Inter tidal zones: The intertidal zone is one of the most dynamic zones because it is the 
interface between the sea and terrestrial environment. Waves and the duration of exposure 
to sunlight influence the activities and life of organisms in the intertidal zone (Balakrishnan 
& Sivaleela, 2022). Mangrove patches dominate the intertidal zones such as estuaries, 
mudflats, rivers etc. It supports rich biodiversity with a total of 4011 organisms which 
includes 3091 floral species and 920 faunal species in India. This signifies the importance 
of inter tidal zone7.  
➢ Water spring, pools, riffles: In Western Ghats the aquatic insect diversity in a habitat is 
depends upon the interaction of intrinsic habitat variables and extrinsic environmental 
parameters. Microhabitats such as riffles support high species richness in the cobbles and

➢ Myristica swamps: Myristica swamps are rare primeval ecosystems, with rich 
biodiversity. They have unique root system which can withstand perennial water-logged 
conditions. An important ecosystem service they provide is maintaining the perennial water 
flow of streams. Additionally they possess higher potential to store carbon which helps in 
minimising the threat posed by global warming.8 Streams of Myristica swamps host a rich 
and endemic biodiversity of fishes such as this striped killifish (Aplocheilus lineatus). The 
Myristica swamp also sustains prolific breeding ground for many species that depend on 
water such as night frog tadpoles (Nyctibatrachus sp.).9 BrahmaKarmali, Valpoi village, 
and Bambar of Satari Taluka in Goa is the home for Northern most part of Myristica 
swamps of Western ghats hosts some vulnerable species such as Syzygium travancoricum, 
Myristica fatua Houtt. var. magnifica,Semecarpus kathalekanensis, and Gymnacranthera 
canarica10 
 
➢ Dead log: The decaying wood found on forest floor serves as a crucial microhabitat for a 
variety of organisms. They sustain a different ecosystem of fungi, insects, and tiny 
mammals with their abundant nutrients and moisture. Mycorrhizal fungi, woodlice, 
mosses, and fungus beetles flourish and aid in the decomposition and nutrient cycling of 
this ecosystem. These logs support the forest ecosystems through decomposition of organic 
matter and replenishing the soil with vital nutrients. 11 Invertebrates such as crickets hides 
under the bark of the log while giving out call. It may be to avoid predator the other reason 
could be empty space in between the bark and the log to amplifies its calls (Jain & 
Balakrishnan, 2011).12 
 
➢ Seagrasses: Seagrass is an important yet often undervalued resource with a significant 
ecological role in coastal waters. In addition to shielding our coastlines from waves and 
tides, seagrasses play a vital role in nutrient cycle that supports fisheries. It serves as habitat 
for various marine species, including fish, shellfish, dugongs, and green turtles. Seagrass 
beds offer shelter and refuge to fishes, crabs and epiphytic sedentary organisms such as 
sponges and tube-dwelling worms. Two species of seagrass have been identified from the 
Goa coast, namely Halophila beccarii and H. ovalis (Usmani & Ansari, 2020).13

➢ Seaweed: Seaweeds are the marine macrophytes belonging to three major groups of Brown 
Red algae (Rhodophyta), algae (Phaeophyta), and green algae (Chlorophyta). They provide 
habitat, breeding and feeding ground for many faunal groups and helps in maintaining the 
high coastal biodiversity. Goa coast has rich source of seaweeds. There are 145 species of 
seaweeds reported from Goa coast. Species of Sargassum, Ulva, Gracillaria and Porphyra 
are found in abundance at the Goa coast (Usmani & Ansari, 2020).1415 
 
➢ Corals: Corals and coral reefs support one of the highest biodiversity observed in marine 
environments. Corals have been documented around Grande Island, and Goa is known to 
host approximately 24 varieties and three species of Azooxanthellate scleractinian corals. 
Typical inhabitants of coral reefs include snails, clams, sponges, anemones, crabs, starfish, 
shrimp, sea lilies, and various types of algae (Usmani & Ansari, 2020) 16. Epiphyte mat: 
Epiphyte mats are non-parasitic plants that grow on the trunks and branches of other trees. 
They create a unique microhabitat by forming dense mats that hold a lot of moisture. They 
support a variety of plants, including mosses and ferns, and serves as homes for insects and 
small organisms such as tree frogs. They form a crucial part of ecosystem due to its ability 
to provide resources and cover variety of species.17

There are four basic types of shore distinguished along the Indian coast, (8129 km coast line) viz., 
1) sandy shores, 2) rocky shores, 3) muddy shore (estuarine region), and 4) coral formations. 
Though the west coast of India is with predominantly rocky shores, there are also stray of sandy 
region (Krishnamurthy & Subbaramaiah, 1972)18. 
Rocky coasts contain tiny tide pools, also known as intertidal rock pools, and tiny gullies in the 
intertidal zone. These intertidal rock pools support a variety of marine ecosystems, particularly 
fish, while representing a very difficult environmental state. (Castellanos- Galindo et al., 2005)19 
Tide pools are created when seawater becomes trapped in depressions along the rocky coast's 
shoreline as the tide recedes. Even though the average depth and width of these tiny oceanfront 
basins are only a few inches to several feet, they are teeming with hardy marine creatures like sea 
stars, crabs, seaweed, snails, barnacles, mussels, anemones, urchins, and small fish.  
 
The marine life that lives there has to withstand hours of exposure to the sun, low oxygen levels, 
rising water temperatures, and predators like wading birds, which are specialized in feeding on the 
shallow pools created by the retreating ocean water outside the tide pool during low tide. The

➢ Sand dunes: Sand dunes are protected by vegetation on and around it. They play crucial role of 
protecting the beach. Without vegetation, this natural protective barrier would be lost to the effects 
of wind and coastal erosion. Dune vegetations are adapted to live in an environment exposed to 
salt spray, sand blasts, strong winds, high temperatures and flooding by adapting their root 
systems, protective waxy and hairy coverings on their leaves and stems to reduce water loss. 
There are 91 genera and 106 species of dune vegetation found in Goa. The common and abundant 
genera include Spinifex, Ipomea, and Pandanus. Dune vegetation is vulnerable to mechanical 
impacts caused by tramping. This tiny vegetation also supports many life (Usmani & Ansari,

The last few decades have seen an acceleration of the global coastline's large-scale development 
(Lundin and Linden, 1993; Nordstrom, 1994) 2324. It seems that Goa has not fallen behind in this. 
In less than 20 years, a number of coastal areas that were virtually undeveloped in the 1970s have 
transformed into haphazardly developed stretches full of concrete buildings and related structures. 
A well-known example of frantic development is the coast between Baga and Candolim 
(Mascarenhas et al., 1997; Sawkar et al., 1997) 25.  
Numerous shorelines have been constructed and designed in a way that they bear  
scarcely resembles the coast that once existed. Consequently, many coastal communities  
saw a sharp increase during this time, with the construction of high-rise buildings  
structures, vacation spots, and residential homes that sprung up practically everywhere along the 
coastal region of Goa. Thus, over the past 20 years, the emergence of tourism, population growth 
combined with construction activity, and contemporary societal demands have significantly 
changed the geological and ecological setup and permanently changed

Crevices of Trees  
Tree cavities can host several taxa, providing ecological niches. Birds often hide in tree holes and 
crevices, even mate and nest there, for it provides them with quiet safe space and often even insects 
to feed on. Even some insects that trees host (like grasshoppers, beetles, crickets, worms and ants) 
become the food for birds.28 
Primary cavity nesters are birds that create their own nesting cavities, such as woodpeckers, which 
are skilled excavators. In contrast, secondary cavity nesters do not make their own cavities but 
instead utilize existing ones, including those created by primary cavity nesters, natural cavities 
from broken branches or decaying wood, or artificial structures like birdhouses.29 
The quality of nest sites can be influenced by factors such as microclimate, food availability, a nd 
nest predation. The orientation of cavities can help mitigate microclimate effects (Relier, 1972; 
Conner, 1975; Stauffer & Best, 1982). Quality of nest sites can be affected by microclimate, food 
availability, and nest predation. Cavity orientation can ameliorate microclimate effects (e.g. Relier 
1972, Conner 1975, Stauffer and Best 1982, and others). Cavity-nesting birds commonly choose 
nests in areas where foraging substrates, such as snags and live trees, are dense (Mannan et al. 
1980, Davis et al. 1983, Brush et al. 1983, Marzluff and Lyon 1983, Raphael and White 1984, 
Swallow et al. 1986). However, density of snags and live trees could also affect risk of nest 
predation. Nest predation is usually the primary source of nest mortality for both open- and cavity-
nesting birds (Lack, 1954; Nice, 1957; Ricklefs, 1969; Nilsson 1984; Martin 1988, Martin 1991). 
As a result, choice of nest sites with reduced risk of nest predation and more foraging substrates 
should be favoured.30 
Cavity nests offer significant benefits, including improved thermal insulation (Joy, 2000), reduced 
risk of nest predation, and higher nest success rates compared to open nests (Scott, 1979; Nilsson, 
1986; Martin & Li, 1992; Martin, 1995). 
Without human interference, natural forested environments offer suitable cavities in large trees 
and snags. The availability of these cavities increases with the age and decay of trees and forest 
patches, as this process enhances the amount of dead wood and supports cavity formation (Newton, 
1998; Joy, 2000).

Given the sensitivity of cavity-nesting species to specific nesting requirements, the concerning 
rates of forest loss and degradation, and the lack of national breeding bird survey programs, it is 
crucial to assess the number of cavity-nesting species that may be vulnerable.31 
Tree cavities are a vital resource for wildlife species that need them for nesting, roosting (Steeger 
& Dulisse, 2002), and protection from adverse weather and predators (Ingold, 1994b; Newton, 
1994). 
Western Ghats- six were primary cavity-nesters namely, Brown-capped Pygmy Woodpecker, 
Greater Golden-backed Woodpecker, White-naped Woodpecker, Brown-headed Barbet, 
Coppersmith Barbet, White-cheeked Barbet. Secondary cavity-nesters namely, Common Myna 
Acridotheres tristis, Jungle Myna Acridotheres fuscus, Malabar Pied Hornbill, Great Hornbill, 
Malabar Parakeet, Rose-ringed Parakeet, Psittacula kramer, Indian Scops Owl, Jungle Owlet 
Glaucidium radiatum, Common Hoopoe, Great Tit Parus major, Indian Roller (Coracias 
benghalensis), Oriental Magpie Robin, Tickell’s Blue-flycatcher and White-rumped Shama. 
In this study, cavities made by woodpeckers (Golden-backed and White-naped) and barbets 
(Brown-headed, Coppersmith, and White-cheeked) were utilized by various secondary cavity-
nesting birds and other animals, including the Indian Giant Squirrel, Indian Palm Squirrel, Monitor 
Lizard, Garden Lizard, Indian Rat Snake, and Honey bees. Observations by Maheswaran & 
Balasubramanian (2003) and Santhoshkumar & Balasubramanian (2010)32 on hornbill nests reused 
by the Large Brown Flying Squirrel ( Petaurista philipinensis) and Honey Bees suggest that the 
reuse of bird-excavated tree cavities by other animal species is common in various forest habitats 
of south-western India. 
According to Aitken et al. (2002), the size of the cavity entrance and internal dimensions are crucial 
for determining cavity use, as they influence which species can occupy the nest. Larger cavities 
are associated with increased clutch sizes (Rendell & Verbeek, 1996; Stewart & Robertson, 1999). 
Additionally, Joy (2000) and Wiebe & Swift (2001) suggest that large cavities may offer better 
shelter, providing thermal insulation during hot summer days. 
 
Cavity-nesting birds such as parakeets, owls, barbets, hornbills, woodpeckers, kingfishers, 
starlings and mynas favour diseased, dying, or dead trees because these are easier to excavate 
cavities in. In India, over 100 species of birds that nest in tree cavities have been identified. Human 
activities, such as tree felling, collection of non-timber forest products, and agricultural practices 
near forest boundaries, pose threats to birds that nest in tree cavities and canopies. Among tree 
species, Terminalia arjuna was found to have the highest number of cavities, followed by 
Mangifera indica, Melia dubia, and Ceiba pentandra. (Manikandan, P., 2015)33 
Tree holes are produced due to environmental factors as well as biotic pressure.  It is a unique 
habitat for insect breeding and survival. Dendrothelms that is Water-filled tree-holes or their 
analogs are natural microcosms because of their relative simplicity in habitat structure, small size,

Tree cavities play a key role in the structure and functioning of forest ecosystems. They host rich 
and specialized assemblages of numerous vertebrate and invertebrate species. Cavities are critical 
resources for many animal species, including mammals, birds, amphibians, reptiles and several 
invertebrates. (Patel, et.al., 2021)35 
Birds conserve significant energy by roosting in cavities, particularly during adverse weather 
conditions (Caccamise & Weathers, 1977; Du Plessis et al., 1994; Du Plessis & Williams, 1994; 
Cooper, 1999). Studies have shown that cavity- nesting birds beneﬁt re -productively from a 
favourable microclimate. Cavities help buffer eggs, nestlings, and adult saddlebacks against 
fluctuations in ambient temperature. Tree-cavity temperatures are more stable compared to the 
surrounding environment, with ambient temperatures showing greater variation and reaching 
lower minimums. Fluctuations in ambient temperature can negatively impact reproduction, as 
these temperatures often do not reach levels conducive to offspring development, particularly in 
cooler regions (Webb, 1987). Greater exposure to solar radiation can improve the microclimate 
within tree-cavity nests, as trees absorb and retain more thermal energy. (Rhodes, et.al., 2009)36

➢ Lichens and Mosses 
Lichens are highly effective bio monitors of atmospheric pollution due to their sensitivity in 
detecting and measuring the biological impacts of pollutants. By assessing changes in lichen 
communities or populations, they provide valuable insights into environmental changes. 
Consequently, lichens can serve as an early warning system for detecting shifts in environmental 
conditions in the State. (Upreti, et.al., 2015)37 
 
Symbiosis: Lichens consist of a fungal partner (mycobiont) and a photosynthetic partner 
(photobiont). The fungus provides structure and protection, while the photosynthetic partner 
produces food through photosynthesis. 
Mosses are small, non-vascular plants belonging to the division Bryophyta. They are one of the 
oldest groups of land plants, having adapted to a variety of terrestrial environments. 
Although moss and lichens are both called non-vascular plants, only mosses are plants. Mosses 
are included in a group of non-vascular plants called bryophytes. 
Lichens are bioindicators. Lichens are widely recognized as effective bioindicators, particularly 
for assessing air quality and environmental health. Their sensitivity to pollutants and 
environmental changes makes them valuable tools for monitoring ecosystems.  
Recent extensive lichen exploration in the State has identified 160 species. South Goa shows the 
highest diversity of pyrenocarpous lichens, with 71 species recorded, compared to 29 species in 
North Goa, with 21 species common to both districts. South Goa's denser and thoroughly explored 
forests contribute to this diversity. The presence of pyrenocarpous lichens suggests an abundance 
of smooth-barked trees, while the high number of foliicolous lichens indicates several healthy and 
undisturbed forests. Notable pristine habitats include Bhagwan Mahavir Wildlife Sanctuary, 
Cotigao Wildlife Sanctuary, Avem, Bela to Zombolim, Endrem to Tulshimol, Kuske waterfall 
area, Marlem, Nadkem, and Ravan Donger. Additionally, coconut and arecanut orchards, as well 
as cultivated plants, also support lichen growth in Goa.38 
Although mosses do not produce colourful flowers and seem to lack direct economic value to 
humans, they play a crucial ecological role. They colonize bare soil surfaces, helping to stabilize 
the soil and protect it from erosion caused by wind or rain. Mosses commonly inhabit rock surfaces 
and, along with lichens, are pioneers in harsh environments. They also fill niches unsuitable for 
other plants, making them a significant component of tropical rainforest ecosystems. 
Mosses are important for regulating the water cycle due to their high-water absorption capacity. 
They recycle nutrients, provide shelter for various invertebrates, particularly epiphytic forms, and 
help balance the environment by capturing atmospheric pollutants. Mosses, lacking a true cuticle, 
are more tolerant of heavy metals, enhancing their ability to adapt to polluted conditions.39 
 
 
37 Upreti, D. K., Bajpai, R., & Nayaka, S. (2015). Lichenology: Current research in India. In B. 
Bahadur et al. (Eds.), Plant Biology and Biotechnology: V olume I: (pp. 263). Springer India. 
38https://www.researchgate.net/publication/354946480_Pyrenocarpous_lichens_in_Goa_with_fiv

39https://www.researchgate.net/publication/216672803_Status_of_Mosses_in_Nilgiri_Hills_Wes
tern_Ghats_India 
 
 
371 
 
Sensitivity to Pollutants : Lichens are highly sensitive to air pollutants such as sulfur dioxide 
(SO₂), nitrogen oxides (NOₓ), ammonia (NH₃), and heavy metals. These pollutants can damage 
lichen tissues and disrupt their symbiotic relationship. 
Indicator Species: Because of their sensitivity, the presence or absence of certain lichen species 
is often used as an indicator of air quality. Declines in lichen diversity and abundance can signal 
deteriorating air conditions. 
Extreme Weather: Increased frequency of extreme weather events, such as droughts and heavy 
rainfall, can stress lichen populations and lead to declines. 
Heavy Metals : Accumulation of heavy metals from industrial emissions, mining, and other 
sources can be toxic to lichens. 
Pesticides and Herbicides : The use of chemicals in agriculture and forestry can harm lichen 
populations. 
Sensitivity to Pollutants: Mosses are also sensitive to air and water pollutants. Acid rain, heavy 
metals, and pesticides can adversely affect their growth and reproduction. 
Bioindicators: Like lichens, mosses are used as bioindicators to monitor environmental pollution, 
particularly heavy metal contamination. 
Temperature and Moisture : Mosses require specific temperature and moisture conditions. 
Changes in climate can alter their habitats, making them less suitable for moss growth. 
Drought and Desiccation: Mosses are highly dependent on moisture. Prolonged drought periods 
can lead to desiccation and death. 
Deforestation and Urbanization : The destruction of natural habitats reduces the available 
substrates and suitable environments for mosses. 
Wetland Drainage: Draining of wetlands for agricultural or urban development can eliminate 
crucial moss habitats. 
Soil Compaction and Erosion : Activities such as logging, construction, and heavy foot traffic 
can compact soil and erode areas where mosses grow. 
Trampling: Mosses are particularly vulnerable to trampling by humans and animals, which can 
crush and kill the plants.

➢ Wind Blown Seaside Cliffs- 
Windblown cliffs are the cliffs which are directly under influence of wind coming from the oceans 
towards the land study of such ecosystem is important to study to know more about biodiversity 
residing in areas like such. Goa has many cliffs like this be it Vagator, Baga, or Cabo de Rama 
species residing in such area are under direct threat due to following reasons. 
 
Impact of Climate Change: 
• Changes in wind patterns and storm intensity due to climate change can impact erosion 
rates and the stability of cliff ecosystems. 
 
372 
 
• Rising sea levels and increased storm surges can exacerbate cliff erosion and alter habitat 
availability. 
Human Activities: 
• Coastal development and recreational activities can disturb the fragile cliff ecosystems, 
leading to increased erosion and habitat loss. 
• Conservation efforts need to focus on protecting these areas from excessive human impact 
and preserving the natural processes that maintain their unique characteristics. 
By understanding the multifaceted role of wind in shaping seaside cliff ecosystems, we can better 
appreciate the resilience and adaptability of the organisms that inhabit these environments and take 
informed steps to protect and conserve these dynamic and beautiful landscapes. 
Coastal cliffs occur as a marked break in slope between the land and the sea. They may have 
sloping to vertical faces and form when slippage and/or coastal erosion take place. They have a 
range of geomorphological features depending on their resilience, structure and exposure to 
weathering and the action of the sea.40

➢ Hypersaline Environment of Salt Pans 
The salt production takes place in agricultural land near estuaries called khazan. Earlier there were 
36 villages in Goa involved in salt production, it is reduced to 9 villages claimed in a study 
published in year 2012. Now only 6 villages involved in salt production, namely Ribandar, Curca, 
Batim, Nerul, Arpora and Agarwada. (Kabilan Mani et.al, 2012, Flory Pereira, et.al. 2024)5051 
Hypersaline environments, which are saltier than seawater, vary greatly in salinity, ion 
composition, temperature, pressure, and nutrient levels. These environments host a wide variety 
of halophiles. Salinity significantly affects community composition, making some hypersaline 
ecosystems among the most diverse on Earth. High salt concentrations can both inhibit and 
promote different microbial processes, making their consideration essential for accurate global 
biogeochemical cycle models.52  
 
49https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/goa/grande-island-underwater-soundscape-reveals-eco-
threat/articleshow/93259474.cms 
 
50 Flory-Rereira, S., Gaonkar, S., Naik, S., Sayed, M., & Shirodkar, S. (2024). Vital role of mangroves in sustaining and 
protecting the salt pans. 
51 Kabilan mani , et. al. (2012), Community solar salt production in Goa, India. Aquatic Biosystems, 8(23), 1-8. 
52 Terry J Mcgenity and A. Oren, Hypersaline environments. March 2012.

Salt pans are part of traditional farming system called khazans which used for salt production. Salt 
pans are home to a vast colony of extremophiles that can survive in conditions of extreme salinity, 
low nutrition supply, high temperature, and low pH. During the salt harvesting period, 
temperatures of 35°C to 36°C in Goa’s salt pans facilitate evaporation in the crystallizer pond, 
achieving the necessary salinity for salt production. The salinity ranges from 400 to 450 PSU, and 
the pH levels from 7.6 to 8.25 indicate a halophilic and alkaline environment. In the sediments of 
Nerul salt pan, 53 distinct phyla were found, followed by Curca (50) and Agarwado (42). Salt pans 
bacterial composition showed that the phylum Pseudomonadota dominated the three sediment 
samples found there. Pseudomonadota, Bacillota, Desulfobacterota, Planctomycetota, 
Halanaerobiaeota, Chloroflexota, Verrucomicrobiota, Cyanobacteriota, Acidobacteriota, 
Myxococcota, Nitrospirota, Bacteroidota, Actinomycetota, Gemmatimonadota are some bacterial 
phyla recorded during study. 
These hypersaline natives exhibit resistance to osmotic stress, as evidenced by genes in their 
predicted functional gene profile. This allows them to actively participate in the carbon, nitrogen, 
and sulphur cycles within these hypersaline environments.53

➢ Microecosystem 
 
Microecosystems are small, multispecies systems, consisting of a subset of the biotic community 
and abiotic properties of a larger ecosystem and have the common features of ecosystems such as 
 
53 Priti Gawas and Savita Kerkar, Bacterial diversity and community structure of salt pans from 
Goa, India. 2023. Frontiers in Microbiology, Sec. Extreme Microbiology Volume 14 – 2023. 
54 https://www.treebo.com/blog/springs-in-goa/

food chains, production–consumption cycles, and hierarchies.55 Goa hosts many such ecosystems 
like tide pools, tree holes, moss patches, Biomeliads, and many more these ecosystems support 
numerous organisms including invertebrates and vertebrates. They provide conditions that 
encourages the growth of algae, fungi, and microorganisms which feed insect larvae and other

ecosystems is very important to utilize it restore biodiversity.  A study claims that species richness 
or single–species populations can be maintained, or at least extinctions can be minimized, by 
boosting rates of immigration. One possible way of achieving this is by establishing corridors of 
suitable habitat between reserves. Using moss patches as model microecosystems, corridors can 
reduce the rate of loss of species, and therefore help to maintain species richness. Connecting 
patches of habitat with corridors did indeed slow the rate of extinction of species, preserving 
species richness for longer periods of time than in disconnected habitat patches. Predators are 
predicted to be more susceptible to fragmentation because of their greater mobility and smaller 
population sizes.57 
 
➢ Ravines  
Ravine and gully erosion threatens large tracts of the world’s agricultural land and contributes to 
huge amount of soil loss and sediment production under different climatic and land use conditions. 
The damage is greatest in the alluvial plains of the semiarid and arid zones. In recent times, global 
attention has been paid to solve the problem of land restoration, and several techniques and models 
have been used for measuring the extent of gully erosion and their management for livelihood and 
environmental security. Many techniques have proved to be effective for gully prevention and 
control including vegetation cover, minimum tillage, terracing and check dams. However, these 
techniques are rarely adopted by farmers and other stakeholders in the long run because of several 
bottlenecks in extension services and policy implementation. Rehabilitation of these lands requires 
an integrated approach of using appropriate site-specific soil and water conservation measures and 
putting land under vegetation cover involving afforestation, horticulture, pasture and energy 
plantations depending upon the land suitability class following watershed approach. There is an 
urgent need of policy interventions at different levels to handle this menace.58

➢ Ecotones  
Ecotones are areas of steep transition between ecological communities, ecosystems, or ecological 
regions along an environmental gradient. Ecotones occur at multiple spatial scales and range from 
natural boundaries to human-generated ecotones. It has some of the characteristics of each 
bordering biological community and often contains species not found in the overlapping 
communities. An ecotonal area often has a higher density of organisms of one species and a greater 
number of species than are found in either flanking community. Some organisms need a 
transitional area for activities such as courtship, nesting, or foraging for food. Examples of 
ecotones include marshlands (between dry and wet ecosystems), mangrove forests (between 
terrestrial and marine ecosystems), grasslands (between desert and forest), and estuaries (between 
saltwater and freshwater). Mountain ranges can also create ecotones due to the changes in the 
climatic conditions on the slopes. 59 Goa is a home of such ecotones be it mangroves, Estuaries, 
 
 
59 https://www.britannica.com/science/ecotone 

 
378 
 
Riparian zones, Lower ghat region, and more. These ecotones can sometimes behave like buffers 
that can reduce the impact of disaster and climate change, Mangroves is one of the examples which 
has been highly studied due to its impact in withstanding tsunami waves and as a remedy of climate 
change but study of other ecotones is limited.  
 
 
Figure 3: Picture depicting ecotone 
Source - https://www.insightsonindia.com/environment/basic-concepts-of-ecosystem/ecotone-
ecological-niche/ecotone/ 
 
Characteristics of Ecotones 
Some of the major characteristic features of ecotones are discussed below: 
A. They can be natural or man-made. Example: agriculture field and forest (it is a man-made one).  
B. They may vary in size from narrow to wide. 
C. They are known to be zones of tension as they show conditions intermediate to the bordering 
ecosystems.  
D. They may also contain those species which are totally different from those found in the 
bordering systems.  
 
Importance of Ecotones 
Ecotones have so many important roles in the ecosystem, some of them are listed below: 
A. Ecotones show greater variation in an organism.  
B. They provide a comfortable habitat for different organisms i.e. by providing space for nesting 
for those animals who roam here and there in search of food or a place for a nest.  
C. They act as a bridge or mode of transportation of gene flow from one population to another as 
they show larger genetic diversity. 
D. They offer protections to the bordering of an ecosystem from various damages and that's why 
they are known to be the buffer zone. 
E. Ecotones also show sensitivity toward global climate change. Climatic changes take place 
because of the shifting of boundaries between ecosystems.60

➢ Burrows  
A burrow is a tunnel or hole that an animal digs for habitation and Goa’s varied landscape from 
high lands of Western Ghats to Coastal region host a lot of burrows and these burrow makers. 
Species like Bengal monitor lizard, some species of snakes, rodents, and fiddler crabs makes their 
burrows in forests or in damp soil in mangrove areas. These burrows sometimes also hosts species 
like otters, it has been seen that otters uses abandoned burrows along side waterbodies which they 
use as a shortcut to get into water in case of confrontation from predators. Burrows also plays a 
crucial role in expanding water streams around river banks. Burrows also improve soil structure, 
aeration, and water infiltration, facilitate the movement of organic matter through soil layers, 
Burrows provide shelter for various species, increasing local biodiversity, and serves as thermal 
refuges for many species during extreme weather event. 
 
➢ Termite mounds 
Mounds are nests for their inhabitants, which are colonies of small potentially vulnerable insects 
such as termites, and ants, which are susceptible to environmental fluctuations. Thus, the mound 
protects against enemies and hostile environmental condition. Mounds vary in shape, between 
and even within species. Yet, different species might also build similar mounds.61The termites' 
building behavior is influenced by environmental elements like heat flow and gas exchange 
during mound development. This alters the mound shape, which in turn changes the interior 
mound environment's reaction to external thermal oscillations.62  
Many experts in Goa have focused on termitomyces genus, mushrooms that grow around termite 
mounds, these mushrooms are also famous for their religious importance and are Goan delicacy. 
These mushrooms are plucked off termite mounds in forest areas, grasslands, plateaus and hill 
slopes in Goa and Karnataka. This symbiotic relationship is very fragile if termites get deprived 
of the fungus, they will starve and die.63

The ancient Indian tradition of anthill worship holds a significant place in Goan Hindu culture, 
intertwining local beliefs, linguistic history, and ecological awareness. This practice, deeply 
rooted in the region's past, continues to influence contemporary cultural and agricultural 
practices in Goa. 
In Goan praxis, the anthill is revered as a manifestation of the Earth Goddess. She is known by 
various names, including Sateri (or Santeri), Bhoomika, and Ela. This worship is so integral to 
local culture that it has influenced place names; for instance, the Goan village Bhoma derives its 
name from Bhoomi, meaning Earth, due to the presence of a worshipped anthill. 
The Konkani word for anthill is "ro'in" or "roen," which originates from the Austric word "rono," 
meaning "with holes." This etymology highlights the ancient roots of this practice, predating 
Indo-Aryan and Dravidian settlements in the region. When later settlers adopted this worship, 
they translated the concept into Prakrit as "Santara," from which the name Sateri likely derives. 
Interestingly, despite being commonly referred to as "anthills," these structures are not made by 
ants but by termites, sometimes misleadingly called "white ants." Termites, in fact, are 
entomologically closer to cockroaches than to ants and are primarily found in tropical and 
subtropical regions. Some of the most impressive examples of these termite mounds in active 
worship can be found in the village of Virnoda and at the Sateri temple in Morjim. 
The cultural respect for termites and their mounds extends beyond religious practice to influence 
agricultural methods. In many parts of Goa, particularly within the Dev Rai or sacred groves, the 
termite species Odontotermes obesus, locally known as "rawlu," is venerated as Rawalnath and 
given free rein of the land. This reverence has practical ecological implications: the Konkan 
culture traditionally avoids using pesticides to eradicate termites. 
This practice of coexistence yields an unexpected benefit. During the Hindu holy month of 
Shravan, the Konkan region, including Goa, is blessed with an abundance of Termitomyces 
species of mushrooms. These mushrooms have a symbiotic relationship with the termites, 
growing from their nests. The Termitomyces mushrooms vary greatly in size, from the massive 
T. titanicus, which can grow up to one meter in diameter, to the tiny Shringar Ollmi (T. 
microcarpus). 
In recent years, the Goa government has been promoting organic farming practices. While direct 
causality is debated among specialists, there's a belief that these organic agricultural methods 
may lead to an increase in the population of local mushrooms, including the prized 
Termitomyces species. This potential increase in mushroom biodiversity serves as another 
example of how traditional cultural practices and modern agricultural approaches can work 
together to enhance local ecosystems. 
 
381 
 
This complex interplay of ancient worship, linguistic history, ecological awareness, and modern 
agricultural practices demonstrates the unique and multifaceted significance of termites and their 
mounds in Goan culture and biodiversity.646566 
In Mongabay’s study it is estimated that roen or termite hill recycles about 500 kg of organic 
matter from the forest each year and the mineral and nutrient-rich soil are returned to the forest 
soil pool. Over 50 percent dead plant material on the forest floor and in grasslands, millions of 
tons each year is converted by the powerful enzymes of these species inside the fungus gardens 
of the termite hill. Each hectare of forest in the Western Ghats has about 810 termite hills. In 
mixed forests, like in Western Ghats, where there is a lot of tree diversity, creating mixed leaf 
litter on ground for termites to decompose, termites invade between 21 and 79 percent of trees.67

Introduction – 
Goa's remarkable biodiversity, characterized by its diverse assemblage of mammals and 
herpetofauna, represents a critical component of the state's natural heritage and ecosystem 
functioning. The inclusion of these species’ groups in the Goa State Biodiversity Strategy and 
Action Plan's 10-year framework is paramount, as they serve as key indicators of ecosystem health, 
provide essential ecological services, and face mounting anthropogenic pressures. From the 
charismatic Indian Bison  to endemic amphibians like the Mhadei Toad, these species collectively 
maintain crucial ecological processes including seed dispersal, pest control, and food web stability. 
Their conservation is not merely about preserving individual species but ensures the resilience of 
entire ecosystems that support Goa's biodiversity and human well-being. As these species face 
increasing threats from habitat fragmentation, human-wildlife conflict, and climate change, a 
comprehensive strategy within the GSBSAP becomes essential to secure their future while aligning 
with national and international conservation commitments.

1. Scope of sub-committee (What all the sub-committee covers?) 
Considering the unique geological history of Goa and the state being a mosaic of 
interdependent ecosystems, to the extent possible and within the limits of this 
subgroup cover the known aspects of microbial diversity, including the non-living 
host-dependent zoonotic and plant viruses based on available publications from the 
Portuguese colonial period and after the liberation of Goa and understand the gaps 
remaining at the ecosystem, species and genetic level to identify in situ and ex-situ 
conservation requirements at habitat and community level and beyond taxonomic 
knowledge explore the bioeconomic and bio-industrial potential of microbes in Goa 
useful in human welfare and all the related aspects of research and development 
which future workers in the field need to prioritise considering the challenges, 
opportunities and threats created by global warming and climate change. The 
paradigm for such work integrates bygone biospheres with present sixth biosphere 
and looks challenges in the area of microbial diversity in future in view of high rate of 
urbanization, sea level rise and threats to known and unexplored microbial habitats 
and micrihabitats.  
 
2. Current scenario for the State of Goa for that particular sub-committee. 
During the Portuguese colonial period, some efforts were made to study 
microorganisms, especially the microbial pathogens harming humans, animals, and 
crops in Goa. The data generated after the liberation of Goa on microbial diversity lies 
scattered in dispersed publications, unpublished reports, dissertations, and theses. 
Urbanization has caused heavy fragmentation of the landscapes in Goa thus impacting 
the microbial habitats. So, there is an urgent need to save what remains. But that can’t 
be done unless we know what is existing. Compared to macroflora and macrofauna it is 
difficult to work on microorganisms. But if we can get many ideas from the published 
work and existing microbial species. This data can guide future microbiologists to use 
novel techniques and technologies systematically. The broad microbial classification 
which would guide this work is shown in figure 1. 
 
452 
 
 
Figure 1 Broad Microbial classification to be used for this work 
Swiss biologist David Thaler (2021) (Is Global Microbial Biodiversity Increasing, 
Decreasing, or Staying the Same? Front. Ecol. Evol. 9:565649) has mentioned –“Animal and 
plant biodiversity is decreasing. In contrast, the global direction, and the pace of change in 
microbial, including viral, biodiversity is unknown. Important niches for microbial diversity 
occur in highly specific associations with plants and animals, and these niches are lost as 
hosts become extinct. The taxonomic diversity of human gut bacteria is reported to be 
decreasing. On the other hand, SARS-CoV-2 variation is increasing. Where microbes are 
concerned, Darwin’s “tangled bank” of interdependent organisms may be composed mostly 
of other microbes. There is the likelihood that as some classes of microbes become extinct, 
others evolve and diversify. A better handle on all processes that affect microbial biodiversity 
and their net balance is needed. Lack of insight into the dynamics of microbial biodiversity 
evolution is arguably the most profound and consequential unknown about human knowledge 
of the biosphere.”  
Setting out the parameters of the work on Microbial diversity  
Thaler’s (2021) comments cited above and especially his concerns on “dynamics of evolution 
of microbial biodiversity ‘are essential because Goa is a mosaic of different rock formations 
and soil groups which all come under the Archean Western Dharwar Craton (WDC) therefore 
any work on Microbial diversity here needs to look at 1. Geological time scale 2. 
Evolutionary time scale and 3. Plate tectonics and continental drift. 4. Paleoclimate changes 
and sea level fluctuations. Besides there is another interesting dimension of post Columbian, 
post A.D. 1492 intercontinental exchange of species resulting in introduction of exotic, 
foreign plant and animal species in Goa including exotic microorganisms. Finally, there is 
bioinvasion by non native species- and in this case there is very little knowledge in the 
microbiological realm. Table 1 sums up the approach to the present work. These are new 
metrics to be used in such works (Kamat, 2023, unpublished).

Understanding of Microbial diversity during the Portuguese period 
The task of this subgroup is special because Goa was not ruled by the British and got 
liberated from the Portuguese so in discussing the status of the work the contributions to the 
knowledge of microbial diversity during the Portuguese colonial period, especially in the first 
half of the 20th century can’t be forgotten. A review of this work follows mostly as work 
done by the pioneer microbiologist Froilano De Mello. We can say that this was the real 
beginning of getting an understanding of tropical microbial diversity in Goa which laid down 
the foundation for more extensive research after 1961.  
 
454 
 
Froilano De Mello’s work on a variety of microorganisms 
Froilano investigated Cholera from 1912 to 1918 and identified Vibrio as main causative 
agent of the disease. Cases of diptheria and bacillary dysentery were also detected by him. He 
isolated causative organism of cerebrospinal meningitis identified as Meningoccio 
Weichlelbaum, types A & B. From human intestines he identified four species of Spirochetes.  
From the intestines of Indian termite, he isolated a new dysentery causing protozoa named as 
Entamebe Goheeni. He contributed to several species of microbial parasites in family 
Trypanosomidae, in Indian birds. These included 10 species in the genus Trypanosoma, 
discovered between 1935-40, two species in Leptomonas, found in 1921-22, a single species 
each of Bodo identified in 1921 and in Leishmania, discovered in 1922. He found 
Dimastigomatix, in 1938, and Trimitus, in 1930's. He named three species in Gen. 
Devescovina, in 1929. He found a single species in Gen. Pseudotriconympha, in 1927 and 
three more in 1935.  He got a single species in Gen. Holomastigoides, in 1918, four in 1927, 
and seven in 1935. In Spirotriconympha, he got two species discovered in 1927 and three in 
1935.  In 1929 he found a single species in Gen. Metastephanonyma. His work on human 
malaria was significant. He discovered eight new species of plasmodia. From local birds he 
did pioneer work to understand the 29 species he discovered under genus Haemoproteus.  
New species Haemocystidium kopki de Mello is named after him. A new species of 
toxoplasma was discovered in 1914 and two in 1935, in the same year he reported seven new 
species of Leucocytozoon in Indian Birds. He turned his attention to the parasites of Indian 
tortoises in which he found four new species of haemogregarina, in Indian tortoises; the first 
one was reported in 1917 and three between 1931-1936. Then by studying the Indian lizard-
Calotes versicolor he found a blood parasite in genus Karyolysus. The parasites from Indian 
frogs included a single species from Racophorus maculatus identified in 1930; two species in 
Bufo melanostictus discovered in 1932; two species in common local Rana tigrina - found in 
1932; a single species in Rana malabarica- identified in 1937 and a single parasite in Rana 
cyanophylcytis identified in 1932.  
Pioneer work in Mycology 
At the old Goa Medical College De Mello carried out pioneer work in medical mycology. 
Mycological research in India did not begin with E J Butler in 1907. Infact 
Indian mycologists have completely ignored contributions of doctors in Portuguese Goa to 
modern mycology. Goa and rest of India has not produced a microbiologist, pathologist, 
epidemiologist and medical mycologist like Dr. Indalêncio Froilano De Melo (1887-1955). 
Half of previous century is illustrated by his prolific research work. Google scholar scientific 
search engine shows 128 papers in his name for the period 1914 to 1955. Professor Christina 
Bastos, Institute of Social Sciences, University of Lisbon as part of her project Empire, 
centers and provinces: the circulation of medical knowledge.  Christina wrote a beautiful 
monograph- From India to Brazil, with a microscope and a seat in Parliament: the life and 
work of Dr. Indalêncio Froilano de Melo (History of Science and Technology, 2008, 2: 139-
189). Christina wrote- “he became one of the most famous Goan doctors ever; he combined 
clinical work, research and public health; he taught medicine, attended international 
conferences, directed medical services and headed the medical school.”  At age of 27, he had 
attended the All India Sanitary Conference and the Third Entomological Meeting, both in 
Lucknow, 1914, where he lectured on the very recently formed field of medical mycology by 
invitation of the Viceroy of India. On the invitation of the then government of British India 
 
455 
 
he participated as a delegate, in the second conference on Mycology held at Pusa. Dr. E.J. 
Butler, who is considered a pioneer of modern mycological studies in India was the President 
of the Conference. He referred to work done by De Mello in his inaugural address. Butler 
said ". In Captain de Mello we greet not only the distinguished scientist but the representation 
of our most ancient ally, Portugal. I am sure that all will join me in thanking him for coming 
from Goa to attend our meetings and to tell us something about the results of his studies in 
the subject of medical mycology, in which he is the leading authority, indeed, almost the only 
worker, in the Indian continent."Froilano De Mello is one of the pioneers of modern medical 
and tropical mycology in India. He discovered several species of yeasts and fungi. To provide 
some glimpses of his research- In 1914, he published papers on Trichophyton which affect 
skin and identified a new species viannai. In 1917, he went to Lahore to present a paper in 
Indian Science Congress on ‘Blastomyces and Blastomycosis” which infect lungs. With his 
student Paes in 1918, he published description of new yeast Endomyces cruzi infecting 
respiratory system. In 1920, he published research on Apsergillus polychromous and 
Epidermophyton salmoneum. With his student Carmo Vaz, he was pioneer to publish 
research on medically important Indian strains of Aspergillus. In 1929, he was invited to 
deliver a lecture at Seth G. S. Medical College of Bombay on medical mycology and the 
large field it offers for research work in Índia. Same year he published, with his student 
Rodrigues, a preliminary note on a Case of Dermatomycosis. In 1932 he described several 
novel species of infectious Scopulariosis. In 1939, he created a sensation in the medical world 
by publishing a paper on the parasitism of feminine Genital organs by yeasts and yeast-like 
fungi (Feminine genital Levurosis) about which the rest of India knew nothing. In the same 
year, he published a report on the characters and identification of the yeasts living in 
commensalism in the intestine of some laboratory animals and followed it by a report on 
experimental studies on diets deficient in vitamin B and their influence on the intestinal yeast 
flora of animals. He also published two novel species of Aspergillus. Interestingly the 
pathogenic dimorphic yeast which he and Fernandes had identified in 1917 as Cryptococcus 
costantini was confirmed in 1975 as asexual stage of fungal pathogen Filobasidiella 
neoformans. Medical world knows this yeast today as Cryptococcus neoformans. He 
migrated to Brazil in 1951. In August 1954, he went to Perth, Australia. He gave an excellent 
presentation on mycological and helminthological studies in Portuguese 
India at Comunicações portuguesas ao II Congresso da Associação Científica do Oceano 
Índico. 
Microbial diversity studies post De Mello 
From 1945 till 1961 microbiological studies continued at Old Goa Medical college and these 
reports mostly on human pathogens and parasites are available in the old documents. 
Gaps in the knowledge till 1961 
No studies are available from 1910 to 1961 on microorganisms like actinobacteria, halophilic 
bacteria, Iron and Sulphur bacteria, cyanobacteria, mycorrhiza, macrofungi, soil microbes, 
marine and mangrove microflora, lichens, plant pathogens and plant viruses. People were 
employing various microorganisms in traditional processes such as production of coconut 
vinegar, feni and various fermented foods without any scientific understanding.  
Status of microbial diversity after Goa’s liberation in 1961 
 
456 
 
The specific details of status in form of preliminary checklists of known microbial species is 
given in various annexures at the end and includes viruses of humans and plants, archaea and 
eubacteria, actinobacteria and cyanobacteria, microfungi and macrofungi, algae and lichens 
and mycorrhizal fungi.  
Known viral and microbial diversity of Goa (refer the annexures at the end for details) 
Taxonomic group
