Lichens 
 
199 
Total 2025 
 
This is not a complete and fully verified and validated list as such work is a time-consuming 
process. The species listed form a tip of the massive iceberg of microbial diversity of Goa. 
We have just provided a glimpse of about 2000 species but actual estimate may cross 5000 
species and an All Taxa Microbial biodiversity survey may reveal more than 10-20000 
species. This estimate is based on studies carried on Earth elsewhere.  
Microbial diversity began to be studied seriously after Goa became a Union Territory. 
However, most of the studies were confined to newly established National Institute of 
Oceanography and CPIR under University of Bombay.  
Later a centre of ICAR was established. Then various colleges began microbiological 
projects. The Foundation of Goa University boosted microbial diversity research from     
1985-86. Most of the present knowledge of the microbial diversity of Goa can be attributed to 
published and unpublished work at NIO and Goa University and Goa Medical College. Then 
the colleges affiliated to Goa University also contributed through various projects and 
programs. There is a huge bank of unpublished work on different aspects of microbial 
diversity in the form of various project reports, graduate and post-graduate level dissertations 
and PhD theses. It is a time-consuming task to validate this work and get some idea of 
microbial diversity not available through peer-reviewed publications.  
Major research areas and researchers  
Ecosystem specific research  
This has been covered by different researchers at NIO and Goa University who have 
identified several microbial species from diverse ecosystems such as marine area, near shore 
waters, intertidal zones, beaches, sand dunes, bays, coves, estuaries, rivers, lakes, salt pans, 
forests, grasslands etc.  
 
 
457 
 
Micorbial habitats explored  
Hundreds of microbial habitats have been surveyed, sampled and screened for microbial 
diversity. These include from human skin and blood to soils, fish, shellfish, seashells, marine, 
estuarine, lake, stream sediments, ores, sands, water, foam, fruits, vegetables, flowers, nectar, 
juices, trees, wood, leaves, roots etc.  
Extreme habitats and extremophiles 
NIO and Goa University microbiologists have done wide-ranging work to study the diversity 
of microorganisms in extreme environments. These include salt pans, tar balls, paint films, 
industrial effluents etc.  
Actinobacteria 
Most of this work has been done at Goa University and NIO leading to good idea of the 
extent of diversity of this group.  
 
Microfungi or anamorphic forms of higher fungi 
Goa University has done considerable work in this area since 1986.  
Unicellular and dimorphic yeasts 
Lot of work on yeasts diversity from sampling floral nectar, fruits, plant storage organs, 
beetles, freshwater lakes, fountains has been done at Goa Unuversity  
Lichens and mycorrhiza 
There is a considerable amount of work done at Goa University on lichens and mycorrhiza.  
Cyanobacteria and algae 
Most of the work on cyanobacteria and algae has been done at Goa University, affiliated 
science colleges and NIO. 
Wild edible, non-edible, medicinal and toxic mushrooms 
Most of the work has been done at Goa University in microbiology and botany departments  
Animal, human and plant viruses 
Lacking facilities to identify viruses most of the work has been outsourced and the 
publications indicate huge diversity of viruses in Goa. 
3. Priority areas/species/habitats- (a bulleted or pointwise list), Traditional wisdom from 
sector if applicable? 
Priority areas include the full exploration of microbial habitats in the following list 
• Microbial diversity exploration of the full continental shelf near Goa at 
different depths as its repository of ancient sediments  
• Microbial diversity of coastal waters of Goa within the exclusive economic 
and active fishing zone at different depths and before, during and after the 
monsoon season  
 
458 
 
• Complete cataloguing of marine viruses in nearshore and offshore waters of 
Goa 
• Thorough sampling of the tropospheric air environment over the Arabian Sea 
to identify microbial signatures in dust samples blown off from deserts in 
Saudi Arabia and the middle east. 
• Controlled sampling of the rainwater to detect BIN (biological ice nuclei) and 
microorganisms carried by the clouds. 
• Deep drilling of the ocean floor in a transect between Goa to Eastern 
Madagascar along the track of continental drift and detection of culturable and 
non-culturable microorganisms in the cores drilled from different depths to 
reconstruct the bygone microbiospheres 
• Complete survey of the beaches of Goa and sampling of the sand deposits at 
different depths in a north south and subcoastal transect and identification of 
culturable and non culturable microorganisms 
• Complete cataloguing of the mycorrhizal fungi and actinorrhizal bacteria in 
sand dunes of Goa. 
• Sand dune microbial diversity mapping. 
• Sampling of waters at different depths and sediment by cores of bays and 
coves for detecting microbial diversity. 
• Complete microbial diversity mapping of offshore marine islands of Goa such 
as Anjediv island under Indian Navy with due permissions, surrounding 
smaller islands near Anjediv, Kunco island of Canacona, Grande island, St 
Georges island, bat island in Marmagoa bay. 
• Sampling and inventorization of microrganisms associated with sunchi coral 
reef in Marmagoa bay. 
• Sampling and identification of microbial diversity in intertidal zones such as at 
Anjuna, Palolem, Agonda with special focus on cyanobacteria and halophiles. 
• Specific sampling of wind blown seaside cliffs of Goa for detection of 
microorganisms in soil stressed by wind and other factors. 
• Specific detection and isolation microfragments of plant amber from placer 
deposits and alluvial sand deposits to separate amber fragments with biogenic 
inclusions such as microfungi. 
• Detail study of calcimycocavite species infecting and colonizing fragments of 
seashells on beaches receiving heavy seashells deposits and identification of 
the fungi and isolation of their cultures. 
• Detail studies of endolithic and cryptoendolithic microorganisms from 
different rocks in Goa. 
• Complete inventorization of microbial diversity of salt pans of Goa. 
• Complete inventorization of microbial diversity of estuaries and estuarine 
sediments to fill in gaps left by NIO microbiologists. 
• Comprehensive survey of all lotic and lentic freshwater resources and their 
sampling for isolation of eubacteria, cyanobacteria, actinobacteria, yeasts and 
fungi and protozoa.  
• Mapping of microbial diversity of all the waterfalls, springs and fountains of 
Goa. 
 
459 
 
• Exhaustive focus on Microbial speleology and cave microbiology to fill the 
vast gaps in knowledge about unique microflora found in the natural and 
manmade caves, caverns, tunnels. 
• Covering all 25 soil types identified by National Bureau of soil survey and 
land use mapping (NBSSLUP) for detail microbiological examination to 
identify the soil microflora and culture the same. 
• Systematic isolation of endophytic bacteria, yeasts and fungi from all the 1650 
plant species of Goa. 
• Systematic cataloguing of animal and plant viruses of Goa including viruses 
found in bats and birds. 
• Systematic sampling of flowers to map nectariferous yeasts.  
• Mapping of microflora of plant storage organs, tubers, rhizhomes and bulbils. 
• Building an inventory of extremophilic microorganisms of Goa including 
halophiles, acidophiles, alkaliphiles, thermophiles, magnetotactic bacteria. 
• Filling gaps in knowledge about microorganisms causing food spoilage. 
• Full inventorization of freshwater fungi of Goa.  
• Full inventorization of Iron and Sulphur bacteria, Manganese oxidizing 
bacteria from mining region of Goa. 
• Subjecting all the area under government forests to mapping of microbial 
diversity with priority for cynobacteria, lichens, mushrooms and litter 
degrading fungi and fungi found in forest streams. 
• Identification all viral and microbial pathogens of all the cultivated crops in 
Goa. 
• Complete checklisting of all the human and animal microbial and viral 
pathogens identified in Goa.  
• Establishment of a state level public funded Goa Microbial Culture Collection 
repository for ex situ preservation of the germplasm. 
• Detail metagenomic studies of important microbial habitats. 
• Production of DNA based molecular identification catalogue of all the 
culturable microorganisms isolated from Goa. 
• Top priority for DNA based identification of all the novel species of 
microorganisms.  
• Systematic georeferencing, marking and in situ conservation and protection of 
habitats where novel microbial taxa have been reported and published. 
• Microflora associated with all the organs of introduced plant species. 
 
Traditional wisdom in this sector 
 
Ethnomycological and sociobiological traditions  
 
• Goa has a defined ecotheological tradition related to the sacred nature of 
mushrooms known as Roen Olamis. Roen depicts the termite mound and 
Olamis denote the spore bearing teleomorphs of the edible mushrooms. Like 
the Santhal tribals in West Bengal Goa worships the goddess of mushroom 
producer termite hills as Santeri or Bhumika.  
 
460 
 
• The ecotheological traditions of worshipping the goddess of mushrooms thus 
links Goa to Aztec and Mayan culture in central America which worshipped 
different species of mushrooms such as Psilocybe cubensis and Psilocybe 
Mexicana. 
• Tarangas or sacred umbrellas the sacred insignia of the goddess of termite hill 
Santeri is umbrella-shaped and is inspired by the shape of a typical fully 
grown epigeal stage of teleomorph of Termitomyces heimii or Termitomyces 
albuminosa. However, the community has no historical memory about origin 
of the design.  
• Goa’s ethnomycological and ethnomycophagic traditions are pre-agricultural 
and over 5000 years old. These traditions show that without any knowledge of 
microbiology and awareness of the microscopic world around them, people 
have been considering macroscopic bodies of fungi known as macrofungi as 
wild edible plants which they uniformly named Alami, Olami, or Ovamis 
depending on pronouncement in different parts.  
• By considering mushrooms as some special kind of seasonally occurring wild 
edible plants the local communities, especially forest dwellers and grasslands-
dependent agro-pastoral communities, developed a mushroom lore with local 
terms identifying the mushrooms by habitat, habitat, season, colour, shape, 
size etc.  
• Ethnomycologically we can identify at least 100-150 species of macrofungi 
known to the local people as edible, medicinal and toxic or purely ornamental 
species however the traditional knowledge of harvesting, marketing and 
consumption was limited to only the proven edible species.  
• Interestingly, no tests for differentiating edible species from toxic species is 
done by the local wild mushroom collectors indicating the continuation of the 
traditions which has survived from the hunter-food gathering stage of human 
cultural evolution without any changes. 
•  System of taboos ensuring judicious and balanced collection of wild edible 
mushroom existed about 50 years ago compelling the collectors to leave 
behind at least 50 percent behind but these ethical traditions laid down by oral. 
• As compared to any other state or union territory in India only in Goa we find 
very high and consistent demand for the wild edible Termitophilic mushrooms 
which people never knew as fungi cultivated by subterranean mound building 
termites.  
• Traditionally people discovered what they label as “olamo or ovmo”, the 
cerebroid, convoluted, foul smelling brain shaped mass, the fungus garden 
created by the fungus cultivator termites as the source of the harvested wild 
edible Termitomyces mushrooms. However, they didn’t make any such 
connection to smallest species in this group locally known as Shiti, shitol, Xitt, 
Xitov, Xitol, chhiti, Shingar, sringar Olamis, scientifically known as 
Termitomyces microcarpus. 
• A solitary mushroom was named Khut or khutyale, A red coloured Tambde, 
one with a sharp bird like beak as Chochale, a bronze coloured one as Sonyale, 
a fat mushroom as fugo due to its ballooning size, inedible ones by general 
term Kuski.  
 
461 
 
• Priority area in this sector is systematic ecotheological, ethnomycological and 
mycophagic studies using standard ethnological and anthropological and 
sociobiological methodology.  
• Priority area is also planned eco-conservation of wild habitats of all the edible 
mushrooms inside and outside the government forest areas. 
• Priority area is a total ban on wild edible mushroom species identified by 
experts as novel taxa- either as novel species, forms, or varieties. These should 
never be permitted for harvesting either by local communities or by collectors 
who market these crops without any regulations whatsoever. 
 
`  Traditional wisdom in fermentation knowledge  
• Without any understanding of the fermenting microorgnisms involved the local 
communities have been engaged in following processes and production. 
 
• Use of leavened bread with use of coconut toddy sap which has saccharophilic 
fermenting yeasts 
• Use of a complex microbial community of endogenous yeasts and bacteria in primary 
fermentation of cashew apples.  
 
• Use of halophilic bacteria and yeast for salting the raw mangoes and in pickle 
production. 
 
 
• Use of beneficial fermenting microorganisms in baking Sannahs. 
 
• Use of Acetic acid bacteria like acetobacter and gluconobacter in production of 
vinegar from fermentation of coconut toddy. 
 
• Use of a community of microorganisms like Lactococci in making cheese. 
 
Priority areas include documentation of these traditional processes and products, 
metagenomic studies to identify the culturable and non culturable microorganisms 
involved in the process, isolation of the key microorgnisms essential for the product, 
obtaining their pure cultures, standardizing the traditional process with better 
knowledge of all the members of microbial community used. 
There needs to be a state level pure culture bank to conserve and preserve the 
microorganisms isolated from all these traditional processes. 
 
Traditional knowledge of biofertilizers 
 
• People have been using the mud from salt pans of Goa without understanding the role 
of Sulphur reducing bacteria and cyanobacteria involved in deposition of compounds 
like Iron Sulphide and other nitrogenous metabolites. 
 
462 
 
 
• People have been using dry algal mats known as “shelo” in local language as manure 
without knowing its cyanobacterial diversity. 
 
• People have been applying bone meal or powder of bones to fruit trees without 
incorporation of any fungus and leaving it to nature to dissolve the matric of the bone 
and release the phosphate. This is possible because they have indirect knowledge that 
organic acid producer microfungi like soil Aspergilli would do the job of reacting 
with the powder and releasing the phosphorous.  
Priority area in this sector is to identify the beneficial phosphate solubilizing 
microorganisms and nitrogen rich cyanobacteria from soils.

researchers in the area to provide 
necessary information on microorganisms 
in their domain thus leaving big gaps in 
actual knowledge 
 Institutional policy reforms to make public disclosure of public

7. Socio-economic aspect- people’s contribution towards the sector and 
implications on people 
  
(How does the sector affect general public and how will they be affected if this sector 
was not conserved/ protected? - for example for Marine Sector-many coastal 
communities are depended on fisheries for livelihood, threat to them because of rising 
sea temperature would adversely impact their livelihood)  
 
Socio economic aspect  
 
Considering the raw deal received by microorganisms in the discourse and decision 
making of biological species there is a long way to go the convey the direct and 
indirect impact of :- 
1. Lack of understanding of habitats and microhabitats of microorganisms in 
different ecosystems in the state. 
 
2. Lack of knowledge of culturable and non-culturable microbial diversity of the state. 
 
3. Lack of understanding the full magnitude and dimension of microbial diversity in 
the state may lead to direct and indirect impacts such as :- 
(1) Loss of novel species yet to be explored and identified 
 
(2) Loss of economically beneficial species yet to be prospected  
 
(3) Loss of ecosystem services rendered by these species for millions of years     
resulting in dangerous impact on health and environment  
 
(4) Loss of patentable knowledge acquired through systematic bioprospecting 
and bioeconomic analysis of the culturable microbial species leading to 
valuable intellectual property rights for the country.  
 
In a state with more than 68 percent urban population the consequences of loss of 
microbial habitats and species would be dangerous. 
 
 
 
Peoples’ contributions to the sector 
 
People have duty to be microbiologically literate and first volunteer to reveal the full 
knowledge about traditional fermentation processes so experts can identify the 
scientific principles and microbial agents behind these. Besides people through BMCs 
need to understand the meaning and importance of any novel microbial taxa found in 
their area and extend unconditional support to conserve, preserve and protect the 
habitat where it gets discovered and stop interference in the location. People have a 
special duty not to be tempted to consume what their ancestors were consuming 
thousands of years ago especially the difficult to domesticate wild edible termitophilic 
mushroom species of Goa or at least based on expert advice undertake sustainable 
harvesting and never touch any species found to be a novel taxa. People can 
contribute by getting training to produce wild cultivable strains of local adapted edible 
mushrooms, produce algal biofertilizers, use salt pans for production of halophilic 
 
472 
 
bacteria and yeasts, learn new techniques for Cashew, coconut feni production, 
improve the primary process of cashew fermentation, vinegar production, production 
of traditional leavened Goan bread or wines from different locally grown fruits. 
Various algal biofertilizers can be produced by utilizing available biodiversity of 
nitrogen rich local cyanobacteria and algae. There is limitless scope to utilize locally 
available economically, industrially and biotechnologically beneficial microorganisms 
for people centric bioentrepreneurship, biobusinesses and bioemployment. People 
need to conserve their soil resources for precious soil microbiota.  
 
Implications for the people from this sector 
 
The positive economically beneficial implications are vast and discussion on the same 
would be voluminous as beneficial microorganisms found in the state have 
tremendous potential in biobusiness and biotechnology.  
 
The negative implications stem from existence and knowledge of microbes which are 
viewed as foes of humans and animals, and these include zoonotic viruses and various 
pathogens and parasites of humans and animals found in the state. This negative list 
of “microbial foes in Goa” is also important for safety and security of the whole 
population and to prevent any disease outbreaks or epidemics in future.

9. Role of BMCs 
BMCs need to be first made micribiologically literate as beyond knwoedge of 
mushrooms they are not aware of other species in the microbial world. Only after this 
educational and training phase is over then systematic actions can be planned for 
conservation and exploration of microbial habitats and  
 
10. Success Story/ies of any successful intervention for 
conservation/protection/sustainable use of bioresources in the respective sector in 
the state of goa for the sector (if any) 
 
• It is generally observed that microbial diversity is automatically conserved, 
preserved and protected in community sacred groves as evidenced by a novel 
genus of hyphomycetes microfungi named as Vanakripa found at Paikacho 
vhall on the hill of Morpirla village.  
• By systematically following the instructions issued over more than four 
months the wild natural habitat of a novel species of Termitomyces was 
conserved and protected by BMC member in his private property at 
Galajibaga Canacona. The novel species on basis of DNA based molecular 
identification is named Termitomyces putuense sp, nov 2023 
• A long term collaborative effort in association with members of Bandoda 
BMC and Shiroda BMC under the supervision of GSBB resulted in 
identification of several novel taxa of ascomycetes and basidiomycetes 
mushrooms from June 2021 to July 2023. This is claimed to be first such 
community based microbial diversity inventorization experiment in India.  
• A mass awareness workshop by GSBB on ecoconservation of Termitomyces 
mushrooms in Goa was first of its kind in India aided by an educative 
informative poster 
• An online webinar for officers of forest department explaining the ecology, 
biology, diversity, taxonomy and conservation needs of widely marketed and 
highly prized local wild edible Termitomyces mushrooms was first of such 
kind in India organized by GSBB  
 
11. Good practice example from other states / Interesting discoveries/ did you know 
facts or any other interesting piece related to the sector 
 
Many states like Tamil Nadu, Kerala are promoting community based production of 
algal biofertilizers and pharmaceutically important Spirulina. Many states have 
promoted large scale cultivation of several varieties of edible mushrooms. Similar 
potential and possibilities exist in Goa.  
 
12. Additional information required -Maps, graphs, data, pertaining to the sector 
These aspects are already mentioned under 3 and would not be repeated. Additional 
information is available in form of huge amount of unpublished dissertations, project 
reports at several educational institutions and Goa University and at NIO, ICAR, 
GMC etc. and acquiring the same needs lot of administrative efforts at GSBB level. 
This is impossible without support and cooperation from all public funded 
 
476 
 
institutions. Active individual and superannuated scientists must also be persuaded to 
submit useful information to fill in our knowledge of known microbial diversity gaps. 
The medical practitioners and pathological laboratories, private hospitals and nursing 
homes may have a lot of clinical data on all pathogens. This data is not yet in public 
domain. Zonal agriculture offices have spatiotemporal data on crop diseases from 
which the microbial and viral pathogens can be gleaned. But this information needs to 
be made available. The soil atlas of Goa is also not made available. The detail 
geological and mineral map of Goa essential to undertake long term 
geomicrobiological studies is also yet to be available.

Annexure I  
Viral Diversity of Goa  
Although viruses are not covered as “life forms” or as “biological species” under CBD, 1992 
and NBA, 2002 these impact living species. Since there are no mechanisms established for a 
national or state mapping and inventory of viruses, its Important to bring together available 
data for knowledge of stakeholders in economy, health and pharmaceutical sector.  
The following is quick list of human and non human animal viruses reported from Goa.  
1.Japanese encephalitis- under control 
2.Chikungunya- on rise  
3-6 Dengue DEN four serotypes- on rise  
7. Yellow fever arbovirus -rare 
8. Rabies – under control 
9. Rubella virus – under control 
10. Measles virus- under control 
11. Mumps virus -under control 
12. Kyasnur Forest Disease Virus KFDV 
13. Hepatitis B – under control 
14. Hepatitis C- under control 
15-16 Herpes simplex and zoaster no testing 
17. Human papilloma virus HPV – common 
18. Adenoviruses causing conjunctivitis 
 
477 
 
19. Rotaviruses – many strains possible 
20. Enteric adenoviruses – many strains  
21-22. coxsackievirus a16 and enterovirus 71 Causing foot, mouth, toe diseases in children 
but specific testing missing 
23. Influenza virus specific testing absent 
24-25. HIV-2 (causes AIDS) dominant other strains HIV-1 rare testing data known  
26. Rhinoviruses causing common cold at least 160 strains nobody cares for testing 
27. Swine Flu H1N1 testing data known 
28. Bird flu suspected no data 
29. Covid-19 testing data known  
30. Many other rare viral diseases systemic or affecting different parts of body but no testing 
data Published  
By a rough estimate we in Goa get exposed to at least 150-200 strains of different viruses.  
Metagenomic viral studies of our sewage and wastewater would reveal very high diversity.

Traditional knowledge system of Goa 
Traditional knowledge systems represent the know-how of the indigenous communities, gathered 
through day to day walk of life, that emerged in a specific location within a certain physical and 
socio-cultural environment, displaying the specific knowledge and understanding, having 
linkages with necessary skill and technology. It refers to the knowledge, innovations and 
practices associated to biodiversity practiced by the indigenous as well as the local communities 
living in the specific areas. 
There is need for the identification, documentation, scientific validation along with evaluation of 
future scope of the traditional knowledge. It represents: Traditional ecological knowledge, 
traditional technical knowledge and traditional institutions and values for the sustenance of the 

 
489 
 
ecosystem, economy and society, through the sustainable use of resources for attaining clean, 
green and healthier growth. 
Traditional water harvesting system in Goa 
1) Sacred tanks:  The traditional water harvesting system in Goa, particularly the sacred 
tanks, stands as a testament to the ecological wisdom of the region's ancestors. These 
tanks, also known as "Devachi Tali," were not only vital for water management but were 
also intertwined with religious significance, being associated with local temples. 
Constructed collectively by villagers, they were annually desilted before the monsoon 
season to ensure their functionality. Initially serving practical purposes like irrigation, 
over time, their religious significance overshadowed their utilitarian role. 
Despite the advent of modern irrigation methods, these tanks still play a crucial role in 
storing rainfall, particularly in regions like Ponda, where their numbers are notably high. 
Unique features characterize these tanks, such as locally sourced materials like laterite 
and architectural elements like arched spaces and steps for easy access. However, 
historical events like Portuguese colonization led to the destruction of many temples and 
associated tanks, disrupting traditional practices.
 
490 
 
Social taboos surrounding these sacred tanks, such as prohibitions on spitting, urinating, speaking, entry of womenundergoing menstrual cycle,and consuming non-
vegetarian food, maintains their sanctity. However, with the decline of old customs and the convenience of piped water systems, these tanks face neglect, threatening their 
existence. Yet, they remain vital biodiversity hubs, supporting various flora and fauna, including medicinal plant reserves, and contributing to the ec ological richness of the 
region.1 
 
1https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/goa/temple-tanks-a-life-giving-link-between-man-and-god/articleshow/70518583.cms

2) Bhousulo bandh, means impounding rain water runoff from the hills for irrigating 
agricultural fields, through collective efforts by erecting bund. 
3) Suranga, is a horizontal tunnel excavated in hard laterite formations from which water 
seeps and flows out to be used by the local community staying downstream. 
4) Bharal, the hollow trunk of the Caryota urens cut into half and is used to bring water of 
the river or stream for the autumn agriculture. 
5) Paat, the canal excavated in the hard laterite formations for bringing water from the river 
or stream downward. 
6) Check Basin Method (Mherãni) is a method of irrigation used for levelled fields. The 
field is divided into basins based on the water capacity which are connected by a small 
drain. The highest basin is the main source of water. This method is feasible, less 
expensive and prevents soil erosion, since the rainwater remains within the basin. 
Mherãnican is used to irrigate large areas efficiently.2 
7) Furrow irrigation (Bhandiani) method is utilised for crops planted in rows. At the side 
of crop field, furrows are created to allow the water to flow between two rows of the 
planted crops. Once these furrows are filled, there will be enough water for at least two 
days. Though this method is comparatively cheap, it is labour-intensive.3 
8) ‘Char’ system (passages for water) is an irrigational practice observed in coconut groves 
of khazan areas. Chars are trenches created alongside khazans which get filled up during 
high tides providing a regular supply of water to the coconut trees around. 
Traditional Housing 
Before the arrival of the Portuguese in Goa, the Goan landscape had a unique vernacular 
architectural style and design based on local needs, availability of construction materials, and 
displaying local traditions. Houses that were constructed by using local clay, burnt brick, laterite 
stone and wood, very suitable for the heat and humidity as well as the climatic conditions of the 
lands with environmental sustainability. With the coming of the Portuguese, Goan houses 
witnessed the influence of Latin architecture. Many of the old houses standing in various parts of 
Goa, showcases the influence of the Latin architecture and have been known for its immense 
heritage values. 
 
 
Traditional agricultural practices

Goa is a small State in India's west coast. Goa has a unique ecological status based on its 
geographic borders. Goa has an abundance of natural resources and a rich cultural history. Its 
land is rich in agriculture. Goa's agricultural history dates back thousands of years, to the time 
when food gathering gave way to food cultivation.4 
 
1) Kumeri cultivation: The Kumeri, is the slash and burn practice of agriculture done on 
the hill slopes for growing a variety of millets like Vari, Pakhad, Kango, Kulith, 
Udid.After learning about pattern cropping and land usage, the seasonal activity chart is 
examined. The seasonal chart suggests that the rustics work in various agricultural 
pursuits all year round. Sanvsar Padva (Hindu New Year) in March or April marks the 
beginning of their agricultural practice for the upcoming season. Preparing agricultural 
plots is the first step. These areas serve as nursery beds for tubers and chilles. mostly 
made with a simple technique called "slash and burn," or "jhumimng," as it is called in 
the Northeast. It is called Kumeri cultivation in Goa. A cleared area undergoes a cyclic 
change after two to three years.5

2) Puran sheti: 
The landless farmers in Sattari, Dharbandora, and Bicholim Taluka formerly relied 
heavily on Puran Sheti, or silt-based paddy farming (Rabi crops), as their main source of 
income. This farming method was used on the banks of the Mhadei River and its 
tributaries, such as the Nanoda, Velsachi, Valvanti, and Ragada Nhai. It was a traditional 
farming method that used solely organic manure, such as kusharem, clay, and cow dung.

3) Khazan: the agriculture evolved mainly in the coastal areas of Goa, wherein the 
nutritious and salt tolerant rice varieties were grown. 
 
 
4) Vaigan: Vegetable cultivation done mainly during the autumn season by irrigating fields 
with water available in the vicinity. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
There were different shapes and sizes of ploughs and hoes used for tilling of soil. There were 
varied designs of sickles and other tools and implements used for agriculture. There were 
different methods of weather forecasting followed by the local communities.

Traditional animal husbandry 
Domestication of various livestock like cattle, buffalo, goat was prevalent, by feeding these 
animals with crop residues, crop thrush, crop by products and seasonally available grasses & 
leaves. Animal husbandry was integrated with agriculture and livestock diseases were treated 
using local medicine like herbs, roots, and shoots locally available. 
They were making use of different leaves as fodder. Different types of sheds were made for 
keeping the domesticated animals. Waste generated by livestock such as cow dungs and urine 
were used for growing crops organically.

● Varied techniques and gears used for fishing 
a) Porxevopp: 
Many Goans will have grown up learning how to capture fish with their bare hands during the monsoon season, when fish swarm in shallow water. This strategy is used by 
more experienced fishermen during the monsoon season in Goa's river system. To keep salt water out, retaining walls are created between paddy fields and rivers. 
Fishermen utilize the walls as a trap, muddying the waters around them and catching fish with their hands or by dropping a net into a muddy riverbed. 
 
b) Gorovap: 
Gorovop (rod-fishing) and poler (line-fishing) are two types of angling. In the former, a nylon thread with a hook is attached to a wooden or bamboo pole. The type of fish 
to be caught determines the bait and hook used. Smaller fish and rice dough are commonly used as bait. To catch a wider range of fish, the later method uses a nylon string 
without a rod and more tempting bait, such as a giant prawn or crab. 
 
c) Khutani or Khutavanni 
The native method of stake fishing is called khutani or khutavanni. To trap fish, wooden poles are anchored into the river and a net is tied across them. The fish are then 
harvested around low tide. It is frequently employed during the monsoon season to catch tambuso (red snapper), chonak (sea bass), and dodiyare (croaker). 
 
            d)Kanni or Zaali: 
Kanni or zaali (barrier net fishing) is another method that requires only two or more persons to complete, depending on the catch. Two fishermen hold up a rectangle net 
with two bamboo sticks on either side while moving through shallow waters. More men can be utilized to trawl a larger net across the waterbed of a deeper body, such as a 
pond. Kanni, like khutani, is used to harvest monsoon-appropriate fish such as tambuso, dodiyare, and muddoshi, in addition to tambdem bhalem (red eel). When a semi-
circular net is fastened to a bamboo frame, the process is known as zaali. Fishermen use zaali to catch shrimp in muddy shallow waters.  
 
 
 
548 
 
e) Kaathali: 
Cast net fishing, also known as kaathalli, requires a 200-300-metre-long net. Small floats run the length of one side of the net, allowing it to fall over the water as a screen. 
Fishermen use kaathalli to catch khorsani (butter fish), shevtali (mullet), conge (apple snails), and tigur (walking catfish), all of which can be consumed during the monsoon 
season in Goa. Paguer refers to a smaller net cast by a single person. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Picture depicting use of Cast net 
 
 
549 
 
f) Ramponn: 
Ramponn is a practice in which fisherman use a canoe to draw a net in a circular pattern across a big area of water. Ramponn is ideally suited to catching huge fish such as 
snapper, grouper, barramundi, shark, barracuda, and lobster during the monsoon.  
 
 
550 
 
 
Picture of Cannoe and Net Use for Rampon 
 
 
551 
 
g) Jhaari: 
To catch crabs for crab curry, you'll need jhaari equipment. In jhaari, a net is laid against a circular metal frame known as kobulem and put on the river in clusters. The 
metal frames, which are kept 50 metres apart between jhaari, allow the traps to be put at a constant level in the water. A string is connected to the sets of jhaari. When 
fisherman notice movement in the string, they act to remove the nets. Free divers catch clams with their hands, whereas oysters are dugged on seashores and riverbanks. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Traditional  Jhaari 
 
 
552 
 
h) Manas or Poin: 
Manas or Poin are Konkani words for fishing with sluice gates. The gates are used to control the ebb and flow of the tides in Goa's river, as well as to trap fish at low tide 
when they close.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Manas or Poin at Mandur Dongrim Tiswadi- Goa 
 
 
553 
 
i) Dipkavnni: 
Dipkavnni is a technique that uses light sources to confuse fish. Traditionally, paraffin or kerosene lamps were used to shock fish before catching them with a portable net. 
Today, people utilize high-beam flashlights in shallow water to do the same task. 
 
According to community wisdom, the best fish to eat in the winter include kingfish, pomfret, doumer, tuna, mackerel, crab, prawns, tiger prawns, shark, lobster, squid, and 
mussels. During the summer, Goans consume shark, kingfish, squid, crab, bombil (Bombay duck), and prawns.8

● Kaavi art of Goa 
The term "Kaavi" comes from the local name for the maroon-red pigment, also known as 'uramunji,' which is e xtracted from laterite soil.  
Kaavi art is an exquisite style of mural artwork that thrives in the Konkan region, particularly on the ancient monuments and temples of Goa.  With its beautiful reddish-
brown paintings, Kaavi art, also known as Kaavi Kale, is a tribute to the region's rich history.  
Essentially, this art form includes the laborious carving of lime plaster over a red oxide-treated surface, resulting in elabora te murals and designs inspired by the region's 
distinct folklore.9 
Kaavi, characterized by intricate inlay work on temple and house walls, defines sacred spaces and reflects Goa 's cultural ingenuity, developed as an alternative to painting 
in Goa's challenging climate, kaavi employs locally available 
materials and techniques, embodying the region's resourcefulness. 
Kaavi designs encompass borders, corners, and figurative art, 
influenced by Yakshagana theatre motifs from neighbouring 
Karnataka. The art's migration from Goa to Karnataka and back has 
enriched its repertoire, blending local and external influences 
seamlessly. Kaavi's intricate patterns, from lotus borders to cobra 
medallions, imbue Goan architecture with beauty and symbolism. 
 
9https://rooftopapp.com/kaavi-art-unearthing-goas-forgotten-folk-art-form/ 
 
 
556 
 
Sadly, many Kaavi works suffer neglect or vandalism, highlighting the need for preservation efforts. Despite this, Goa's architectural art serves as a testament to centuries of 
cultural evolution and adaptation. Preserving these treasures honours the legacy of those who entrusted their work to the divine and future generations, ensuring their enduring 
legacy.10

● Chitari art and painting on wood 
The basic Goan Chitari Art is a simple style of art that has been passed down through centuries in Cuncolim hamlet. This art form gains popularity around the annual 
Ganesh Chaturthi, when wooden things sell at numerous fairs held a few days before Chaturthi.  
The traditional design of two parakeets or two flowers painted freehand by artists in brilliant red, yellow, and green on mango, jackfruit, or hedi (local white wood) surfaces 
is a staple of any Goan Hindu home.11 
 
In Cuncolim, the Chitari and Chari communities of Demani are renowned for their skilled craftsmanship, particularly in wood c arving and painting, which has been passed 
down through generations. This ward is a shining example of Mahatma Gandhi's village industry concept, with around 80 families c ontinuing the tradition of artisanal work 
inherited from their ancestors. Specializing in crafting wooden children's toys, baby cradles, Ganesh Chaturthi decorations, traditional seating mats, and various other items, 
these artisans have also maintained the age-old practice of repairing and painting temple chariots and decorations. Their workshops are hubs of creativity, producing a wide 
range of wooden articles, from cradles for newborns to kitchen utensils and decorative items. However, despite their rich heritage and craftsmanship, Cuncolim's toy 
artisans face the threat of extinction. The modern preference for electronic and digital toys over tradit ional wooden ones has led to a decline in demand. Additionally, 
challenges such as scarcity of wood and lack of government support have further jeopardized their livelihoods. Ye t, these artisans are not merely craftsmen; they are 
custodians of cultural heritage. Their work has garnered recognition both nationally and internationally, with some artisans even receiving awards for their exceptional skill. 
They continue to play a vital role in cultural practices like the tradition of gifting wooden items to newly marrie d couples and crafting decorations for festivals like Ganesh 
Chaturthi. 
Despite the lack of formal training, the younger generation in these communities carries on the family tradition, showcasing their talent and creativity. It is imperative for 
governments and policymakers to recognize and support these artisans, not just for economic reasons but also to preserve and celebrate Goa's rich cultural heritage.12 
 
 
11https://aratigoa.wordpress.com/2018/08/29/goas-vibrant-chitari-art/ 
12(https://www.heraldgoa.in/Goa/The-magic-hands-of-Chitaris-from-Demani-give-life-to-dead-wood/197322)

● Artifacts of the Chari 
For generations, the temples of Goa have showcased remarkable woodwork crafted by skilled artisans primarily from the Chari community. This tradition is passed down 
through families, with stunning examples of woodwork adorning temples across the state, often revealed only during special occasions like annual festivals and fairs. 
On the auspicious occasion of Gudi Padwa, the Hindu new year, Chari artisans perform a sacred ritual wher e they cut a piece of wood from a mango tree trunk, which is 
then worshipped as 'Holi'. Using traditional tools like chisels and hammers, they meticulously carve out an image of 'Giroba' throughout the day, creating a revered deity 
that is worshipped throughout the year by locals and attracts devotees from neighbouring areas along the Goa-Maharashtra border. 
The artistry of wood carving extends beyond temple decorations to include roofing, furniture, and decorative panels found in temples throughout Goa. The Chari 
community, also known as 'mest', relies on manual craftsmanship to create intricate motifs that showcase their skill, talent, and diverse range of craftsmanship. 
Recognizing their significant contributions, temple committees and community institutions have historically allocated agricultural fields to Chari families, enabling them to 
thrive in villages and continue serving temples. During annual celebrations across Goa, representatives of the Chari community, known locally as 'Barazan', are 
acknowledged for their cultural heritage and dedication to their craft. 
Prakash Chari from Sal, Bicholim, emphasized the community's ongoing commitment to preserving traditions, stating that despite engaging in various occupa tions, they 
continue to honor their heritage by participating devotedly in annual celebrations and festivals. 13 
 
● Bamboo art work 
In the realm of scientific inquiry and biodiversity conservation, the traditional craft of bamboo and cane weaving practiced by the 'Mahar' community artisans in Goa holds 
significant ecological relevance. A couple hailing from Aldona has been actively engaged in bamboo craft for the past 30 years, carrying forward a legacy passed down by 
their parents for generations. 
Bamboo, a rapidly renewable and versatile natural resource, forms the basis of their craft. The artisans skillfully utilize simple tools such as hacksaws and bill hooks to 
shape and fashion bamboo stems into various utilitarian objects like 'patlo' baskets and 'dalli' mats. These products serve multiple purposes in daily life, from storing grains 
to transporting goods, embodying the sustainable use of natural materials. 
 
13https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/goa/chari-community-keeps-alive-traditional-woodwork-art/articleshow/90830427.cms 
 
561 
 
However, the widespread adoption of plastic containers and products in modern society has posed challenges to the demand for traditional bamboo crafts. The decline in 
market demand due to the convenience and accessibility of plastic alternatives not only impacts the livelihoods of artisans but also raises concerns about the environmental 
implications of plastic pollution. 
From a biodiversity perspective, the dwindling demand for bamboo products reflects a disconnect between human cultural practices and the preservation of natural 
ecosystems. Bamboo forests provide essential habitats for a diverse array of plant and animal species, playing a crucial role in maintaining ecological balance. The decline 
in traditional bamboo craftsmanship could potentially contribute to habitat degradation and loss, further exacerbating biodiversity loss in the region. Despite these 
challenges, the artisans remain committed to preserving. 14

● Art of zele making from the paddy pinnacles 
Agriculture has long been the cornerstone of livelihoods in Goa, and even today, the cultural practices of Goans reflect the dee p-rooted agro-heritage of the region. During 
Ganesh Chaturthi, a significant festival, families participate in rituals that honor this agricultural legacy. On the second day of the festival, the head of the family and other 
male members venture into the paddy fields barefoot, following a tradition that symbolizes reverence for the land and its bounty. The y harvest the newly grown ears of 
paddy, offering them to Lord Ganesha by placing them on a wooden plank beside his idol and by tying them to the entrance door-frame. 
In Ponda, another ritual adds layers of traditional knowledge and biodiversity significance to the celebration. Here, the harvested paddy panicles are used to weave a 'zelo,' 
a traditional ornament, which is then tied to the wooden canopy over the Ganesha idol. This practice not only showcases the fusion of cultural and agricultural traditions but 
also highlights the sustainable use of natural resources. It underscores the intimate connection between agriculture, biodi versity, and traditional knowledge, preserving both 
cultural heritage and ecological balance.15

● Art of garland making from locally available flowers 
One of Goa's most appealing crafts is the weaving of flowers and flowery wreaths into temple and church decorations. Grand temples take on an ethereal air as floral 
decorations change each night for the nine ritual nights of Navratri, which precede the martial celebration of Dussero. For the most exquisite decorations, go to the Mahalsa 
temple in Mardol for the zayam puja, when decorations made entirely of star-shaped jasmines (zayos) adorn the temple in the most creative ways.16

● Jewellery art tradition of Goa, 
Goan jewellery was introduced to the globe by "Daivadnya Brahmins," who were well-known for their jewelry-designing abilit y. They were the first to introduce Goan 
traditional jewellery designs to Europe. Since then, the popularity and demand for Goan jewellery has only increased. 
Goan traditional jewellery has a wide range of pieces for practically every area of the body. 
 
For the Arms, 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
566 
 
The name Bajubandh refers to an armlet worn by women on their upper bodies. A traditional gold bajubandh features flower and peacock designs skillfully created by 
local artists. 
A classic Goth bangle made of gold has a basic design and is adorned with flowery designs created by artisans. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Tode are hefty gold bangles worn by Goan women at festivals, poojas, and weddings. These bangles are adjustable with a pin. The screw makes it easy to wear, adjust, and 
remove the bangle. 
Pichodi is a type of bangle used by ladies in Goa. A common Pichodi style consists of pearl or gold patterns arranged in the shape of a crown.  
 
 
 
567 
 
The beaded gold bangles are called as Piddukachi Kakna. The classic form combines gold motifs with a variety of colored beads, including orange, yellow, and red. 
While the beads used in these bangles come in a variety of colors, the most popular patterns feature black beads.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Coin Bangles are gold kadas decorated with patterned motifs, colored or gold bead motifs, and coins. The coins feature sacred depictions of Goan deities.  
 
 
 
568 
 
Jewellery for Neck 
A mangalsutra is an essential item of wedding jewelry for every Goan bride. The mangalsutra worn by Goan brides is referred to as "daul." A typical mangalsutra consists 
of a gold chain embellished with coral and/or gold beads, as well as a pendant.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Galsiri is a necklace fashioned up of pennies. A typical Galsiri consists of coral and gold beads strung together in a gold chain (with a string fastener) and gold coins. A 
galsiri necklace adorned with traditional religious symbols and images of Goan deities. 
 
569 
 
Jewellery for Ears 
Pake are traditional ear cuffs that ladies wear on special occasions including poojas, family gatherings, and weddings. They are traditionally decorated with Konkani 
designs and patterns. A typical pair of Pake is constructed of gold with floral designs and pearls strung together to form a mesh-like pattern. Diamonds and precious 
gemstones are used in more expensive fashions. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Kaan are another type of earcuff used by women during traditional Konkani weddings. Kaan earrings are composed of gold and feature gold motifs such as leaves. 
 
570 
 
 
Ved are simple gold stud earrings adorned with diamonds or precious jewels. Jewelry for the nose 
 
Goan women wear Nathinis (nose ornaments) at weddings, religious rituals, and family gatherings. A classic Gold Nathini consists of pearls with a pink or white stone in 
the center.

Jewellery for the feet.

● Sacred groves and sacred flora 
Gavda, Kunbi, Velip and Dhangar – Gouly, the tribals of Goa have worshipped various forms of nature. They have a tradition of sacred cow, sacred goat, sacre d banyan 
tree, sacred hill, sacred stone, sacred pond and also sacred grove. By considering them sacred, they have protected them, since many generations. 
There are many instances of the occurrence of rare plant species in the grove. In the De vachirai of Derode, Sattari magnificent specimens of Dhup tree (Canarium strictum) 
are well preserved by the local community. In original form protection forbade any interference with the biota of the grove whatever, and not even leaf litter was allowed to 
lift up from it, nor was grazing or hunting practiced within the grove and hence they represented a sample of vegetation in its climax state. Earlier, human beings were 
relied on sacred groves for supply of various medicinal plants, shrubs, creepers. In order to pluck these plants whenever required they had to pe rform some rituals to please 
the forest God. Even today, in the remotest parts of Goa, locals who are still far away from any rural health services, rush to sacred grove for herbal medicines to get cure 
on their ailments. 
The trees beings beneficial for humanity, to protect them became a religion and were converted into the abode of trees spirits or Vanadevatas. To cut down trees meant 
depriving the spirits of its home and very often if it became imperative to cut down any trees, special prayers of forgiveness we re performed before a tree was cut down or 
another abode offered to the Vanadevata invariably. It is not the tree that is worshipped but the spirit residing in them. 
In Goa, the tradition of sacred Grove is the pre-Portuguese heritage, existing since the hoary past. The cluster of banyan trees lying in the vicinity of the Gokarn Sansthan 
Jeevottam Math at Partagal in the Poinguinim of Canacona is appeared to more than one thousand years. Holiyechi Rai of Caranzol in Sattari was known since the hundreds 
of years. th During the 18 century, the Ranes of Sattari and peasants before initiating the revolt against the Portuguese  used to visit Caranzol and were entering into the 
sacred Grove called the Holiyechi rai where they were worshipping the sacred slab. By doing the ritual inside the sacred Grov e, they believed that they were getting the 
moral boost up to fight against their rivals. In the land record, there are some areas mentioned as 'Rai' and all these a reas were once respected by the locals as the sacred 
Grove. 
FESTIVALS AND RITUALS ASSOCIATED WITH THE SACRED GROVES 
Like others part of India, in Goa too, there are various rituals, festivals associated with the sacred groves since many cent uries, as these are regarded as the institutions 
having the sacredness and that is why the communities involved in conserving and protecting these groves on different occasions performed rituals, rites to appease the 
presiding deities and get blessings. The people have built up the faith on the presiding deities as well as the guarding spirit. There  are various rituals, festivals performed 
 
574 
 
with the strong belief that the presiding deity or guardian spirit should not cast the wrath. In India, even after development in the fie lds of science and technology, people 
have the belief in the religious practices, rites and rituals. In Sattari taluka, in the chains of th e mountains of the Western Ghats, there is village of Dongurli. On every 
alternate year, villagers from Charavane, Rive, Pali, Golawali, Hivre Khurd, HirveBudruk and Dongurli assemble infront of the twin religious shrines of Mundalgiro and 
Kolgiro of Thane in Dongurli for celebrating the folk dance of Ghodemodni during the Shigmo festival. The persons dressed with the traditional costume  holding the 
swords in the hand and sitting on the wooden effigy of horse perform the dance as if he is riding a horse on the tune of the Dhol and Ta so, the percussion instruments. This 
dance makes one aware about the tradition of the warfare that prevails once in this land. It is performed infront of the twin shrines of the folk deities of Kolgiro and 
Mundalgiro. In the past the area known as the Mundalgiryache mol was covered with the forest. However today, very few trees are left that are the testimony of the past 
remnants of the sacred grove. The shrine of Mundalgiro is under the centenary old huge Jambhul tree to the left h and side where as the shrine of Kolgiro is lying under the 
tall, towering tree of Satvin. There are also Jackfruit, Kumyo, Salai, Kusko and other trees. All these trees are consi dered as the sacred and protected by the locals. During 
the night, the villagers dare not to sit in the area. However, during the festival of Ghodemodni, not only the villagers of Dongurli and surrounding six villages, but also from 
other parts of Sattari thronge in a big number to the twin shrines to make offerings of various items after fulfillment of their respec tive wishes. Today, work of 
beautification under taken, has degraded the natural setting as some exotic species of trees have been planted and cement concrete fencing have been erected Devotees visit 
Thane to witness the biggest Ghodemodni of Goa. 
Koduvaparab of Verle  
Inside the Netravali Wildlife Sanctuary lies a beautiful village of Verle. This tribal dominated village has the settlement of other forest dwelling communities who are living 
in tune with the nature and environment involved in protection and conservation of the sacred grove known as Bhuipann. As the villagers do not dare to collect even minor 
forest produce, the sacred groves have been protected through generations. However, during some of the religious ceremonies, the village rs enter the sacred grove and 
collect the forest products. During the sixth month of the lunar calendar, Bhadrapad, after the celebration of Ganesh festi val has been concluded, the main villagers 
maintaining the temple of presiding deity, enter into the sacred grove in the evening and collect various herbs, roots, shoots, leaves believed to possess medicinal properties 
and distribute all these items among all the families residing in Verle.  
 
 
575 
 
The next day is celebrated as Koduvaparab. All the family members get up early in the morning and prepare d ecoction and drink the bitter liquid first before having tea or 
other breakfast. The villagers have the belief that the bitter decoction has various medicinal properties which h elp them to get rid of diseases by curing health ailments. 
While collecting roots, herbs, tubers from sacred groves they are supposed to avoid any parts of Huro [Sapium insigne] and Ka ro [Strychnos nux-vomica] trees. Since these 
trees possess toxic elements. Except on the occasion of Koduvaparab, the villagers rarely enter the sacred grove of Verle. In the past, ethnobotanist or traditional healer 
before entering the sacred grove for collecting any roots, shoots, tubers or leaves were involving the presiding deity and assuming that the permission has been granted after 
invocation, were collecting it and preparing the medicine. These medicines were given in past by taking just a coconut or min imal money. However, today, the traditional 
healers and ethnobotanists are fast disappearing.  
 
Every year, villagers of Mulgao in Bicholim celebrate Pethechi jatra in the second month Vaishakh where in the idol of goddess Kelbai use d for the festive occasion is put 
into the specially weaved cane box and is taken in procession to neighbouring Mayem for few days for the veneration and then the deity is brought back and on the way to 
the temple, she is kept for one night in the sacred forest dedicated to Daddev. This area today has been badly affected by iron-ore excavation.  
 
In Goa, Keri of Sattari has the highest numbers of the Sacred Groves. Among these sacred groves, the Ajobachi Rai and Pisha chi Rai are the largest and untouched, as they 
are situated outside the periphery of human settlement in the hilly region. Beside these, Baldyachi, Abdurgyachi, Mithasher, Komachi, Birmanyachi are the other sacred 
groves. Three decades ago, the villagers annually were going to the Ajobachi and Pishacho Rai to perform the ritual. However, the tradition today has not been observed. 
 
In the mining affected village of Surla in Bicholim, the villagers have till this date guarded zealously B arazan and Ajyachi Rai. While going to Barazan hamlet from 
Kadchal, the grove is situated on the left side of the road. Villagers, offer the vegetarian as well as non-vegetaria n food items to the guardian spirit of the grove. Since, the 
village has been badly affected by the iron ore mining; the Barazanachi Rai is only testimony of the rich forest. I n the grove of Ajyachi Rai at Gaonkarwada of Surla, one 
can experience how the rural folk offered the protection to trees, creepers, lianas, bushes trees and vegetation that ha rdly can be seen in other areas of Surla is found here 
and also enjoy the cool shade in the grove. It has the aged ficus bengalensis and ficus religiosa along with many species of the ever green trees. In the vicinity of the grove, 
 
576 
 
there exists a small temple of Narayan dev and a sacred lake. However, today, concretization of the tank has threatene d ground water sources. At Ghadiwada in Surla, 
villagers kept few ficus trees and built a new temple in the honour of the Holy Spirit Aadcho Ajo and recite devotional songs on every Sunday.  
 
In Pissurle, there is sacred grove known as the Pejali-devichi Rai. This mining affected village was once domina ted by agriculture and villagers were growing a variety of 
indigenous species of paddy. There was a tradition of relishing on the rice gruel before going for the manual work in  the morning. As per local belief goddess who was 
flying in the sky, had seen rice fields laden village and came down to relish on the rice gruel. When she ate the rice  gruel, she decided to stay in Pissurle for ever, from then 
onward the folk deity got the name as the Pejalidevi and was living in the forests that gained respect as the Pejalidevichi Rai.  
 
 
Kumbharkhanitalya Ajyachi Rai  
Kudne, village already on the map of archaeological heritage of Goa, before onset of the mining activities has intimate bond with the environmental values and hence 
villagers have protected the patches of the forest through the tradition of the sacred groves. At the outskirt of Deulwada of Kudne a  sacred grove exists locally known as the 
Kumbharkhanitalya Ajyachi Rai. 
 
As the villagers have strong belief in the guardian spirit, they rarely make entry in to the grove. While going from main road of S ankhali-Amona, the right turn takes to 
Kudne. To the left side of the village road, a small shrine has been established where locals prey to the deity Ajoba. When their wishes are fulfilled they make offerings of 
the earthen votive figure like horses and bells to Ajoba. Kudne attracts a large crowd of devotees during the Shigmo festival, when two days before the full moon day of the 
Phalgun the last month of the lunar calendar; celebrate three nights’ festival of Gadeutsav. Devotees with traditional attire  believed to be possessed under the trance run on 
the directions of the Holy Spirit known as the Devchar in the darkness. According to the villagers, for the three nights of Gade utsav the holy spirit of Kumbharkhanitalo 
Ajoba plays significant role and that is why various rituals are performed to appease him. 
 
 
577 
 
 In his honour villagers of Kudne have guarded, the sacred forest having tall and towering trees and shrubs. There are  centuries old Kazro trees, and fish tailed palms in 
large number. In whole of Kudne, this sacred grove is only forested area that has significant tree cover and is the natural habitat for different species of birds and animals. 
 
 In the hamlet of Dharge of Dharbandora, there are many sacred groves but today some of these groves became extinct as they had formed the parts of Mahavir wildlife 
sanctuary. One such groves that is lying few meters away from the temple of Mahadev of Tambdi Surla has become target of degradation as villagers constructed temple 
structure and after few years, left it neglected. Today, the area of the sacred grove has been disturbed as the temple structures are totally in dilapidated condition. Villagers 
on the festive occasions visit the grove to perform various rituals. The stone sculptures that are without any shelter are on the way of degradation. 
 
ECOSYSTEM SERVICES OF SACRED GROVES 
Sacred Groves are important forest ecosystem possessing high bio-diversity and conservation value. They are protected by the locals through deep religious and cultural 
sentiments. Ecosystem services provided by them are perhaps the greatest and the most crucial contribution to the society and community.  
 
The All India co- ordinated Research Project on sacred Grove Ecosystem Services Assessment (SGESA) initia ted by the Ministry of Environment and Forest has attempted 
to quantify and value the eco-system services of sacred Grove in India based on their relative importance and in the context of sacred Grove eco-system the following 
ecosystem services were selected for SGESA. 
 
 PROVISIONING  
Fresh water: Many sacred Grove has the origin of the perennial springs that provide fresh water to the local communities living in the vicinity. In Keri of Sattari, Ajobachi 
rai is responsible for keeping alive the springs of water tank at its foothills and also the wells. The sacred Groves being an intact forest, forest floor of which is covered with 
litter and humans is expected to have better infiltration then grassland, scrub and quickly areas. On account of dense r and deep roots network, various kind of burrowing 
soil organism and incorporation of decomposing organic matter into the top soil, the soil tends to be more porous and spongy with greater water infiltration capacity. In 
maintaining local hydrological balance, the sacred Grove play important role. 
 
 
578 
 
 NTFP AND TIMBER 
 In some areas, locals are allowed to make use of non-timber forest produce as well as timber in rare c ases. There are some sacred groves, where even extraction of non-
timber forest produce like honey, wax, and herbs too is not allowed. But for extracting medicinal herbs, the locals by invoking the presiding deity, make use of it. 
 
 SUPPORTING  
(1) Nutrient cycling  
an adequate supply of essential elements needed for life is provided through the ecological process of nutrient cycling. Various  processes such as decomposition, 
weathering uptake and leaching are involved in nutrient cycling. The Sacred Grove helps in enhancing crops productivity in adjacent agro eco-system as the nutrients are 
transported through spring originating from the Sacred Grove to the agricultural field. 
 
 (2) Pollination 
 A set of species involved in the pollination such as bees, beetles, trips, midges, flies, bats, birds and others take refuge in the  Sacred Grove. These pollinators provide an 
essential eco-system service that result in the out-crossing and sexual reproduction of many plants. They improve the field of crops and play and important role in 
conserving the biological diversity agriculture and natural eco-system.  
 
 
(3) Biodiversity  
Bio-diversity provides a large number of eco-system goods and services like food, potable water, medicine and fibre essen tial for humans. Sacred Groves are repository of 
rich bio-diversity, threatened flora and fauna taxonomically unique plants and animals and are often remnant representative of the bio- diversity of the region. The 
Myristica swamp forest inside the Sacred Groves of Nirankarachi Rai of Maloli and Ajobachi Tali of Brahma Ka rmali in Sattari indicates how bio-diversity has been 
protected. 
 
 
579 
 
Regulation 
1. Carbon sequestration: Sacred Groves are important for long term storage of carbon. Most of the carbon is stored in vegetation including litter a nd soil compartments. 
Sacred Groves has the potential value in terms of their contribution to regional carbon stocks particularly those of old growth forests.  
 
2. Maintaining hydrological balance: The Sacred Groves make contribution in maintenance of the water balance in eco system also improves water quality. The perennial 
spring that originates in Nirankarachi Rai of Maloli quenches not only thirst of local villagers but water possesses medicinal value. They are significant in recharging grand 
and surface water in their vicinity.  
 
Cultural 
1. Spiritual: Most of the Sacred Groves are dedicated to deities or to ancestral spirits and are associated with the concept of nature worship. They have important socio- 
cultural functions. In addition to the religious function. In Poriem of Sattari the members of temple committee visit to th e ruin of Sattari temple surrounded by the 
sacred trees and perform various rituals during the full main days of Shravan, the fifth month of the Hindu calendar and after sacred threads to the folk deities. 
2. The Sacred Groves too have recreational value. Some of the festivals, folk dances in the past were performed inside the Sacred Groves. 
 
Besides, these functions Sacred Groves provides health services directly and indirectly traditional health care syste m existing in surrounding areas of Sacred Groves 
was making use of different part of plants, shrubs, climbers in the Sacred Groves for the treatment of various ailments. There a re also cases of psychological healing 
after visit to Sacred Groves villagers too enjoy peace of mind due to the existence of Sacred Groves. 
SACRED GROVES DEDICATED TO THE GODS  
The practice of dedicating groves to deities is the most common in Goa. In Sacred Groves, all forms of living cre atures are given protection through the grace of any 
one deity. The presiding deity of the Sacred Groves is generally feminine, as indication of its origin in ea rly times. The red paint smearing the goddess represents of 
course the blood of sacrificial victims. These victims were no doubt humans in bygone time. In Shigao of Dharbondora, Rangaidevi, the presidi ng deity of the Sacred 
 
580 
 
Grove is always smeared with red powder. In order to please the unseen holy spirit of the Sacred Groves, annually sacrifice of cock, goat is done. Majority of the Sacred 
Groves in the Western Ghat parts of Goa are dedicated to the female goddesses.

BIODIVERSITY IN THE SACRED GROVES OF GOA  
In Goa, the forest dwelling communities have excellent knowledge of the floristic wealth of their surrounding who make use of these  plants for satisfying their daily needs 
by maintaining their relationship with biodiversity rich areas. There existed among them a symbiotic relationship between the local community a nd biodiversity who with a 
wealth of knowledge on the utilization and conservation of food and medicinal plants have guarded it.  
 
In Bardez, Tiswadi and Salcete, the new converts to the Christianity have kept their linkages with the c ultural rooted in the environment. The Tavashache Feast celebrated 
in Santan Bhati of Tiswadi in the monsoon is the cultural event wherein both the Christian and Hindu participate. They pray to Our La dy for the male child. If the son is 
born, the next year the couple make offering of Cucumbers to the Our Lady. In Raia village of Salcete the Christian community c elebrate Konsache Feast where in the 
panicles of new paddy are offered to the goddess and then among all the villagers. 
 
Among the Muslim community of Goa, there are memorials built in honour of the pious saints who are venerated by Muslims as well as the Hindus of the locality. There 
are trees which are considered as the holy and protected in the vicinity of the Durgah. In Sankhali, there  is a Durgah dedicated to Babar Pir where in the Kosam tree 
(Schleichera oleosa) is protected. In Bicholim Savar (Bombax ceiba), mango and other indigenous species of trees are protec ted. In Bicholim town and Keri (Sattari) there 
are water bodies inside the river, regarded as the sacred and they are known locally as the 'Pirachi Kond' 
Sacred Groves have important socio-cultural dimensions beside religious functions. Various rituals, festivals are observed inside the sacred groves only on certain days in 
the year. In Verle there is Jaita Pann in which annually rice is cooked and is eaten by the tribals after making offering to the presiding deity. In some sacred groves on a 
particular day in a year, leaves of medicinal plants are plucked and distributed among the villagers who after grinding it with water drinks the mixture. There is a tradition 
of making offering of cock, goat or buffalo annually to the deity. 
 
Earlier the women of forest dwelling Velip tribals were performing the eco-feministic festival of 'Dhillo' inside the sacred groves by singing, reciting and dancing for about 
seven days, in between period of Dussera and Diwali. Many cultural beliefs relating to fertility find expression in vows and prayers made at sacred groves. Different moral 
support and guidance for individuals are derived from cultural values associated with the sacred groves. 
 
582 
 
Social, cultural and environmental ties with the adjacent forests are a sensitive and sentimental affinity among the forest dwellers that have preserved some patches of the 
forests on religious grounds. There they have protected not only trees, shrubs, herds, climbers but all forms of vegetation along with geological wealth. Removal of even the 
dead wood or stone is taboo. The faith of these indigenous communities in Nature's creation has helped in many ways natural ecosyst ems in India as the sacred groves. 
Some of these sacred groves are so important that they are perhaps the last refuges of the endangered and vulnerable biological wealth. As access to and interference with 
the sacred groves has been culturally restricted and thereby reduced the human impact in terms of harvesting of natural resources. The result of such restriction has been 
that sacred groves have evolved as significant reservoirs of biological diversity and permitted the complex and diverse arr ay of ecological processes to continue 
uninterruptedly over long period of time. Some of the sacred groves constitute pristine vegetation, and are particularly rich in flora and fauna. 
 
SACRED GROVES-WITH UNUSUAL BOTANICAL MARVELS 
The Sacred Groves in some areas exhibit unusual botanical marvels and rare and endangered specie s. The climbers locally called Garkani (Entada phaseoloides) are found 
in the Sacred Groves of Holiyechi Rai of Caranzol, Devachi Rai of Coparde in Sattari. It has th e climbers showing ropy twisted stems swinging from one tall tree to the 
others, sometimes forming impenetrable thickets. The climber has the pods which seem to be the longest one among leguminous plants. The Pach Amyachi Rai of Surla has 
giant mango trees looking magnificent, lofty banyan like tree. In the Sacred Groves of Pirapeth in Ibrampur of Pernem, there are more than two dozen of the Indian fishtail 
or Sago plant (Caryoto urens) once every part of this trees was used by the aborigines. 
In Maulichi Rai of Vagheri in Sattari there are wild relatives of species of spices are there whereas the Ajobachi Tali of Brahma Karmali has the thick growth vegetation of 
wild species of turmeric. There are some Sacred Groves in the Western Ghat of Goa, where species of wild bamboos are noticed. Bamboosa arundanacea (Velu) and 
Oxytenanthara ritcheye (Chivar) are there. Devachi rai of Surla in Sattari has the shrubs of Karvi , that blossom every after seven years.

The forests were virtually under the control of village communities with well-defined territories. The sacred groves acting as sanctums for wildlife would have also 
provided ample food especially for frugivorous animals. 
 
The sacred groves are the treasure trove of the floral diversity, though, there are plants with the rich medicinal value, there are  some known to be causing illness in man or 
livestock. These plant though not actively poisonous cause painful irritation and eruption if they came in contact with the skin or mucous membrane since they possess the 
phosphoric acid. Though, some parts of these plants have poisonous elements, they possess usefulness and aesthetic value. 
 
During the sixth month of the Hindu calendar, the Bhadrapad, the forest dwelling Velip tribals extract leaves, roots, shoots, ba rks of the most of plants that are inside the 
sacred grove called 'Bhui pann' except the huro and karo , plant having poisonous elements , while celebrating the festival o f Koduwa Parabs. Though, the sacred groves 
have the plant with the rich medicinal value, there are some sacred groves with the number of poisonous plants like Huro and Karo. In spite of poisonous value, these plants 
are protected by the local communities living in the vicinity of the sacred groves.18

● Window pane oyster art. 
Windows serve several important functions. Primarily, they filter air and sunlight, 
providing a passageway for both, yet they also hold a significant place in the artistic 
landscape of Goan architecture. In some Goan homes, window screens made from nacre 
are a hallmark of traditional upper-class residences. The precise origins of these 
windows are unknown, but mother-of-pearl nacre was favoured over glass because it 
allowed filtered light to enter while maintaining privacy. This gave the windows a 
warm, translucent appearance from the outside and reduced glare on the inside. While 
high-quality timber was typically reserved for altars and fine furniture, the wood used 
for windows was often of lower quality. 
The nacre, otherwise considered waste, was cut into lozenge shapes and fitted into 
wooden battens, enhancing the windows' value and beauty. Today, Goan craftsmen 
create miniature replicas of these windows, sold as souvenir picture frames and 
decorative wall pieces. Mother-of-pearl windows can be custom-made to fit specific 
measurements, showcasing the ingenuity and skill of Goan artisans who elevate house construction to an art form. Despite their ethnic beauty and potential to enhance 
urban architecture, these windows are in low demand today, and the craftsmen who make them are rare and mostly out of business.21 
 
 
 
 
21https://www.dsource.in/gallery/mother-pearl-shell-windows#33301

● The Matoli tradition of Goa  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Matoli 
 
 
612 
 
The Ganesh Chaturthi festival, known as 'Chavath' in Goa, was forbidden by former Portuguese rulers beca use to the widespread worship of Lord Ganesha among people 
of all ages, genders, and social classes. As a result, after freedom, the event is celebrated with great enthusiasm and grandeur. Essentially, it is a harvest festival that is 
celebrated by the agro-community to show their joy over the harvest-ready paddy crop. Worshiping Ganesh is a symboli c act of respecting the sacred bond between nature 
and humanity. The Goans have incredible traditional knowledge (TK) about how to use all the fruits and flowers connected to the "Matoli." They have learned this 
information via their first-hand experience and their centuries-old association with the plants through trial and error.  
Following the dry dormant season of the Hindu months of Chaitra, Vaishakha, and Jyeshtha, Matoli is a celebration of the renewal and rebirth of nature. Then comes 
Shravana, Bhadrapada's verdant, flowering, and fruiting season. Therefore, as a sign of reverence for the proof of life's continuation and progeny, Goans celebrate the 
Ganesh holiday and craft the exquisite Matoli.  
The whole point of Ganesh's symbolic devotion is this: Ganesh: An idol sculpted from the rich soil of the riverbed; Matoli: Displa y of fruits, flowers, stems, roots, and 
foliage that are found in that particular season; Sunday worship: PatriPooja, or leaf worship, honors the littlest creepers and bloom ing plants and establishes a connection 
between them and the feminine folk.  
This worship of nature in the form of ‘Matoli’ is unique to Goa and rest of Konkan. 
 
Earth (matter) and plant life (energy) are worshipped as Ganesha. The worship of matter and energy, therefore, indicates that our ancestors understood that mass could be 
converted into matter and vice versa and that humans had a responsibility to preserve nature.  
It is necessary to preserve and safeguard even the tiniest creeper. All of God's creations, no matter how tiny or insignificant, must be protected. Nature cherishes and 
preserves polyculture; it cannot stand monoculture. This is Matoli's ecological significance. 22 
 
 
 
22 Source: “Matoli and Biodiversity” by Dr. Bhushan Bhave submitted to Goa State Biodiversity Board
