● Various fairs and festivals of the land too closely related with the environment and ecology of the areas, which indicates the eternal bond of the people existing 
with it. 
▪ Kalotsava 
In Goan culture, the yearly Kalo celebrations hold a unique significance. It is a time of year whe n temple devotees worship the village god by offering prayers. The 
temple's most important cultural event is Kalo. It's a feast where villagers and members of a certain temple committee participate  in a variety of social, cultural, and 
religious events. Between November and February, some temples celebrate the Kalo festival. It is celebrated for one, two, or even more in various places. For a 
maximum of 3 days. Everyone participates in the celebration with a great deal of religious fervor and zeal. In Goa, the st art of winter marks the beginning of the 
Kalo season. People prepare to celebrate Kalo the day following the ceremonial marriage ceremony of the basil plant pedestal, also known as Tulshi vivah. 
When Kalo is celebrated, the young people build human pyramids and climb on each other's shoulders to get to a clay pot that is kept high within the temple 
grounds and contains yoghurt, fruits, and sweets. Prior to the ceremony, the young actors perform a folk play called "Gavalan Kalo," in which events from Lord 
Krishna's early years are carried out using customary music and dialogue. In certain places, the deity set aside for  the celebration is drawn by the devotees while 
chanting and playing music in a beautifully painted chariot.  The temple is decked out in flowers on the day of Kalo, and in some regions, the idol of the deity 
intended for the celebration is carried in a palanquin and paraded around the community. In keeping with the promises given to her, the deity receives offerings from 
everyone of the devotees who participate in the procession. A traditional folk drama known as "Dashvatari Kalo" is performe d during the evening. In a folk drama 
performed by the artists, Lord Vishnu is seen killing the demon Sankasur during the battle. After the Dashavatari Kalo, the re is a unique theatrical performance.  A 
Marathi musical drama based on historical or mythical tales was performed earlier. 23 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
23 https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/city/goa/kalo-celebrations-an-expression-of-gratitude-to-the-village-deity/articleshow/5582249.cms

▪ Jatrotsava: -1) Devi Lairai jatra: Shirgaon Jatra commemorates the journey of Goddess Lairai, also called Saibin, and her siblings to Goa across the Western 
Ghats. While her siblings settled at Mulgaon, Mayem, Mapusa, Morjim, Lairai made the decision to remain in Shirgaon. According to legend, Lairai once requested 
her brother Khetoba to get firewood, only to discover that he was playing with kids. She kicked him out of anger, then felt bad about it and decided to walk through 
fire as a form of self-punishment —a practice known as "Agnidivya" or "Agnitun-chalne." This custom continues today, with 600-700 new Dhonds joining each 
year. A massive bonfire titled "Homkhand" is built, and devotees known as Dhonds walkacross it. The Jatra, celebrated annually in April or May, attracts many 
devotees and is a prominent event in the local cultural calendar.24

2)Redechi Jatra:  
Mayem village in Bicholim is known its yearly "Redyachi Zatra" festival. This 'zatra is celebrated with a great deal of religious ritual and festivity that showcases 
the socio-cultural legacy of the region.  
There used to be a tradition of buffalo sacrifices during the fair. The fair is called the "Redyachi Zatra" or the "Vhodali Zatra" even though this practice has been 
outlawed for more than 25 years.  
Between the Kelbal temple in Kelbaiwada and the Mahamaya temple in Gaonkarwada, the local deity's sacred pitcher, or Kalas, was carried in a procession. The 
devotees carried a basket filled with wooden masks of the folk deities to the Kelbai temple at midnight, along with a massive, lit earthen lamp known as "Maale."  
A country canoe carried the insignias, known as "tarangas" in the local language, of Pisso Ravalnath, Devaki, and Krishna f rom Marcel of Vargao to Mayem for 
the fair. Due to the village's forest, certain fair customs still honor the connection that people have with the environment and biodive rsity.  
At Chavatho, where devotees swarm for blessings, the "tarangas of Ravainath, Bhutnath of Mayem along with Devaki, Krishna and Pisso Ravalnath of Marcel 
were kept." Marcel received the "tarangas" back in the canoe following the blessing ceremony. 25 
 
   3) Malyachi Jatra: On the Chaitra Shuddha Ashtami, Malyachi jatra is held in Mayem, wherein a lamp is lit and held on the head by the devotee. 
 
4) Pethechi Jatra:The Kelbai deity is in Mayem from Chaitra Shuddha Panchami to Chaitra Shuddha Ashtami (the eighth day). She is carried in a cane basket        
procession from Mulgao along a customary route that leads to the nearby Mayem hamlet. In the community, a cane basket adorned with Kelbai insignias is kept for 
religious purposes. The distinctive wooden masks of different deities, which indicate the goddess's presence, are carried in the cane basket and are a reflection of 
Mulgao's rich cultural legacy.26

▪ Diwja 
In many parts of the Goa, it is the day marked by ‘Divajanchi Jatra’ in which married women having husbands observe fasting. Together with other ladies, they light 
the traditional five-wicked lamp known as Divaja and offer it first to the village's ruling deity. Mother Earth is repre sented by the lamp, which is lit in all directions 
to represent the dispersal of light or the displacement of darkness.  The purpose of this light is to help humanity transition from darkness, hatred, grief, and 
intolerance to light, peace, joy, and knowledge.27

▪ Gade utsav: The Gade Utsav is a unique festival celebrated in Goa as part of the Shigmo festival. It is a tribute to demons, ghosts, and spirits, particularly the deity 
Devanchaar. The festival is celebrated in various parts of Goa, including Cudnem, Sal, Pilgao, and Adpai.28 The gade are people who undergo purification rites and 
observe various kinds of abstinence before and during the festival. They are believed to be possessed by a godly spirit during the festival.29 
▪ Siddheshwarachi Bhagut: According to the Hindu calendar, this rite takes place twice a year, during the summer and the rainy season. The purpose of this 
celebration is to offer prayers to Lord Siddheshwar for the protection of the village and its inhabitants. In the forest whe re the Almighty dwells, chickens are offered 
to God during celebrations, cooked, and then served to devotees. During the performance of this rite, only men from the village are a uthorized to enter the forest 
where God resides; women who have reached puberty are not allowed to visit for prayers.

▪ Shigmotsava 
The Shigmo celebrations in Sattari and Bicholim talukas, as well as the border regions of Maharashtra and Karna taka, are not complete without the festival of 
Karvalyo. The Karvalyo festival, which is primarily observed on the third or fourth day of Holi Pournima and is linked to the sati ritual, honors womanhood. 
Although sati remained popular in Goa informally into the 16th century, Afonso de Albuquerque Constantino de Braganza opposed the wicked practice. 
Following her husband's death, the widow was expected to jump onto his blazing pyre. This custom, which is considered sacre d, raised the deceased woman's 
standing in society.  In remembrance of Sati, the festival of Karvalyo is thus observed during Shigmo. 
People in the villages of Sattari and Bicholim greet the Karvalyo with open arms and wash their feet before worshiping them. The phrase "karvalyo" describes two 
boys, ages 10 to 12, who are dressed in sarees and other feminine-symbolizing accessories. Crossandra flower (Aboli)  garlands are used to adorn their heads.  The 
two children are dressed in temple , made to sit on the shoulders of two people who are holding them, and then taken in a procession to several locations. 
A group of folk musicians who sing sakarat' (local geet) and beat the 
dhol, taso, and kasale continually accompany the procession. 
The local setting and mythological tales connected to the 
deity are extensively detailed in these songs. The connection between 
the karvalyo and the god is also clarified by the songs. Karavlyo is 
celebrated for two days and nights in a r 
 
Karavlyo in Shigmotsav at Sattari Taluka

▪ Ghodemodni:The peculiar celebration known as Ghode Modni, or "horse dance," is observed in the villages of Thane, Sattari, and other locations. This centuries-
old custom features a breathtaking exhibition of martial arts and horsemanship, with players dressed like warriors mounted on ornamented horses. The spectacle 
that enthralls audiences is a result of the rhythmic sound of hooves and the colorful costumes worn by the performers. A p rominent feature of the Shigmo festival, 
which is held in Goa during harvest season, is the Ghode Modni folk dance. From an etymological perspective, “ghode” means “horse,” and “modni” means 
“joyful,” which perfectly captures the spirit of the festival.30 
 
▪ Chorotsav 
Chorotsav, sometimes referred to as the "festival of thieves," is a peculiar holiday celebrated in Sattari Taluka's Car anzol and Zarme village. Chorotsav provides a 
playful window into the fun and inventiveness of Goan culture, complete with humorous acts and simulated thefts. Eight villagers who represent "chor" (thieves) are 
buried in the ground at Chorotsav; four of them have their heads buried so that their torso and sword-wielding hands are exposed, and the other four are buried up to 
their necks so that their faces are visible. At night, this ceremony is performed in front of the goddess Brahmani Maya's shrine. The horrible event of robbers being 
wrongfully put to death centuries ago is symbolized by this symbolic gesture. Both residents and curious onlookers flock to the scen e, watching with a combination 
of interest and excitement as the eight people are buried alive.  The story underlying this strange custom states that many centuries ago, four men with two children 
from a separate village were traveling through this community. However, these four adults were beheaded and two youngsters were hanged because locals thought 
they were robbers. When the men's parents arrived in this area during their search, however, it was discovered that they wer e not thieves and that the situation was 
one of mistaken identity. Upon realizing this, the villagers acknowledged the mistake they had made. Therefore, as part of th is Holi celebration rite, the villagers 
pledged the parents that they would remember and preserve them in their minds in order to do justice to their spirits.31 
 
 
 
 
30https://goa-tourism.com/event/ghode-modni/#:~:text=Ghode%20Modni%2C%20meaning%20’horse%20dance,the%20essence%20of%20the%20performance. 
31 https://www.heraldgoa.in/cafe/the-%E2%80%98festival-of-thieves%E2%80%99-at-caranzol/219566#:~:text=The%20forested%20village%20of%20Caranzol,this%2C%20they%20accepted%20their%20mistake.

▪ Chikhal Kalo : at Vitthal Temple Sanguem 
The religious celebration known as Chikhal Kalo, celebarated in the Goan village of Marcel, is a unique fusion of fun and de votion. It takes place in the vast 
grounds of the Devki Krishna temple every year on the eleventh day of the Hindu month of Ashadh. When the monsoon arr ives, the temple grounds are guaranteed 
to turn into a muddy landscape, which is an essential part of the subsequent excitement. The celebration includes traditional activities like gilli danda and chendu 
fali, which resemble cricket, in addition to exciting dance. The name Chikhal Kalo comes from the fact that the slic k mud surface causes players to fall and get 
covered in mud repeatedly, which is an essential aspect of the ritual. 32 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
32 https://goa-tourism.com/festival/chikhal-kalo/

▪ Shirshranni  
One of the rich customs known as "Shisharanni" is performed at the Shri Mallikarjun Temple in Avem-Khotigao, Canacona, every three years during the traditional 
Shigmo festival.  
Three men lie on the ground to create a traditional cooking area, and the cooking utensil is placed on  their heads while rice is cooked using human blood.  
The term Shisharanni is derived from two words: "ranni," which denotes a traditional cooking location, and "shisha," which refers to a  type of tree.  
Three "gades," who are thought to temporarily represent God on earth, are associated with the ceremony.  
Layers of plantain trunk and a damp cloth are placed over the heads of these three selected gades.  
After that, the three men formed a typical cooking area by lying down on the floor. An earthen jar is set on top of the three heads when they are rendered 
unconscious.  
To simulate a conventional cooking stove, the Shisha tree's branches are burned beneath the pot. Because the people thi nk that the three gades are filled with God's 
spirit and are under God's protection, they remain unaffected even when the burnt shisha is maintained near their heads.  
Following the cooking of the rice, another participant in the rites cuts the crown of the head of another gado with a sword. After that, the blood that comes out of 
this wound is mixed with the cooked rice. A sacrifice is symbolized by the head being cut open and blood being used.  
At last, the cooked rice is hurled at the populace. Nonetheless, because the rice is prepared with sacrificial blood, it is seen as unlucky, and people avoid being hit by 
it in order to prevent the blood-stained rice from falling on them.  
 
 
 
 
 
 
624 
 
▪ Homkhand 
The celebration involves lighting a pyramid-shaped pile of wood, usually five to six feet high. To the rhythmic a ccompaniment of traditional percussion 
instruments like as the dhol, tasha, and cymbals, local men and boys engage in a fascinating rite where they walk barefoot across the flaming embers once the wood 
has been reduced to smoldering ashes. Hundreds of people participate in this energetic and captivating spectacle as they courageously walk the flaming trail.33

▪ Dhendlo 
Dhendlo is a representation of Shri Krishna, a cowherd companion. Around the hamlet, they carry Dhendlo, an idol of Krishna, in a square box called a "Devaro," 
which is held aloft by a man. As they wander around singing, other villagers join him. Every home in the village is visited by a person carrying the Dhendlo, and 
the lady of the house washes his feet when he arrives. After that, Lord Krishna is offered flowers and kumkum is applied. Rice, jaggery, and coconuts are offered, 
Aarti is done, and in the evening, women prepare Godshe, which is then given out across the village.34

▪ Jagor

▪ Intruz celebration at Dongrim Old Goa. 
During the colonial period, particularly under Portuguese leadership, the Hindu communities of Goa suffered significant challenges and restrictions on their 
traditional customs.One such limitation was imposed on the celebration of Shigmo.  
Shigmo was a time for Goans to celebrate the coming of spring, with colorful parades, ornate costumes, vibrant music, and lively dances. It was a celebration that 
drew communities together, instilling a sense of belonging and cultural pride.  
However, Shigmo was looked with distrust by the Portuguese colonial rulers. They were afraid that the celebration could be used to promote Hindu nationalism and 
cultural identity. In reaction to this perceived threat, the Portuguese government prohibited Shigmo celebrations.  
The prohibition of Shigmo was met with opposition, particularly in Dongrim. Even under the oppressive colonial administration, the people were c ommitted to 
retain their cultural history and traditions. They developed a strategy to avoid the restriction while still celebrating their beloved holiday, demonstrating tenacity and 
ingenuity.  
This idea resulted in Intruz, an occasion that closely resembled Shigmo but with strategic changes. Intruz wa s skillfully arranged a month before Shigmo to avoid 
arousing suspicion among Portuguese authorities. The inhabitants of Dongrim retained the spirit of their celebration despite conforming to the limits impose d on 
them. 
 
 
 
627 
 
The festival lasts five days, each loaded with unique events and cultural expressions:  
1. The Procession of Deities: The Intruz festival begins off with a magnificent procession of village deities. This colorful and spiritually significant ceremony sets 
the tone for the upcoming festivities.  
2. Folk Dances and Songs: Intruz is a period when cultural manifestations take center stage. 
Folk dances and traditional tunes, passed down through generations, are performed with zeal and fervor. 
These expressions represent the essence of Goan culture while also reflecting the festival's cheerful atmosphere. 
3. Suvari Vaadan: Perhaps the most engaging feature of Intruz is the Suvari Vaadan, a musical performance showcasing Goa's distinct rhythms and melodies. This 
music is performed on traditional instruments such as the ghumot, a typical Goan drum. The Suvari Vaadan reflects Intruz's joyous atmosphere and demonstrates 
the village's cultural richness.

▪ Sao joao 
The São João Festival has its roots in the 16th-century Portuguese invasion of Goa. The event, which has its roots in C atholic customs, honors Saint John the 
Baptist, who is said to have jumped for pleasure in his mother's womb when Jesus' mother, Mary, paid him a visit. Additiona lly, it is a celebration of the monsoon 
rains that provide the land with nourishment and a sign of the value of water. The colorful crowns, or "kopel," that the participants wear are  fashioned of fruits and 
flowers and symbolize happiness and the wealth that the monsoon brings.  
Exuberant celebrations abound during the holiday, and one of the most notable traditions is the playful jumping into wells, streams, and ponds by young Goan men 
wearing these kopels. This action represents the cleansing properties of water as well as John's exuberant leap. The day is marked by singing, traditional music, and 
the contagious laughter of gathering groups. Sao Joao is a veritable feast for the senses, with parades, processions, and music and danc e performances filling the 
streets and the aroma of mouthwatering local specialties like "sannas" (steamed rice cakes) and "feni" (a local spirit) filling the air.35

cowbells around their waists and on their ankles, which ring loudly enough to be heard far away. Their altered speech and mannerisms make them unrecognizable to 
crowds.

▪ Virabhadra 
In Goa, people worship Lord Shiva in a variety of ways. Virbhadra is revered in Goa, despite the lack of a  temple or shrine devoted to him. Virbhadra folkdance is 
performed throughout Goa on various occasions. It is evident that Karnataka had an influence on the cult of Virbhadra worship a nd Virbhadra folk performance. 
Virbhadra Anna, Houdu, and Kailasvalige are Kannada-derived words that are still used today when referring to Virbhadra. During the Vijaynagar dynasty, the 
Virbhadra folk dance is thought to have originated in Goa. 
Every year, people in Bicholim, Ponda and Sanguem talukas perform the Virbhadra folkdance.  The Virbhadra folk dance is performed in Bicholim town the day 
before Gudi Padwa, the Hindu New Year. In Borde, Virbhadra is presented on the final day of Shigmo, while in Vithalapur, which is near Sanquelim, a performance 
takes place on the final day of Chaitra Utsav, which is the full moon day in the first month of the Hindu calendar.  
The most well-known performance in Goa is the Virbhadra folk dance of Vithalapur, which is accompanied by a ch ariot parade and draws sizable crowds. The 
dance is performed by a folk performer wearing royal robes and a cardboard with numerous small flags tied to him, to the rhyt hms of the dhol (drum), taso (drum), 
and kasale (cymbals). He also gets his face painted to resemble Virbhadra, has long hair, and wears a crown on his head. After taking a few rounds, he enters a 
trance while wielding two swords as if engaged in combat.  
According to a mythology, the father of the goddess Parvati Daksha had planned a sacrifice ceremony. Except for Lord Shiva, all the gods and goddesses were 
invited. Daksha publicly insulted Parvati and Lord Shiva when they went to the ritual. Parvati turned into ashes after jumping into the flaming fire since she could 
no longer stand the insult. In his rage, Shiva conjured out Virbhadra, who not only ruined the ritual of sacrifice but also began a reign of terror. This episode is 
commemorated with the Virbhadra folk dance.  
In Ponda, Virbhadra performs following Navaro-Vhakal's performance. The Virbhadra is performed in different sections of Ponda at the eco-feministic festival of 
Dhalo, which falls in the tenth month of the Hindu calendar, Paush.

▪ Kelenchi Jatra 
Every year, the distinctive celebration of the god Sri Dev Bhabreshwar takes place in Khobrawado, Calangute, North Goa. Because devotees present a whole bunch 
of bananas to this deity, the event is well-known as "Kelyanchi" or "Ghadanchi Jatra" (event of Banana Bunc hes). The shrine is situated on the well-known 
seashore between Baga and Calangute.The deity receives more than 2500 bunches of bananas every day. A beautiful roof of banana bunches is then created by 
tying these bunches to a makeshift wooden frame over the deity. Every evening, the extra bunches —raw or ripe—are put up for auction. Every year, thousands of 
residents and visitors go to this celebration, which takes place in February.38

▪ Maange Thapni 
"Mange" means "mugger," which refers to an Indian crocodile. The Konkani word "thapne" refers to the process of creating a  clay sculpture. This means that "a clay 
mugger is sculpted and worshipped." In the Hindu calendar month of Pausha, on the moonless night known as Pausha Amavasya, "Mange Thapne" is celebrated. The ritual, 
which is performed on the river's mangrove embankments, is overseen by particular social groupings. When the mud is still wet on the e mbankment, it is removed and used 
to create a sculpture of a crocodile. The sculpture is embellished with thorns and shells that are found nearby. Afte r that, people revere the statue. Puffed rice, jaggery, and 
an offering of a chicken or egg are offered. Following that, the villagers offer a prayer to the mugge r, asking it to keep people safe who work near and enter the river. The 
offerings are delivered as prasad after the prayer. Following a customary procedure, the relatives that are direc tly associated with the ceremony are subjected to an 
attendance check. Family members who fail to show up are punished by working in the fields for a maximum of one to five days. 40 The conservation ethos is abundant in 
these seemingly archaic folk religious expressions, which also instill a sense of brotherhood and denizenship within the common area in the folk mentality.41

prepared by using  (‘Gavathi Suruyu tandull’)  which means locally grown rice. This variety of rice is locally cultivated by many local farmers in their fields.

Kunbi saree: 
The Kunbi saree was invented by two Goan aboriginal tribes, the Kunbis and the Gawdas. These tribes were mostly farmers, cultivating rice a nd owning paddy fields. As a result, 
the saree is shorter in length, allowing women to do household tasks and agricultural work without becoming dirty. This simple clothing has steadily evolved over time, and its use 
has reduced dramatically. Today, it only serves as a memory of the culture of the tribal communities who resided in Goa's hilly hills. 
Usage: 
This brilliant red checkered saree was originally worn by ladies from the Kunbi and Gadwa tribes. These women worked in paddy fields, and they wrapped the saree so that it did 
not fall below their ankles. The Kunbi saree is draped by tying the fabric below the shoulder, then crossing a strip of material over the left shoulder and fastening in the back. This 
draping design enabled these ladies to easily carry out their daily duties and harsh fieldwork. Some farming and working-class women in rural Goa continue to wear the Kunbi 
saree because it is so comfortable to wear and work in.  
These sarees were worn without blouses until the 1940s, when the colonial Portuguese government established a legislation requiring them to be worn. These sarees were formerly 
solely woven in red and white, but they are now made in a variety of colours. The saree is now reserved for folk performances and special occasions.  
On important events like festivals and weddings, Kunbi women dress in silk textiles. Since women perform the majority of their labor by hand, they only wear one ring on each 
hand.  
 
Significance: 
There are numerous ways to interpret the Kunbi saree's significance. According to popular belief, every season has its own curtains, and the arrival of a new season is indicated by 
a kunbi drape. The fundamental color scheme of the Kunbi saree is thought to represent life, and the materials used to make these garments were gathered locally. The saree's red 
colour represents fertility and the brightness of life. Its dye came from a fruit that grows wild in the forests of Goa called "Japani fruit." In addition, the saree was dyed in lilac and 
 
640 
 
yellow hues, which were traditionally worn by widows and derived from haldi. These dyes are claimed to have positive effects on skin health because they are produced from 
organic sources. Hence, the saree’s material would not cause rashes on one’s skin. 
The Kunbi sarees are distinguished by their very simple designs. These sarees merely contain patterns of squares and checks; they don't have any themes. It's interesting to note 
that these saree patterns differ from one group to the next. For example, the saree worn by the Christian Gawda ladies have enormous squares, whereas the sarees worn by other 
tribes have smaller squares. 
 
Given that checkered fabric is seen as pure, holy, auspicious, and potent, this Goan Kunbi cloth is also dedicated to the gods and used in religious rites. Without this fabric, the 
yearly Veerabhadra ceremony, which takes place during the Shigmo festival in March and April, is genuinely 
incomplete. In addition, these cherry red Kunbi sarees are used for a variety of other dances, including Dhalo and 
Fugdi. Kunbi sarees are a staple of festivals and special events in addition to everyday life.42 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
42https://gaatha.org/Craft-of-India/kunbi-saree-weaving-goa/

Shravan in goa: 
Shravan, named after the Nakshatra (constellation), is linked to significant historical and religious events in Hindu mythology. The Shravan festival, also known as Sawan, is one 
of the holiest months in the Hindu calendar and is largely dedicated to Lord Shiva. The Shravan Festival takes place in the fifth month of the Hindu lunar calendar and is very 
religiously significant. It combines fasting and dedication.  
 
History of Shravan Month 
The Shravan month gets its name from the Nakshatra (constellation) "Shravana." This Nakshatra is prevalent during this time period, which is normally between July and August 
on the Gregorian calendar. Shravan Month is believed to be the time when Lord Shiva drank the poison "Halahala" that originated from the churning of the cosmic ocean (Samudra 
Manthan). Samudra Manthan is one of Hindu mythology's most crucial events. Symbolizing the unending conflict between good and evil forces. Lord Shiva ingested the fatal 
poison and held it in his throat, which became blue as a result. Since Lord Shiva sacrificed his well-being for the benefit of all beings. He became widely known during Shravan 
Maas as the preserver of life and the protector of the universe. 
How Shravan Month Started? 
Shravan Month dates back to ancient times, and the celebrations have evolved throughout centuries of custom and religious practice. In early Vedic literature, the month was 
observed for agricultural ceremonies and strongly tied with nature worship. The emphasis is on cosmic forces and their interactions with Earth. As a result, Shravan Month became 
a significant season in agrarian civilization. 
Shravan Month originated as a symbol of penance, piety, and devotion that embodied the ideas of spiritual development and disengagement from worldly desires. 
 
Significance of Shravan Festival 
• Spiritual Cleansing: Fasting during Shravan helps believers purify their minds, bodies, and souls. It provides a route for self-discipline and devotion. 
 
642 
 
• Harvest Time: Shravan signals the start of the monsoon season in several parts of the country. During this critical period for agriculture, rituals are performed to ensure a 
bountiful crop. 43 
 
Rituals and Customs During Shravan Festival 
Shravan Maas is observed with a variety of ceremonies, customs, and religious activities that vary differently depending on the location. The most common festivals observed 
during this holy month are listed below. 
1) Shravan Somvar (Mondays): Mondays during the Shravan Month are reserved for fasting and prayers to Lord Shiva. Many devotees fast from sunrise to sunset(Sawan 
Somvar Vrat) and make special offerings at Shiva temples.  
 
2) Aytar Puja:  On Sundays during the Hindu lunar month of Shravana, women in Goa do Aytar Puja (Aytar is a Konkani name for Sunday, derived from Sanskrit 
Adityavasara). Known as Aditya Vrata in Aytar Puja. 
 
3) Abhishekam: Abhishekam is a ceremonial bathing of the Shiva Linga with water, milk, honey, ghee, curd, and Bilva (Bael) leaves. Devotees present these items, which 
are considered pure and sacred, to Lord Shiva. Pouring water and milk on the Shiva Linga represents cooling the Lord after he consumes the poison Halahala. 
 
4) Fasting:Fasting is an important aspect of Shravan Month. Devotees observe several forms of fasts, including full-day fasts, half fasts, and consuming just fruits and milk. 
These fasts are thought to cleanse the body, mind, and soul, allowing the devotee to focus on their spiritual practice.  
 
• Shravan Somvar fasts: Every Monday of the month, devotees fast. The fasts typically last for four Mondays, but they can occasionally go for five, depending on 
the month.

Directorate of Art and Culture Efficient - The scheme “Financial Assistance for preservation of Goan Maand 
Culture” have been designed with an objective to encourage Goan folk artists and 
to revive , preserve and protect the Goan Maand culture consisting of folk forms 
viz. Zagor, Ranmalle, Kallo, Pernizagor, Talgadi, Tonyamell, shigmo, Challe, 
Naman, Jatigayan, Goff, Dhallo- Fugadi and folklore and folk music Viz. Suvari 
vadan, Ghumatvadan, Shamelvadan and Dholvadan and any other folk forms, 
folklore and folk music as selected by the committee of experts which are basically 
originated from Goan Maand. 
Limitation- The Maand group should have legacy of practicing folk art forms for at 
least past thirty years at such traditional Maand place.

ofIndia 
The Ministry of Culture has formulated a Scheme titled “Scheme for Safeguarding 
the Intangible Heritage and Diverse Cultural Traditions of India”, with the 
intention of reviving and energizing a variety of organizations, associations, 
people, recognized non-MOC institutions, non-governmental organizations, 
researchers, and academics in order for them to participate in initiatives and 
programs for bolstering, safeguarding, conserving, and advancing India's rich 
intangible cultural legacy. 
 
The scheme will include all officially recognized ICH domains, including 
performing arts, social practices, rituals, and celebrations; knowledge and practices 
related to nature and the universe; traditional craftsmanship; and oral traditions and

I. BACKGROUND  
  
1. PARADIGM SHIFT AND DIRECTION OF NEW WORLD VIEW  
The last century model of development has observed failures, non-
sustainability and dead ends in many areas of development. Although the 
contemporary human activities are following the same management 
structure there is a marked shift of paradigms in many areas due to 
consequences of serious damage to ecosystem and sustainability.   
712  
  
712 
 
In the mid of last century  As on now in 21st century   
a) Hunting a tiger was given a big 
re ward  
  
Now a biggest fine  
b) Any serpent noticed was killed 
immediately.   
  
Killing all the insects was in the 
practice using  poisonous 
pesticides.  
Now reptile catchers are called, it is caught, and released 
in its habitat area.   
  
Killing the insects without discrimination of good or bad 
is disturbing  natural food production. Honey bee is 
more for pollination than far honey. Therefore now pest 
control is with alternate methods and organic pesticides 
are recommended.    
  
c) Clearing the forest, cutting hills 
and leveling the ground was 
the set method of 
development. Removing 
bushes, grass was the priority  
activity for development   
  
Now it is an offence as an un-ecological activity causing  
• Soil erosion and silting   
• Washing out the nutrients  
• Destroying the micro-fauna beneficiary chain of 
supply of plant food.   
• Eye sore of wounded earth.    
Therefore conservation methods are recommended   
  
d) Filling the marshy land for 
development was the practice.   
  
e) Mangroves had no special 
consideration and their 
destruction was going on till 
third quarter of last century.   
  
  
  
f) There was nothing serious 
about flattering of sand dunes 
and sand extraction.  
Wetlands are now valued as hotspot of biodiversity and 
conservation programs are promoted.   
  
Positive role of mangroves has been acknowledged as:  
• To protect land from Tsunami   
• To protect estuarine water body from human 
pollution  
• To provide breeding place fish and marine species.   
• Habitat for birds  
  
Important role of sand dunes has been acknowledged  
• To protect interior land from sand shifting 
Interphase belt between marine and terrestrial 
ecosystem, Providing segregation as well as food – 
chain, breeding places and habitat

 Natural/organic farming without chemicals has been 
preferred.

2. CITY AS A BIOLOGICAL ENTITY  
Cities as living organisms can be viewed through the lens of James Lovelock's GAIA 
theory, where urban settlements share the same fundamental needs as living entities: land, 
air, water, food, energy, and security. Urban areas function as mini versions of GAIA, with the 
collective needs of residents mirroring those of living organisms. 
Like biological entities, cities require periods of rest, particularly during the night. This 
rest enables natural processes like air purification, dust settlement, and temperature 
regulation. The nighttime also provides practical benefits for urban maintenance, such as 
conducting road repairs with minimal disruption to daily life. This natural rhythm helps 
maintain the health of the urban environment, including its flora and fauna. 
Uncontrolled urban sprawl resembles obesity - an unhealthy condition leading to 
inefficiency and various problems. Creating forest belts around cities, spanning 100-500 
meters, establishes natural boundaries for growth. Historical examples support this concept, 
such as the collapse of certain civilizations in Jordan that grew beyond their sustainable limits. 
Modern urban challenges manifest in various ways. Latur city requires water supply by 
railway tankers, COVID-19 has severely impacted urban slum dwellers, and market s ystem 
inequities force farmers to sell produce like capsicum at extremely low prices while market 
rates remain high. These examples highlight the vulnerability and unsustainability of current 
urban systems. 
Social connectivity has eroded in modern urban settings. Contemporary urban life has 
replaced personal interactions with impersonal transactions - shopping malls instead of local 
shopkeepers, online shopping reducing human contact, and neighbors living in proximity but 
remaining strangers. This social disconnection has led to increased crime rates and security 
concerns. 
Solutions to these urban challenges include developing walkable cities, implementing 
the "fifteen minutes urban form" concept, and using innovative technologies like piezoelectric 
tiles (as demonstrated in Japan) for energy generation through walking. Cluster designs and 
self-management units foster community interaction, moving away from centralized 
management systems. Viewing cities through a biological lens leads to more sustainable, 
healthy, and socially connected urban environments that better serve their inhabitants.

3. URBAN SECTOR IS THE BIGGEST CONTRIBUTOR TOWARDS CLIMATE CHANGE   
A. Urban sector is a parasite community of the world population of mankind   
1. It does not create any of its basic needs but on the contrary consumes and further 
degrades, pollutes and destroys the earth resources at an accelerated rate.   
a) Land: is consumed for urban set up directly for building construction and 
infrastructure like road, dams and canals, mines, industries, warehouses 
and recreation.   
b) Air: heavy consumer of atmospheric oxygen and producer of carbon 
dioxide and other air pollutants making it unsuitable for living beings.   
c) c) Water:  
• High consumption per capita for domestic consumption: drinking, cooking, 
washing, flushing, etc.   
• For industries, farms and recreation.   
Destroy the surface water sources like river, streams, lakes by sewage and 
garbage.  
• Even the ground water in the aquifers is both sucked up for heavy consumption 
needs and are also polluted.  
• Detailed note on water annexure II  
d) Food: More wastage due to consumption of only commercial part of the farm 
production and rest put to waste  
e) Energy: Very heavy consumption of energy causing   
• Pollution of air resulting into unhealthy air and global warning   
• Heat causing heat dome effect   
• Depletion of finite resources and pressure on renewable resources.  
 f) Waste:   
It drives out the various wild life species both floral and faunal and destroys the 
ecosystem of the urban area.   
• By destroying their habitat.   
• By disturbing the delicate interlinks between the different species of life and 
other components of eco-system.   
• By destroying their food base.   
• By pollution of various type including sound pollution.     
 
B. The human population is growing at an exponential rate putting a very heavy 
burden on the nature’s supply system and reserves.   
C. The life-style in the name of modernization, sophistication and comfort is becoming 
more and more burdensome for the eco-system, increasing per capita consumption 
of nature’s resources day by day. With all that the urban sector is a factor taking the

II.  MAIN OBJECTIVES OF STUDY   
TO STUDY THE PRESENT URBAN FORM AND ITS FUNCTIONS IN TERMS OF HEAL THY, SUSTAINABLE 
AND COMFORTABLE LIVING ENVIRONMENT AS WELL AS FUTURE ISSUES  
AND PROBLEMS ANTICIPATED DUE TO CLIMATE CHANGE PHENOMENA   
SUGGEST WORKABLE INSTANT AND LONG TERM REMEDIES INCLUDING RESTRUCTURING 
PRESENT URBAN FORM AND FUNCTIONING PATTERN ALONG WITH PROMOTION OF 
BIODIVERSITY   
1. To protect and strengthen the nature’s system.   
2. To repair, reform, re-structure the urban system to mitigate malefices of climate change.   
3. To re-introduce nature in urban areas by promoting new ways of accomplishing sustainability in 
terms of basic needs of water, energy, food and healthy environment.   
4. To get rid of some of the burning problems of solid and liquid wastes and air pollution.   
5. To reduce the carbon footprint to close to zero situation.   
6. To flatten the heat dome.   
7. To bring down the dependency in basic needs and perasital characters of urban society by sel f-
sufficiency methods and urban-rural tie up organizations.   
8. New form of urban planning for smoothening down the issues of traffic, transport system and 
controlling the urban sprawl. Strengthening the social bondage and human relations through 
planning modes.   
9. Conservation and strengthening the natural elements in urban areas and make them more 
productive for helping the sustainability.  
10. Suggesting some minimum workable changes in the present laws, rules and management 
structure to attain more self-reliance and sustainability.   
11. Accomplish greener, cleaner secure and sustainable urbanization.    
  
 
  
III. BASELINE STUDY    
1. PONDA: TOWN OF MEDIUM SIZE, CENTRALL Y LOCATED TOWN OF GOA (Primary and 
secondary data by survey, site visits and observations)   
a. Location and type: Ponda lies at the centre of Goa State with good connectivity to all 
the taluka of Goa. Employees having possibilities of transfer in any part of Goa prefer 
to reside here. Four industrial estates Kundai, Madkai, Usgao and Bethora are within 
a range of 15km. therefore the town has residential character. It is surrounded by 
horticulture farms and acts as market place for agricultural produce.   
b. History and Heritage:  After Kadambas rule, Adilshaha had established their 
administration unit with construction of a masque Safa Masjid and establishment of 
their officers in the Kota Fortress. There was one more hill fort Mardangad which was 
centre of war between Portuguese and Marathas. That was dismantled by Portuguese 
720  
  
720 
 
for strategic reasons. Due to religions atrocities and destructions of Hindu Temples in 
the adjoining taluka under Portuguese rule, in 16 th century, many temples were 
shifted to Ponda taluka. So Ponda taluka become a centre of temples and consequently 
the cultural centre for Hindus.   
Upto 1930 present Ponda town was a part of village Kawale. Its importance increased 
as travel and transportation by petrol/diesel vehicles started and Ponda become the 
midpoint of North-South and East-West transit lines. Govt. taluka offices were also 
established here. Also Ponda become the pioneer of education with establishment 
brought up by a visionary Dr. Dada Vaidya. After liberation of Goa, Goa Engineering 
College, Industrial Training ‘institute also came up in the vicinity and Ponda became 
an educational hub.   
c. Urban planning   
In 1961 when Goa has liberated from colonial rule of Portuguese, the town was small 
with only two roads one east-west and the other north-south were tarred. Population 
was just 4000. Urbanization was spelt out by Municipal office with a garden in the 
front, Mamletdar office, Revenue and Treasury, Post office, Police, Civil & Criminal 
Court and Military barracks, Central Town Court with bus stand, petrol pump, space 
for weekly bazaar, and a High School. Only one industry of match factory start ed few 
years back which generated electricity and supplied to the town.  The development 
started after liberation. Town and Country Planning Department (TCPD) were 
established in Panaji which prepared Interim Bye-laws and a zoning plan in 1965 
which was perhaps revised couple of times. Subsequently Planning and Development 
Authorities (SPDAs) were constituted under TCPD and Outline Development Plan was 
prepared and is being revised periodically. Topmost authority was Town Planning 
Board chained by minister, C.S, Div. Commissioner, Chief Eng. PWD etc. as member and 
Chief Town Planner as Member Secretary. Regional Plan for Goa was prepared in 
through an expert panel headed by renowned architect Charles Correa.    
2. Presently in Goa the zoning and controls on building construction of the towns is exercised by 
Planning and Development Authority (PDA) as per their Outline Development Plans (ODPs) 
which define the land use of the different zones, road layout, boundary setbacks etc. as per bye 
laws formulated by TCPD.   
PDAs are supposed to be a penal of experts from different planning faculties and some 
social workers. But the same have been profusely occupied by the political workers of 
the ruling party.

In Panaji in the name of Smart city development this belt is thinned of vegetation, paving and 
artificial landscaping is done. Environmental component of smart city concept is damaged. 
Actually since last 40 years the sea is showing fast ingress landwards at the rate of 1m. per 
year. Interference to this is in this belt only   
  
Species:  
Moss and water hyacinth increased in the water bodies. Fresh water aquatic fauna fish, crabs etc. 
vanishing fast.   
Predator birds like variety of kingfishers, especially pied kingfisher, cormorants, vanishing f ast, 
wetland birds like egrets, herons, water foul, etc. reduced drastically.   
Woodland birds like hornbills, drongos, orioles, hornbills, woodpeckers disappeared.   
Water snakes disappeared    
Mammals like other, some of the civets-species, otters have disappeared.  
Hanuman langurs have started visiting urban areas more frequently especially on vegetables and 
fruit plantations causing lot of nuisance and damage.   
726  
  
726 
 
The damage occurred vary on account of various factors at the local level. But the process is the 
same and the factors which cause this phenomenon are almost same.   
In Ponda the generation is still living which used to take the water from Kannewhal stream for 
domestic use. Now even for couple of km. downstream from the urban pollution source the 
farmers do not dare to get down into paddy cultivation as the water pollution damages their 
feet.   
In Margao the urbanites of old age remember that they were harvesting fish from sal river as easily 
as to harvest vegetables from their backyard kitchen garden. Now it is a dead river.   
The lake at Vasco has also been polluted Kushavati river, at Quepem, Valavanti rivulet at Sanquelim and 
Bicholim, Mapusa river and river in Sanguem follow the same trend.   
Entry to Margao from Ponda or Panaji was through wide stretch of dozens of hectares of Paddy 
fields. When these farms were abandoned, lotus flowers of wild varieties were blooming there, 
associated with variety of wetland birds. Now lot of area starting from Margao sports stadium 
has been reclaimed for building construction including Ravindra Bhavan, Collectorate, PDA 
Market and bus stand driving away flora and fauna and natural flood water holding sp ace of 
the town.   
Talegaon near Panaji was a rich orchard of coconut palms and variety of fruit trees and big 
stretches of vegetable plantations. That is disappearing fast with buildings and their growing 
density is taking charge of the scene.

VII. BUILDING UP SUST AINABILITY IN URBAN SECTOR  
1. Quality of air discussed above.  
2. Production of basic living resources and reducing the dependancy  
 a) Water   
Rainwater can be harvested in the underground tanks. Rest to be soaked in 
each plot to enrich ground water source and avoid flooding. Watershed 
development techniques suitably modified to suit urban situation should be 
made applicable. Artificial ponds can be created with multiple benefits as 
wetland, fish farms, recreational garden tanks etc. to create buffer water 
stocks.   
• The ground to be maintained free from pollution, sewage and garbage so as to get 
clean water in aquifers.   
• All the natural surface water sources to be maintained clean, protected and 
ecologically undisturbed by earmarking ‘no development belt’ around.   
• All the sewage and industrial effluents to be treated and fully used for flushing, 
washing, irrigation and industrial use.   
This can make the township largely self-dependent on water.  
• Detailed note on water-Annexure III  
b) Food  
A significant part of food is wasted, creating problem of wet garbage handling, 
transporting and processing problem and disposal of the residue.   
• Urban farming to be promoted along with re-cycling of farm waste.  
• Promotion of urban farming       Annexure V

729 
 
c) Waste Management   
• Waste can be avoided or significantly reduced if handled at the point 
where it is generated. The same can be transformed into a resource by 
aerobic composting into manure, or anaerobic transformation into fuel 
and manure to the extent of 100%. Aerobic conversion is more suited 
for individual household while anaerobic for larger establishments like 
canteens and hotels.   
• Detailed note on Waste Management Annexure IV  
• Program of urban farming can be taken up even in dense city parts in 
various ways to render sustainability to urban sector in certain food 
items like vegetables, spices and even some of the fruits with 100% 
recycling of the organic waste, significant reduction in carbon footprint 
and providing urban indoor and outdoor temperature comfort.

 Energy:   
Sun: Sun has been the prime source of energy for all living beings since 
the time the nature has evolved on this planet, for all the needs of water, 
food and partly habitat. The sunrays, the wood fuel, (the fossil fuels are 
the direct and indirect products of solar energy but it is non-renewable 
and highly polluting) harnessed by the planet during its movement in 
the solar orbit creating seasons of the year. Solar electric energy by 
photovoltaic cells, water heating, drying are direct uses of solar energy.   
Ethanol is again a renewable organic product     
  
732  
  
732 
 
Animals like bullocks, horses, donkey and dogs in polar region are again 
sustained by solar contribution to nature.   
Methane through anaerobic process requires biomass which is again produced by 
solar rays.   
Atomic energy:  It is independent of solar system. But its quantum is very 
less and hazards are highly prohibitive.   
Geothermal is another source which has not found to be so flexible  
for use.  
Hydroelectric is by gravitational force of falling water where again the 
dynamics of water is based on sun.   
Hydrogen as fuel is a possibility but not yet developed for easy harnessing.   
In order to attend the carbon footprint issue in terms of energy use, the following administrative 
tools have been worked out.   
Incentive and disincentive for sustainable use of energy can be worked out through 
administrative tool like green tax. This tax rates need to be based on direct and indirect 
consumption of energy for various goods and activities in the following manner:   
1) Cost of energy consumed to manufacture or process a unit item of the product plus 
administrative and infrastructure cost.   
2) Cost of transportation per kg. per kilometer including handling and warehousing  3)  
Cost of usage including the infrastructure for usage.   
4) Quantification of energy use and its environmental cost need to be worked out 
scientifically and levied on various goods and activities as correctly as possible to 
avoid injustice and impracticability  
 
 
33  
  
Incentives for sustainable use can be worked out (here hypothetical figures given 
to understand the purpose of this mechanism)   
(Government being one of the biggest single institution consuming the energy 
should be included along with the other users)   
a) For direct use of solar energy 90% exemption of green tax. In case of 
transportation from distance that cost to be deducted from exemption 
percentage)  
Solar electricity, solar water heating, solar cooking, drying, solar car etc. are the 
items to be considered.   
b) Thermal power zero percentage exemption on tax and its transportation per 
unit consumed will be taxable.   
c) Centralized hydroelectric power, nominal exemption, say 10% on tax plus nil 
on transportation.   
d) All fossil fuels and their transportation per kg. per km. zero exemption.   
e) For atomic power and transportation zero percent exemption.   
f) Electricity form waste processing plant as their byproduct 50% incentive and 
0% for transportation.   
g) Power from bio-methanation plant 50% incentive and zero percent on 
transportation.   
h) Bio-gas, gobar gas etc. 90% incentive.   
i) Single use plastic goods zero incentive.   
j) Agricultural products from certified organic farms 50% incentive (on 
transportation no incentive).   
On building construction and other construction, tax worked out as per type of 
construction. Exemption to be granted for green building type and for sustainability  
criteria.

VIII. URBAN PLANNING, DEVELOPMENT AND CONTROLS   
1) Overdevelopment and unbalanced development No proper density planning 
causes overdevelopment. It results into inefficiency of infrastructure and damage 
the quality of functioning of urban services. Smooth flow of traffic is disturbed. 
Unbalanced development causes crises-cross traffic, resulting into speed of 
movements, traffic jams etc. This is because proper hierarchy of roads and 
segregations of traffic types cannot be done.   
2) Encroachment on biosphere:   
• Steep hill slops are disturbed.   
• Water bodies are disturbed and polluted. Riparian belt is damaged.   
• Defects, deformation/floods/destruction/blockage of natural rainwater 
drainage system cause floods.   
• Destruction of habitats of faunal sector by destructing of ecosystem.   
• Insufficient green cover to reduce the carbon foot print.   
• Destruction of water bodies and wet lands.   
• Pollution of ground, water and air.  
• Insufficient/defective solid waste and sewage management system.      
Non sustainability of urban sector in terms of basic needs:   
• Clean air and noise level within tolerable limits   
• Sufficient and clean water   
• Energy needs   
• Food and consumption needs.   
• Health and proper living environment with active and passive recreational 
facilities like playgrounds, amusement parks

Social needs not properly/adequately provided:   
• Insufficiency in health facilities (walking, jogging, 
meditation).Insufficient/improper, outdoor recreational areas.  
• Peace and security both physical and emotional is not attended adequately.   
• Social alienation prevails. Social interaction and integration is lacking.   
• Public participation and upgradation of social, cultural, physical and emotional 
needs is not properly exercised. Public consultation is very formal and lacks 
proper spirit.    
  
Planning :  
• Provision for growth, change and upgradation is not properly considered.   
• There is no allocation of space for waste management sewage treatment,

DEVELOPING AN ECOLOGICAL AND SUST AINABLE MODEL  
To replace the non-sustainable centralization model of mass production, by nature’s 
system of de-centralization is one of the basic changes envisaged. Urban society 
which is a consumer society is to be transformed into ‘prosumer’ form (producer + 
consumer). To start with, the resources ignored by the centralized system will be 
harnessed by the new structure. As most of them are natural and imperishable, will 
forge sustainability in the system. This alternate model the contemporary urban 
situation needs to change because of following situation.   
• More than ecology, economy has become more unstable.   
• Himalayan disparity has been created between rich and poor.   
• Mass production has kept no connection with human values.   
• The nature constituted and strongly upheld smallest structure of human 
relationship – family is crumbling.  
• In spite of tremendous research in innumerable human, nature’s and pure 
science faculties, the human senses, skills, capabilities and sustaining power 
have become weaker.   
World renowned architect Frank Lloyd Wright  of mid- 20th Century had put forth the 
concept of one acre house wherein one acre land is sufficient for all the living resources 
of one family. Shripad  Dabholkar and agriculture expert had put forth a 1500sq.m. farm 
program giving 6F: Food, Fire, Fodder, Furniture and Fuel sufficient for one family.  
There can be still better programs.

XII. SYNERGIES MATRIX   
1. Strategy   
Urbanization is a very complex phenomena with large variety of stakeholders each 
having diverse activities, many having independent objectives, some others clashing 
with the others. When the planner puts his hand on planning it becomes very 
difficult to him consider each independently and also with togetherness, due to cross 
interests prevailing between them.   
A famous urban planner says, “Urbanization is a problem; rather a bunch of problem. 
If you try to solve one, it results into new variety of problems. Therefore the best 
way is to go for ‘SCENARIO PLANNING’ . Considering the existing situation and 
futuristic needs, the planner should put forth the picture of what scenario he wants 
to create. This help in tuning each component to achieve this scenario. Synergizing 
this way becomes easier and faster. This should be the role Town Planner (in the 
present case Town and Country Planning Department) to play. But TCPD has been 
assigned power to plan the town and approve/disapprove building plans. But TCPD 
does not have powers to control the overall development. Either this department 
should be given these powers and equipped with additional expertise and allowed 
to perform free from political interference or separate agency or co-ordinating body 
should be constituted. Otherwise development will be a callous disjointed activity 
creating a non-controllable  form as has happened in case of ‘Smart City’ (Imagine 
Panaji) in this 2nd quarter of 2023, with total confusion, with no body to tell what is 
going on and when it will be complete.   
742  
  
742 
 
2. List of Govt. Dept. involved   
Dept. of Environment and Forest

The controlling body should have good expertise in ecology as well as urban and 
rural planning and should be capable handling multi-task activities with 
synergizing capabilities or all of the above should be a part of co-coordinating 
committee which should meet at least twice a year with one meeting in February 
or March to finalize the time table of works before monsoon and the other in 
September to review the monsoon situation and to plan works before next 
monsoon. The committee should be accountable for functioning properly and 
answerable for failures.   
  
3. Role of BMCs  
BMCs will be the end link to organize the participation of the community at the grass 
root level along with the urban civic administration in issues like waste 
management, urban farming, urban greening initiatives and public education and 
participation.  
Municipalities are heavily obsessed with local political in-fights. Town & Country 
Planning Dept. and PDA has got planning expert tuned for development bias and not 
for environment.They are always under pressure from development forces. 
Therefore a separate administrative section may be opened under department of 
environment which should organize additional expertise in synergizing planning 
and development. With the existing specialized sections of forestry, wild, life, waste 
management, pollution, bio-diversity, wetlands it can handle most of the issues 
related to climate change. As regards, other specialized fields, like urban farming, 
Directorate of Agriculture, for water related issues, WRD, for energy Electricity 
Department and GEDA may be consulted. Whatever structure is evolved, it should 
have administrative powers and the officers should be accountable.

and also act as a carbon sink. Productive landscape in 
urban areas will also contribute towards food 
production. Urban-rural participation program 
discussed here can satisfy most of the food requirements 
of the urban needs with the help of adjoining villages 
and achieve mutual benefits.

GARBAGE AND SEWAGE   
This is the most obnoxious 
product of urbanization. It 
pollutes air, water bodies, and 
land.   
With various technologies and 
management systems identified 
and applied all over the world, 
there is no simple acceptable fool 
proof ultimate solution to this 
problem.    
Garbage and sewage is not created at any particular 
time or particular place. De-centralized creation waste 
being brought under centralized system of management 
is the basic problem. Items created by nature starts the 
nature’s process of degradation for transformation into 
another type of nature’s resource immediately. This 
creates obnoxious form for humans till it is lifted to 
centralized place of processing. This is specially for 
organic waste. So the best way is to take up the 
processing at site where it is created. The same is the 
case of sewage.   
If this waste is looked at as resource (in raw form) for 
urban sector , the paradigms shift is experienced. This 
issue is discussed in Annexure IV .

ANNEXURE- I Cheonggyecheon Stream Restoration Project  
Cheonggyecheon is a 10.9 km (6.8 mi)  stream flowing west to east through downtown 
Seoul, and then meeting  Jungnangcheon, which connects to the  Han River and empties 
into the Yellow Sea. During the Park Chung-hee presidency, Cheonggyecheon was covered 
with concrete for roads. In 1968, an elevated highway was built over it.  
After the Korean War, more people migrated into  Seoul to make their living and settled 
down along the stream in shabby makeshift houses. The accompanying trash, sand, and 
waste, and deteriorating conditions resulted in an eyesore for the city. The stream was 
covered up with concrete over 20 years starting in 1958, and a 5.6 km-long (3. 5 mi), 16 
m-wide (52 ft) elevated highway was completed in 1976.   
In July 2003, then-Seoul mayor Lee Myung-bak, initiated a project to remove the elevated 
highway and restore the stream. It was a major undertaking since the highway had to be 
removed and years of neglect and development had left the stream nearly dry. 120,000 
tons of water was to be pumped in daily from the Han River, its tributaries, and 
groundwater from subway stations. There were safety problems due to the deteriorated 
concrete. Still, restoration of Cheonggyecheon was deemed important as it fit in with the 
movement to re-introduce nature to the city and to promote a more eco-friendly urban 
752  
  
752 
 
design. Other goals of the project were to restore the history and culture of the region, 
which had been lost for 30 years, and to revitalize Seoul's economy.  
  
The Seoul Metropolitan Government established several organizations to oversee the 
successful restoration of Cheonggyecheon: the Cheonggyecheon Restoration Project 
Headquarters for the control of the whole project; the Citizen's Committee for 
Cheonggyecheon Restoration Project for the management of conflict between the Seoul 
Metropolitan Government and the union of merchants; and the Cheonggyecheon 
Restoration Research Corps for the establishment and review of the restoration plan.  
  
To address the consequent traffic problem, the Cheonggyecheon Restoration Project 
Headquarters established traffic flow measures in the downtown section affected by the 
restoration work and coordinated changes in the downtown traffic system based on the 
research of the Cheonggyecheon Restoration.……………………………………………………………    
 
Landscape Performance Benefits  
  
ENVIRONMENT AL  
1. Provides flood protection for up to a 200-year flood event and can sustain a flow 
rate of 118mm/hr.  
2. Increased overall biodiversity by 639% between the pre-restoration work in  
2003 and the end of 2008 with the number of plant species increasing from 62 
to 308, fish species from 4 to 25, bird species from 6 to 36, aquatic invertebrate 
species from 5 to 53, insect species from 15 to 192, mammals from 2 to 4, and 
amphibians from 4 to 8.  
3. Reduces the urban heat island effect with temperatures along the stream 3.3° to 
5.9°C cooler than on a parallel road 4-7 blocks away. This results from the removal 
of the paved expressway, the cooling effect of the stream, increased vegetation, 
reduction in auto trips, and a 2.2-7.8% increase in wind speeds moving through 
the corridor.  
4. Reduced small-particle air pollution by 35% from 74 to 48 micrograms per cubic 
meter. Before the restoration, residents of the area were more than twice as likely 
to suffer from respiratory disease as those in other parts of the city.  

753  
  
753 
 
SOCIAL  
1. Contributed to 15.1% increase in bus ridership and 3.3% in subway ridership in 
Seoul between 2003 and the end of 2008.  
2. Attracts an average of 64,000 visitors daily. Of those, 1,408 are foreign tourists who 
contribute up to 2.1 billion won ($1.9 million USD) in visitor spending to the Seoul 
economy.  
ECONOMIC  
1. Increased the price of land by 30-50% for properties within 50 meters of the 
restoration project. This is double the rate of property increases in other areas of 
Seoul.  
2. Increased number of businesses by 3.5% in Cheonggyecheon area during 
20022003, which was double the rate of business growth in downtown Seoul; 
increased the number of working people in the Cheonggyecheon area by 0.8%, 
versus a decrease in downtown Seoul of 2.6%.  
3. The restoration created a 3.6-mile continuous east-west green corridor for 
pedestrians, bicyclists, and wildlife.  
4. Connectivity within the greater transportation network was improved by adding 
22 bridges (12 pedestrian, 10 for automobiles and pedestrians), connections with 
5 nearby subway lines, and 18 bus lines serving the neighborhood.  
5. The restoration reestablished connections between waterways. The 
Cheonggyecheon eventually runs into Jungraechon stream, which leads out into 
the Han River. The wetlands at their meeting point are designated as an ecological 
conservation area.  
6. Because water is only naturally present in the Cheonggyecheon during the 
summer rainy season, 120,000 tons of water from the Han River and several 
subway pump stations is is pumped and treated to create a consistent flow with an 
average depth of 40 centimeters in Cheonggyecheon.  
7. Native willow swamps, shallows and marshes were constructed in 29 different 
locations along the restoration, creating habitat for fish, amphibians, insects, and 
birds.  
8. A fish spawning ground was created where the Cheonggyecheon and 
Jungnangcheon meet.  
9. Terraced vertical walls give visitors access as water levels change, create seasonal 
interest as levels submerge and re-emerge, and provide flood protection for the 
city.  
10. Natural stones bridge the two banks, creating walkways for adventurous 
pedestrians and to helping regulate water speeds and levels and various points 
along the stream.  
754  
  
754 
 
11. Construction materials were salvaged and re-used from the concrete deck 
structure and elevated highway demolition. All of the scrap iron and 95% of waste 
concrete and asphalt was reused.  
  
  
ANNEXURE II                    GREENWAYS OF PONDA   
REJUVENATION OF PERENNIAL ‘KANNEWAL ’ STREAM- BIODIVERSITY CONSERVATION 
FOR URBAN USE  
 This is a concept developed with an intention to conserve and connect the green assets of the 
town more particularly the perennial water bodies to put them to conservative urban use as 
pedestrian path and activities of health and recreation. Simultaneously it could conserve and 
facilitate the bio-diversity of the town. Following initiatives were taken.   
1. A seminar was organized on World Environment Day 2005 by an environmental NGO, 
Nirmal Vishwa (NV), wherein experts in Goa in Architecture and engineering 
representing various organizations like Indian Institute of Architect, Planning and 
development Authority, Town and Country Planning Department, senior scientist from 
NIO, Botanists, etc. participated. The biodiversity study of the 2.5km long part of the 
perennial stream Kannewhal was presented. A project of 750m long central part of this 
stream designed as a pedestrian path along with walking, jogging, cycling and passive 
recreational activities was presented and discussed. Green ways of Ponda (GWP) was 
a comprehensive plan connecting the stream to various perennial springs and green spot 
in the town. Some of the greenways like rainwater drains were identified as the corridors 
of urban wild life. This initiative was welcome and approved after detailed discussion.   
2. The issue of protection of water bodies in urban areas from public neglect, pollution, 
garbage, so-called development activities was brought before the Environment 
Protection Council, the highest Environmental forum of the State Government presided 
over by the Governor of the State. It was resolved to provide NoDevelopment Belt along 
the perennial water bodies in urban area. Thereafter town and Country Planning 
Department was directed to take action.   
3. The matter was pursued with SGPDA and the „No Development Belt‟ was marked in 
outline Development Plan (ODP) of Ponda Town.   
4. A video film „Springs of Ponda‟ was prepared by NV .   
5. One of the spring in the form of dirty puddle was developed by NV through public 
participation and was named as Hanuman Teertha. The public in that area started using 
the water for drinking and on Ganesh festival started using it for Ganesh immersion 
spot.  
6. The spot was destroyed by the construction of Government Highway Bypass. The same 
was got restored. It was damaged second time by flyover construction and now waiting 
for the fulfillment of Govt. promise to restore it.   
7. Bus stand stretch of the stream was the easy spot for the urban crowd, shops, shacks 
and street vendors to throw garbage. NV and Ponda Nagrik Sanghatana (a voluntary 
group) cleaned and beautified the stretch and protected it by 2.5m high steel jali and 
755  
  
755 
 
handed over the project to Ponda Municipal Council for maintenance after proper 
MOU. But it is being neglected by the Council and the pathetic situation continues.   
8. Govt. of Goa decided to take up traffic infrastructure development project in Ponda. For 
that a road was proposed by covering the stream by r.c.c. slab for a length of 2.5km.   
9. The promoters of GWP objected it strongly and presented the case of similar attempt in 
Seoul city of S. Korea for 5.6km stretch which had to be demolished totally and 
restoration of the stream was to be done. The promoters of GWP who were planning 
experts, took part in planning of the said infra-structure project. In the design of this, 
the 2km no development belt was incorporated as pedestrian spine of the town with 
750m. stretch in central part taken up for comprehensive development as passive and 
active recreation for jogging, cycling, etc. Along with the traffic infrastructure plan, this 
green way project was also approved after lot of public consultations with govt. 
departments and public groups. But on account of political priorities the project stands 
shelved.   
10. In the meantime on lot of instances came up where in the GWP was appreciated by the 
political and bureaucratic heads of the Govt. On their assurance the proposal for 
development of GWP for central 750m. part was submitted to them as a development 
proposal. It was appreciated but not taken up so far.   
However the GWP initiative caused to of public awareness about the ecological assets 
of the town. Public was all the time supportive to the new initiatives of nature‟s 
conservation in the town. College students also took up survey and documentation of 
the natural water sources of the town.   
The whole thing has underlined one fact that there is ample scope to harness in 
sustainable way the neglected natural assets of the town.

ANNEXURE III  
Sustainable urban development – Water   
Climate change is inevitable and so also urbanization.  
Year 2021 registered highest temperature 2022 we are already witnessing rise in temperature. 
The water woes are increasing which is evidenced by increased movement of water  tankers.  
Urbanization is considered to be integral to economic growth.(Although its sustainability is 
questionable) as there is good access to various basic facilities in close proximity for 
comfortable lifestyle and job opportunities. This cause rapid growth and puts tremendous 
pressure on the supply of necessities. Traditionally the urban populace depends on rural areas 
for its most basic need including water. This leads to adding carbon footprint , subsequently a 
trigger factor for climate change.  
Sustainable urban development is the way forward for cities to mitigate climate change.  The 
Goal no 11 of SDGs deal with sustainable cities. One of the most important challenge of rapid  
urbanization is the water and sanitation issue .  
  
Present status  
Goa state water policy.  
Goa boast of 100% piped water connectivity. With daily production of 530mld treated water, 
Goa is   already short of almost 70mld for projected population of 19 lakh as per PWD data.  
“AMRUT 2.0 focuses on making the cities 'self-reliant' and 'water secure'. Mission targets 
provision of 2.68 crore tap connections to achieve the intended outcomes. Total indicative 
outlay for AMRUT 2.0 is ₹2,77,000crore including central share of ₹76,760 crore for five years 
from FY 2021-22 to FY 2025-26.”  
Policies are good but in reality far from the target.  
 Projects that can augment the water supply by up to 168 mld are stuck at various stages of 
construction . As per the official records the water lost for reasons such as leakages caused by 
old pipelines and theft is very high at nearly 40%. Fragile and narrow pipelines, unequal 
distribution of water, lack of measures to stop pilferage, poor maintenance and underutilization 
of water treatment plants  left citizens exasperated in summer.  
Considering the sub-judice problem of Mhadei the water wows are going to be worst unless we 
prepare for the situation. Reduction of the excessive reliance on the surrounding countryside 
should be the ultimate goal. The only solution appears to be -  
1. Roof top water harvesting.  
2. Recharging ground water  
Presently the Urban water supply is ensured through 7 different water network viz Opa, 
Assnora, Pernem ,Valpoi Sanquelim, Salaulim ,Cancona .The daily requirement is 401829 cu. 
mts

Daily requirement has increased by 4%per day.With the rapid urbanization the water demand 
will rise further  
Immediate action required   
1. Revive traditional water resources   
a- Every city is having springs flowing through it or ponds and lakes of perennial 
nature. Presently most of this springs are badly polluted .There is urgent need to 
revive and protect these springs. Environment Protection Council, the topmost 
forum for environment protection of state of Goa has recommended a „no 
development belt‟ around each urban perennial water body to keep it protected from 
the development in the land hungry urban areas. This recommendation should be 
enforced fully, urban area in particular.    
b- Every house in the city was equipped with dug well. With the changing scenario of 
old houses being replaced by emerging towers this wells are either polluted with 
seepage of sewage water or filled up totally .whatever wells are existing we need to 
replenish them back again, the water can be used for toilets, gardening washing 
vehicles etc. if not for drinking.  
2. Encourage Rain water harvesting.  
a- There is urgent need to make RWH  mandatory for the new housing projects.  
i. Chennai started this way back in 1994.Chennai metro planning and 
development authority made RWH mandatory in every new construction plan 
with the participation of all the stakeholders and supported by legal framework.   
ii. Japan offers subsidies for RWH. We have a policy in place but awareness 
required.  
iii. Singapur 50% of the land acts as catchment area. We need to seriously 
thinkabout the hill cutting and deforestation.  
iv. Successful stories of RWH in Rashtrapti  Bhavan, CSE New Delhi have given 
positive results.  
b- Recharging ground water has been successfully done through various techniques in 
watershed development programs. These techniques can be reshaped to suit urban 
situation in various ways.   
i. By soak pits to catch roof top water of the buildings. The recharge pits have to 
be1.5m to 3m wide and 2m to 3m deep. Excavated pit is to be lined with brick 
or rubble.   
ii. Recharging groundwater by having soak pits every 2mts in rain water drains.  
iii. Trenches on the hill slope.  Lokvan on the periphery of Ponda town is 
successfully harvesting rain water for more than three decades. Similar is the 
success of other watersheds.  
iv. At individual level many harvest Rain water for recharging ground water for 
augmenting supply through borewell needs to be popularized.This system was 
used by Ambience complex successfully catering to the needs of 15 flats in 
chicalim Vasco.  
  
In different parts of the country the rain water harvesting experiment has 
become successful with the active participation of the environmentally 
conscious individuals, NGOs, Govt. machinery and legal framework.  
771  
  
771 
 
  
There is an urgent need to speed up this exercise in order to replenish ground 
water for the future use. This is essential especially in the coastal urban areas to 
prevent e intrusion of the salt water in the empty fresh water aquifers. It is high 
time that fresh look is taken at our water management policy and systematic 
efforts are made to enhance the water supply not by pressurizing existing water 
resources in far off rural places by creating water sources within urban areas.  
  
Ponda town is blessed with 9 perennial springs if managed properly should cater 
to the needs of at least 50% of the population.  
  
Revival of the traditional water harvesting systems was acknowledged at 3 rd 
world water forum to meet the challenge of water scarcity. These systems should 
be studied and modified (if needed) and applied in the present context.    
  
Waste water processed through STP is a resource which can be re-used for 
flushing, washing and irrigation and attain better sustainability.

ANNEXURE IV  
Sustainable waste management and urban development Climate 
change is inevitable and so also urbanization.  
Year 2021 registered highest temperature 2023 we are already witnessing rise in temperature.  
Directorate of census operation Goa 2021.  
Sustainable urban development is the way forward for cities to mitigate climate change .The  
process of the urbanization should not be the burden on rural sector.  One of the important 
challenge of urbanization is, ‟Municipal solid waste management‟. Urban lifestyle has entered 
in the rural sector of Goa and the solid waste management has become the problem of the rural 
sector also.  
Present status  
The State Government has mandated GWMC to prepare a holistic Solid Waste Management 
Policy for the State. GWMC has set an ambitious goal of achieving Zero-Waste and Zero 
Landfill philosophy adopted by the State. This, amongst others, envisages a State with high 
social awareness on waste and public space hygiene at par with the best tourist destinations in 
the world.  
The Goa Waste Management Corporation (GWMC) functions from their office located within 
the premises of Hindustan Waste Treatment Plant Pvt. Ltd. at Saligao plateau, Saligao, Bardez, 
Goa and are instrumental in coordinating all activities pertaining to solid waste throughout the 
state.  
  
The following data gives a fair idea about the amount of waste generated in Goa.  
The table is as per the survey report available with GWMC,prepared for formulating Solid 
waste management policy.
