The SWMF at Saligao serves as a best practice model for treating waste generated in a holistic 
manner to cater to the needs of local governing bodies.  
Since its inception in 2016, the plant has received more than 1.6 lakh MT of waste, out of which 
32% is dry waste, 45% organic waste, and 23% is mixed. About 99% of this waste is processed.  
The non-biodegradable waste collected by local bodies is sent for co-incineration in cement 
plants through Goa Waste Management Corporation (GWMC). GWMC has also set up three 
bailing stations each at Bicholim, Verna, Cocora. In additions to these, 11 urban local bodies 
and four village Panchayat have bailing facility.  
“Currently, the facility manages 125 TPD of waste as per SWM Rules 2016 with Hindustan 
Waste Treatment Pvt Ltd. For maximum resource and energy recovery, the SWMF has a 
material recovery facility for sorting and recycling dry waste, a waste- to-energy facility 
converting organic fraction into biogas and electricity, generating sufficient energy to power 
the plant; an in-vessel composting facility; and safe handling of residual, inert material. The 
plant recycles its effluents with a net zero liquid discharge. The residual inert material that goes 
to the sanitary landfill is approximately 3 per cent although 10 per cent was allowed under the 
concession agreement.   
Cumulatively, through its activities over four years - recycling, substituting coal with RDF, and 
managing waste with anaerobic digestion, plant has reduced about 35,000 million tCO2eq. 
emissions. Further, the Salmona spring which was earlier polluted, has since improved its water 
quality due to scientific management of waste at the facility. GWMC also provides technical 
support to various ULBs and Panchayat”; TERI report  
  
The GWMC model shows that if managed properly by technically qualified, trained and 
dedicated cadre then the waste will no longer remain waste but becomes a future resource. The 
success depends on participatory approach of all the stake holders.  
  
The project is not free from problems  
  
1. The facility is expensive and has high operational and maintenance costs.   
2. A sustained source of funding is needed to ensure smooth functioning overtime.  
774  
  
774 
 
3. Presently the facility caters to only waste generated in 27 villages in North Goa. And it 
is overloaded. One facility is not enough for the entire state‟s SWM.   
4. Also, having a government-owned SPV does not indicate that local bodies are free of 
their waste management responsibilities. It‟s a co-operation model.  
5. Source segregation and collection lies on waste generators and its enforcement on 
ULBs/ panchayats.  
6. If local bodies don‟t have collection systems, littering and leakages into water bodies 
can be high.  
7. Tourist spots generate more waste and there is institutional pressure to keep these places 
clean.  
8. Not all panchayats  have been able to enforce segregation strictly.  
9. There is resistance from villagers to pay for waste collection services.  
10. In some villages, open burning or dumping in nearby drains is common practice.  
11. Number of local governing bodies fail to collect and send to GWMC for further 
processing, There is no compulsion element.  
The solution lies in „DECENTRALISATION „  
  
The success of waste management lies in a co-operative and participatory approach.  Hence, 
active participation of citizens, ULBs, VPs and all other stakeholders in waste management is 
a must.

Best practices   
There are a number of sustainable methods of waste management within and outside the 
country.  The western techniques are not always suitable for adoption in totality. The waste 
composition differs vastly in India and developed western countries certain practices could still 
be adopted for better wm. The strategic plan for the development of the model should be based 
on the successful models. In view of the situation certain models were examined.  
1. Mega Housing Project - Hiranandani ,Thane  
A number of mega projects are coming up in Goa and are occupied by high income 
group. The life style leads to creation of large amount of non-biodegradable waste. This 
is putting burden on the local community. To seek a solution for the problem an in depth 
study was undertaken in the mega project Hiranandani estate in thane Mumbai.  
775  
  
775 
 
Mega project Hiranandani estate in thane Mumbai. The project has 117 buildings, 
having 18 floors on an average 18 floors, with 4 apartments per floor. Huge amount of 
waste is generated in this complex. It is exemplary to note that there is 100% segregation 
of dry and wet waste. The wet waste is used to produce biogas. The plant presently takes 
care of 2 TPD of biodegradable waste. The plant produces electricity which runs the 
sewage treatment plant to treat 3lakh liters of sewage. The water is recovered back for 
the lush green gardens in the complex. The garden waste is taken care of in the separate 
composting units. The segregated non biodegradables are handed over to the recyclers 
for material recovery. The entire waste management system is taken care of by the 
complex without the help of Municipality.  
The waste management was successful with active participation of the socially 
responsible ladies in the colonies. The mission continues even after the success of the 
program in the colony .Every Friday the highly educated and socially enlightened  
ladies organize a silent  march with plaques in hand in nearby areas to create awareness.  
1. Surat Model  
This one of the filthiest city of India was transformed into cleanest city within  18 
months with a well designedstrategy.theSurat Municipal Corporation got into rapid 
acton under the leadership of the commissioner SuryadevaraRamchandra Rao.1995  
The issue of solid waste management was taken up on urgent basis after the break of 
plague in the city.  
Step I  -To boost the morals of the sweepers clean up drive was first started in the 
sweeper‟s colony. Followed by health officers workplace.   
Survey was undertaken and Dirtiest places were identified by senior staff and sanitary 
inspectors. Worst problems and worst areas were listed. One task was taken up at one 
time for cleanup drive.  
Proper planning and step by step action were under taken. After completion of one task 
next one was undertaken. Morning field work was made mandatory for all the staff. The 
slogan “from AC to DC”-air-condition to daily chores was used. Review meetings were 
held every day in the evening with  all the departments the problems encountered were 
discussed and solved on the spot responsibility of financial authority were delegated to 
the zonal chiefs to speed up the decisions and solve the problems on vital issues. Fines 
were imposed for indiscriminate waste disposal.   Step II -after putting the internal 
system in place and achieving high level of cleaning services, a system of „additional 
cleaning charges‟ to be collected on the spot was adopted. The system was adopted with 
all firmness and fairness. E.g. when persistent defaulters such as large commercial 
establishment refused to pay heavy administrative charges, their shutters were downed 
until they did.   
The strategy- door to door collection, on spot additional charges, encouragement 
for recycling, reprocessing waste   
  
776  
  
776 
 
2. Vellore Model.  
 VELLORE district of Tamil Nadu has been judged the cleanest district in India by the 
government‟s Total Sanitation Program credit goes to C, Srinivasan  
The “Vellore model” of ZWM with separate units which work together for a common 
objective can be described in a nutshell as a “centralized project with decentralized 
processes”. Exnora green cross is the implementing agency.  
It is based on natural ecosystem where sun,water, soil, microorganism ,fungi ,insects, 
fish, animals,take care of biodegradable garbage.  “Vellore Model” of Zero Waste 
Management (ZWM) has nine different individual processes, which are interconnected 
and interdependent and which lead to “zero waste” in the end. The interconnection 
provides maximized efficiency and also sustainability – both economic and 
environmental sustainability.  
The nine different processes or units are separate and well defined. However, the inputs 
and outputs of the nine units are closely linked to each other. When all the units are 
considered together, the only input to the whole system is “undesirable” waste and the 
outputs are useful products. The output of one unit is an input of one or more other 
units. For example, vegetable waste from the secondary segregation unit goes to the 
cattle shed while cow dung from the cattle shed goes to the composting, 
vermicomposting and drying units. We can see the systematic handling of waste from 
one process to another, increasing its desirability at each stage of processing.   
The incredible part is this - Vellore district (area 6077 sq km, population over 3,026,432) 
is now fully into this ZWM experiment – all thanks to Exnora Green Cross (EGC). They 
have trained Self-Help Groups (SHGs) on waste processing and now these groups are 
powering the ZWM movement.  
Garbage is segregated at source  into recyclable and organic waste. The model 
segregates garbage at source, household, farms, villages, municipalities, educational 
institutions, hospitals  
SHG teams collect the garbage and bring it to the processing facility.  
At the processing facility, recyclable waste is separated, cleaned, and sold for reuse.  
Animal edible organic waste (kitchen garbage like vegetable peels, etc.) is separated 
and fed to cows.  
Non edible organic waste is thrown into a compost pit.  
Cow dung (waste from the organic waste eating cows) goes to the biogas plant to 
produce energy for cooking or lighting.  
The slurry (biogas waste) is used as an agent for breaking down the other organic waste 
sitting in the compost pit.  
The resulting organic fertilizer is sold  in the market giving rise to a whole organic 
farming industry. provides employment to 200 people ,provides an income to SHG by 
way of selling recyclables, organic fertilizers etc. exnora green cross.  
  
3. Pune  Municipal Corporation  – compost pit is  mandatory in every new building 
complex. City wide competitions are organized for plastic waste collection regularly to 
create awareness.  
  
777  
  
777 
 
4. Environmentally conscious individuals  are involved in creating Zero waste situation 
even in Goa. to make it 100% legal framework is essential.  
  
5. Across the border  
About 10 years ago, Indonesia‟s second-largest city, Surabaya, was a grey, dirty city 
with overflowing landfills and litter-defaced streets. In 2004, these woes finally 
compelled city leaders to tackle waste seriously. Through several years of collaborative 
R&D with Japan‟s Kitakyushu City, an enhanced method of composting was developed 
based on the science of fermentation. Accelerated decomposition, a key feature, 
rendered the method feasible for deployment in households and in composting centers 
in congested areas. The microorganisms and the formula for making the seed compost 
were derived from local ingredients, while the practices were adapted to fit local social 
systems.  
  
A citywide campaign led by a highly committed leader in collaboration with the private 
sector, NGOs and other actors, enabled composting to be rapidly scaled up. Compost 
stimulated interest in planting and home gardens, which greened and beautified streets 
and parks. Eventually, landfill waste was reduced by 30% in just five years. The famed 
„Surabaya Model‟ of composting is now being replicated to other ASEAN cities. 
Nevertheless, Surabaya‟s city officers are not resting on their laurels – they are 
continuing their international cooperation efforts in many environmental sectors, and 
have recently begun to experiment with community-scale biogas systems at its 
composting centers.  
Urban sustainability should therefore focus on three E’s, Environment, Economy, 
Energy Reduction of The excessive reliance on the surrounding countryside should be 
the ultimate goal. Environmental protection by reducing pollution resulting from 
dumping and littering, Resource recovery for economic gain and energy generation by 
various means by processing waste should be the ultimate goal for sustainable waste 
management.

4. Socio-economic aspect- people’s contribution towards the sector and implications on people  
The general perception of a good and bad lifestyle as well as the system paradigm is gradually shifting. The laid-
back lifestyle has become a habit for the older generation. Dependency on the government and the market is not 
changing significantly, although intellectual acceptability of eco-initiatives is showing positive response. 
 
To speed up this process, we require a multifaceted program. There is enough awareness, but more action 
programs are needed than informational and academic ones in order to transfer it into action. Government is a 
major player in the whole matter and has the power to create a great change if it acts from home. In the case of 
790  
  
790 
 
the government awareness campaign, people will follow if they discover that government is implementing it in its 
establishments and demonstrates that it is serious about the change. 
People will join the government awareness campaign if they learn that govt. is committed to the change and is 
serious about its implementation at government facilities/ depts.  
1. Govt. offices, canteen, programmes etc. should exercise total ban on single use plastic for tea, snacks more 
stringently and under strict guidance issued from to time.              
(Dept. of Environment and Climate Change/ Goa State Pollution Control Board (GSPCB)). 
2. Waste generated in govt. offices (Solid waste as well as sewerage) and establishments should be managed in 
an ideal manner so that, if found feasible the same could be an example to follow by others either as it is or 
with changes, for others. (GWMC, SIDCGL) 
3. The consumption of electric energy and vehicle fuel in govt. offices can be monitored and reduced, wherever 
possible. That can and should be avoided with a genuine target. 
4. In every office one officer should be given this additional task. An efficient officer with this special task to plan 
and monitor this will pay-back the expenses on this unit and make an impact on society. 
5. P.W.D. and other govt. authorities while issuing tender for construction, the tenderer should be compelled to 
identify site of disposal of debris and excavated earth. 
The same can be enforced by Municipalities and Panchayat while giving license for construction. 
There will be sites where earth filling is required. They need to be identified. Some of the components of 
demolished building can be re-used or re-cycled to be used here. The construction proposal should be 
associated with details of what part of the debris will be re-used /re-cycled. 
6. Institutions of higher learning, business headquarters, and industries all have their own workforce and 
management structures. They ought to be closely linked into the program with clearly specified goals and 
deadlines. 
7. Competitions, prizes and incentives should be awarded to the institutions, lanes, wards etc. for best 
performance. 
8. Assistance and incentives should be declared for clean water body, biodiversity gardens, roof top gardens etc. 
involving NGO’s, social clubs, etc. 
9. Various concepts, experiments and programs successfully implemented in the various parts of the country 
and also globe like Global Eco-Village Network, Gaia of Denmark, Auroville in India should be widely 
propagated. 
791  
  
791
